#2741. Bengals Film Room: Chase Brown starting to heat up?

The Cincinnati Bengals survived an overtime thriller 43-36 on Sunday against the Tennessee Titans. No one expected the game to be that close, but that is life in the NFL. If you start out slow, you are typically in for a dogfight the rest of the day. That is something that the Bengals continue to keep doing.

There has been a lot of chatter about trading for a running back, specifically Jonathan Taylor. While Taylor is a great back, I have not been of the belief that he necessarily elevates this team dramatically. For a guy that would cost premium draft capital to acquire, he would be joining a Bengals team that will always be pass-first.

When you pass the ball a lot, you need a player that is a high-level pass protector and can catch the ball out of the backfield. To me, they already have that guy in Chase Brown.

Brown caught eight passes for 46 yards on Sunday. He had a fantastic touchdown reception, but it was called back due to a holding call on Dylan Fairchild. Brown is a reliable target as a pass catcher, and that is something the Bengals will need to continue leaning on as an extension of the running game this season.

The thing that Brown has improved the most on since his time in the NFL is his pass protection. He has turned himself into one of the best pass protectors in the league this season. He has a 78.2 pass-blocking grade and has consistently flashed by picking up blitzes all season. For a team that loves to throw the ball, it's so critical to have guys like Brown and Perine who take pride in being good blockers for Joe Burrow and the offense.

While it wasn't a massively productive rushing performance for Brown on Sunday, it felt efficient. Brown had 12 carries for 55 rushing yards. That totals out to 4.6 yards per carry in the game. I thought he has looked more elusive, quick to hit the hole, and has been running his best of the season over the last two weeks.

If Chase Brown is the running back #1 for the rest of the season, you have to hope that this is the start of him coming on for the rest of the season. He has been a player who has started a bit slower statistically in the past. Just last season, he did not have a rushing game over 50 yards until Week 7. He still finished the season with over 1,000 rushing yards.

If the Bengals want to compete in the playoffs, they'll need more balance in the running game. Chase Brown starting to heat up would go a long way toward accomplishing that.

#2735. How Brian Schottenheimer is failing the Cowboys

Watching the Dallas Cowboys in 2026 has become a tiring experience. We are not even halfway through the season, and things are already looking bleak. Losing is never fun, but watching them underachieve has become a weekly ordeal that has turned into pure exhaustion.

Every Sunday, it's a new level of disappointment. There's talent on this team, but the leadership and tactical execution have brought about regular failures that are tough to sit through. The most recent collapse against the Arizona Cardinals serves as more evidence that head coach and play-caller Brian Schottenheimer is fundamentally not the guy to help this franchise return to glory.

The issues start with Schottenheimer's bizarre tendencies. He routinely fails to make the basic decisions that would maximize his team's probability of winning. One example is his weird habit of running quarterback sneaks down at his own goal line. Instead of trusting his playmakers or scheming an effective play, he plays scared and chooses to waste a down, putting the offense in a tough spot. Every time he does this, the Cowboys have punted three plays later.

Another example is his treatment of Brandon Aubrey. We all know that Aubrey is one of the league's most lethal kicking weapons, but Schottenheimer finds ways to turn that into a disadvantage for the Cowboys.

Rather than pressing and trying to pick up extra yards to give him a more reasonable field goal attempt, the head coach contentedly runs the ball and settles for a short gain. His confidence in Aubrey treats those situations like an automatic three points instead of working for a shorter attempt. He unnecessarily creates high-stress kicking situations that have resulted in blocks and misses.

The team also cannot stop repeating the same mistakes. They look uncoached at times, committing the same self-inflicted errors week after week. Are we sick of neutral zone infractions yet? Every week. Early and often. It's just the same penalties over and over. It's become an epidemic. Whatever the coaches are doing to discourage this practice is not working. They keep jumping early.

As a play-caller, Schottenheimer is equally frustrating. The team doesn't have much of a rushing attack, as the offense has struggled to deploy the physical ground game they so confidently promote during the summer. It's been ineffective, and there have been moments when he has completely abandoned it, essentially acknowledging defeat.

That admission might be a little easier to accept if the offense possessed a high-powered aerial attack that many believe should accompany having one of the best wide receiving duos in the league. But they don't.

For some reason, the team's most explosive receiving weapons are underutilized. Schottenheimer fails to create mismatches, and the offense becomes very stagnant at times. No pre-snap motion or creative blocking schemes. The Cowboys' offense has turned into a predictable entity that defenses can absolutely shut down at certain points in the game, and those moments are extremely harmful.

Under Schottenheimer, the Cowboys constantly invent new ways to lose football games. Against the Cardinals, it was the inability to run out the clock. Earlier in the year, against the Ravens, it was a goal-line debauchery that couldn't win the game. Both instances put the pressure back on a porous defense to come through, and sadly, they did not.

The Cowboys don't just lose. They actively engineer their own downfall through a blend of situational ineptitude and executive panic.

But if you listen to Schottenheimer's postgame press conferences, he seems completely detached from reality. His media appearances have turned into comedy shows, highlighted by delusion and a lack of awareness. He stands at the table and claims to be a problem solver, yet no problems ever get solved. He throws out tired clichés and empty promises about how things need to get cleaned up, but each week the same chaos ensues.

The Cowboys are a 3-5 football team, and sadly, it's fitting for who they are. Each week, they are favored against these bad teams because, on paper, they should be beating them. They have more talent. But none of that matters when the coaching puts them at such a disadvantage.

Star players become average, and average players become bad. So far, the evidence strongly suggests that Schottenheimer is not a head coach capable of leading an NFL team to victory, and with each new week, this is becoming more and more obvious.

Dončić's interior scoring is justifiably revered and has remained potent to begin 2026-27. In a monumental part of the match, Karl created his own moment. After the ball bounced in a scrum following a shot from Bischof, Karl wedged his body in against the Atlético Madrid backline and found himself with a perfect angle to beat Jan Oblak for a 1-0 lead. That 54th-minute effort was the kind of play that can turn a season around for a youngster. A little confidence can go a long way.

Bischof and Joshua Kimmich just bossed the midfield. What an effort by those two — especially considering the late scratch of Pavlović.

Harry Kane and Michael Olise were good, but they were not at their respective bests — and that is why this end result was so impressive.

In the 74th minute, Konrad Laimer, who had his best game of the season, hammered a shot into the net. There were two other instances in the match where you could have argued that the Austrian should have scored. On this attempt, Laimer received the pass from Kane and just absolutely rifled his attempt past Oblak. It was a thunderous strike that was fitting for a guy who delivers so much energy to the squad.

There will be criticism of Josip Stanišić, but this was not a game where you can care too much about what he gave the squad offensively. This was all about him being a stable part of the backline. This was progress for the Croatia international.

It was not a perfect game by any means, but the midfield was extremely strong, the backline was stout, and the attack just worked its collective behind off. What… an… effort.

Maybe the most impressive thing about this win was that Bayern Munich just never stopped. The Bavarians were truly relentless, and even a very good (and healthy) Atlético Madrid side could not match them.

Overall, you cannot get worked up in a bad way with anything in this game. The Bavarians flat-out worked harder, and were more determined in a situation where there were plenty of reasons to just sit back and play for a draw. We wanted to see heart and fight, and that is exactly what the squad delivered.

#2723. Josh Jacobs needs to display more (or any) contrition

In May 2026, Packers running back Josh Jacobs crossed a line that should never be crossed. And neither he nor his representatives are acting accordingly in what should be an effort to seek redemption.

He pleaded no contest to battery of a woman. He’s fighting in court to keep the video secret. He’s responding to additional allegations through a strident statement from his lawyers attacking the accusers.

The most tone-deaf gesture of all came last Thursday night, when he celebrated a touchdown by pretending to wear, and to be released from, handcuffs.

His implausible explanation, which accused Prime Video of not showing enough of the celebration and attacked the media for interpreting the images with their lyin’ eyes, was contradicted by the full video of the event.

That’s not the way to play this. His no-contest plea is equivalent to saying, “I did it.” He should be contrite. He should be apologetic. He should be seeking redemption.

The Packers continue to stand behind him, primarily because he’s the best running back on the roster and they want to win games. Their reported interest in Colts running back Jonathan Taylor strongly suggests that, if the Packers could get Taylor, the support for Jacobs would immediately evaporate.

Here’s the basic reality. If the Packers were to cut Jacobs, would anyone sign him? The Chiefs took plenty of heat last week for adding kicker Justin Tucker to the practice squad; they may not be inclined to give another second chance to a player whose arrival would compound the negative reaction to Tucker’s arrival.

The reality, in every sport at every level, is obvious. If the player has enough skill and ability, someone will find a way to justify behavior that shouldn’t be tolerated by an industry that relies so heavily on support from the public, both directly through ticket sales and TV ratings and indirectly through taxpayer funding for stadium projects.

Still, Jacobs has done himself no favors by adopting a posture of defiance. He did something no man should ever do. He’s lucky he’s good enough at football to not lose his job over it.

If he was at the bottom of the depth chart in Green Bay, he would have been gone a long time ago.

#2721. When the game is on the line, where has Devin Booker gone?

There was an unfortunate trend that began to manifest itself during the back half of last season. When the going gets tough, your best players need to get going. And unfortunately for the Phoenix Suns, that trend involved Devin Booker's struggles to perform in clutch moments.

From February 1 onward, in 11 clutch games in which Booker played, the Suns went 3-8. During those moments, Booker shot 6-of-20 from the field, recorded five assists against eight turnovers, and posted a -34 plus/minus.

That's concerning, especially when you consider that over his previous 10 seasons, which included some pretty horrible Suns teams, Booker owned a -2 +/- in 316 clutch situations. He shot 40% from the field during those moments and maintained a 1.8 assist-to-turnover ratio.

And it wasn't as if Booker had struggled in the clutch throughout the entirety of last season. Through the first 19 games in which he played, the Suns were 11-8 in clutch situations. Booker shot 51.2% from the field, recorded 10 assists against only three turnovers, and posted a +27 plus/minus. But upon returning from an ankle injury on February 7, the nosedive began.

You can make the argument that it's supposed to be tough, that your best player is naturally going to be the focal point of opposing defenses, and therefore his performance will be hindered by the schemes designed to stop him. During that same timeframe, from February 1 onward, Booker ranked dead last in plus/minus among players who attempted at least 20 shots in clutch situations. Jalen Brunson, Luka Doncic, and Shai Gilgeous-Alexander were at the top of the list, with Brunson posting a +41. And there were plenty of other names ahead of Booker, including Jamal Murray, CJ McCollum, Brandon Ingram, and Desmond Bane.

That only adds to the concern about who Devin Booker is and what he represents at this point in his career, particularly within the context of this Suns team. Because you can make excuses all day long about how he's being double-teamed or triple-teamed, but great players make the necessary adjustments that lead to team success. That's why plus/minus, when evaluated over an extended period, carries considerably more value than looking at the number from a single game. The trend we witnessed last season was concerning.

If double teams are being thrown at Devin Booker, why is he turning the ball over so frequently? Does he not see them coming? You know as well as I do that many of those turnovers come from Booker predictably driving into a crowd of defenders and trying to force the issue rather than relying on the finesse that's been a hallmark of his career.

Why do I bring this up? Because on Monday night against the Golden State Warriors, that familiar trend once again manifested itself. Booker's inability to execute in clutch moments ultimately contributed to another Suns loss. Yes, there are multiple variables involved, including other players who failed to perform when it mattered most. But none of those guys are making $57 million a year.

Booker re-entered the game with the Suns leading 106-104 and 4:48 remaining. A minute later, he connected on a nine-foot jumper, accounting for his only two points in clutch time. From there, things unraveled.

With Phoenix trailing 109-108, Booker missed a wide-open 12-foot jumper. On the following possession, he turned the ball over. After Jalen Green committed a turnover on the next trip down the floor, Booker was called for an offensive foul, his sixth and final foul of the game.

His final clutch stat line? In 3.8 minutes, Booker shot 1-of-2 from the field, grabbed one rebound, committed two turnovers, and posted a -7 plus/minus.

It's not the end of the world, but it does raise concerns that Devin Booker is picking up right where he left off last season, when his ability to impose his will on a game appeared to be a fading trait.

You might look at this as a one-game sample, but I see it as a sample of 11 previous clutch-time games. Perhaps that's still not enough to definitively identify a trend, especially when you consider the body of work Booker has put together over what is now his 12th NBA season. But it's the manner in which these struggles recur, time and again, that has become the focal point of frustration for a fan base desperate for success and watching a team that can ill afford to lose.

Booker's game has become predictable, and his execution in these moments has been subpar. And I know that somewhere, somebody is preparing to show me a collection of all the game winners Booker has made throughout his career. I appreciate every one of those moments and what they've meant to us as Suns fans. In the same breath, hitting a game-winner against Oklahoma City last season doesn't equate to a victory last night against Golden State.

Devin Booker has earned the benefit of the doubt throughout his career, but that doesn't mean he's exempt from scrutiny when the results begin telling a different story. The Suns need their best player to be their best player when possessions matter most. That requires better decisions, cleaner execution, and an ability to recognize what opposing defenses are taking away. Booker's past has established what he's capable of. His present is beginning to raise legitimate questions about his ability to consistently deliver it.

#2719. Vic Fangio: J.J. McCarthy was a "steal" for the Giants

In late September, the Vikings sent quarterback J.J. McCarthy — the tenth overall pick in the 2024 draft — to the Giants for only a fifth-round pick. And the Eagles, who are trying to end a six-game losing streak, have to deal with McCarthy on Sunday.

On Tuesday, Eagles defensive coordinator Vic Fangio addressed the various changes the Giants have made since last season, capped by his take on the Giants landing McCarthy to replace Jaxson Dart, who’s out for the year with a knee injury suffered in Week 2.

“They’ve got a really good offense,” Fangio told reporters. “They’ve got skill at the receiving position. They did a nice job raiding the Ravens, not only for John [Harbaugh], but for [tight end Isaiah] Likely and [fullback Patrick] Ricard. They’ve got a lot of the Ravens type offense that they had when [New York Giants senior offensive assistant] Greg [Roman] was there, and they’ve intermixed Kansas City type passing in there with [offensive coordinator] Matt [Nagy]. They’ve got it going right now. They’ve got good wideouts, good tight ends, two good backs. The quarterback has come in, in a short period of time and really done a nice job, for them to get him for a sixth-round pick is a steal.”

It was a fifth-round pick, not a sixth-round. But it was still a steal.

The Giants were desperate for help at quarterback. The Vikings were, apparently, desperate to unload McCarthy. Desperate enough to take a fifth-round pick, even though the Vikings possibly would have needed him to play at some point this season.

The end result is that the tables have quickly turned, and that the Giants are now the top dogs while the Eagles are currently all alone in one of the weakest divisions in football. And the idea that the Eagles beating the Giants in Philadelphia would be viewed as an upset says it all.

#2718. 'Didn’t have freedom to pick my team': Sachin Tendulkar shares his experience of captaining Indian Test team in 90s

'Didn't have freedom to pick my team': Sachin Tendulkar shares his experience of captaining Indian Test team in 90s originally appeared on Cricket News. Add Cricket News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Sachin Tendulkar says he lacked the freedom to pick his team as India captain.

He led India in 25 Tests and 73 ODIs, winning four and 23, respectively.

Tendulkar also praised Temba Bavuma for ending South Africa's 27-year wait for an ICC title.

Sachin Tendulkar has revealed that he did not have the freedom to pick his own team while captaining India in the 1990s.

The batting great, widely regarded as one of the finest players the game has produced, also said the Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) is a far more professional body today than it was in that era.

The 'Master Blaster' went on to refer to the match-fixing scandal that shook Indian cricket as his captaincy drew to a close, and he described that stretch as a dark phase for the national side. His comments came in reply to a fan's question during an 'Ask Me Anything' session on Reddit.

Asked about his leadership years on Reddit, he began by saying it was an honour to lead the country, but then spoke about how little say he had in squad selection and how much the board has changed since.

"It was a great honour to lead the team as captain. However, I didn't always have the freedom to pick my team entirely on my own. The BCCI today is a far more professional organisation than it was in the 1990s. Indian cricket also went through a particularly dark phase during that period," said Sachin.

When he was asked to name his favourite captains, he picked two men who followed him in the role and who were each central to a long run of success for India, Ganguly and Dhoni.

"As far as my favourite captains go, Sourav Ganguly and MS Dhoni would definitely be at the top of my list!" he said.

MORE: Rohit Sharma sets fitness goals: Fans react as India veteran pulls off a diving effort to run out Daryl Mitchell during 1st ODI

Tendulkar's two spells as captain were short and difficult. In his first stint, he led India in 17 Tests and 54 ODIs, and in his second he led them in eight Tests and 19 ODIs.

Selection committee led by Gundappa Viswanath

The root of Tendulkar's complaint lay in the way Indian squads were chosen at the time. Captains did not hold voting rights in selection committee meetings and sat in only as non-voting attendees, which meant that the man responsible for results had no formal say in the team he was handed.

Squads were also shaped largely by zonal selectors, who worked with regional quotas, and that often led to decisions where the captain's tactical preferences and his choice of backups were overruled.

MORE: 'It's too early': Sachin cautions against giving Sooryavanshi key role

One of the most painful moments of the first spell came in March 1997. India were bowled out for 81 while chasing only 120 against the West Indies at Kensington Oval in Bridgetown, Barbados, and Tendulkar has often pointed to the match as one that left him deeply frustrated about the make-up and resolve of the team.

The first stint ended abruptly, with Azharuddin returning as captain and leading the side until the 1999 World Cup. After India's disappointing showing at that tournament, Tendulkar was handed the job again, but he stepped down a year later.

Tendulkar gave up the role voluntarily after India lost 3-0 in Australia in 1999-00 and then 2-0 at home to South Africa in a Test series in February and March 2000. He refused to carry on even though the board tried to persuade him to stay.

Ganguly succeeded him, and the appointment marked the start of a golden era for Indian cricket. It also signalled a shift towards giving captains greater authority over the selection of their squads.

MORE: 'Nee po mone Dinesha': Sachin drops Mohanlal's iconic dialogue for Sanju Samson

Tendulkar also used the Reddit session to praise Bavuma, who led South Africa to their first ICC title in 27 years by beating Australia in the 2023-2025 World Test Championship final at Lord's. The former India captain said he admired the South African leader's spirit and spoke about what the achievement meant for the sport.

"I truly admire Temba Bavuma's spirit. He has led from the front and delivered some remarkable results for South African cricket. South Africa winning an ICC title is great for world cricket!"

South Africa followed that triumph by beating Australia 2-1 at home, which showed that the title was no one-off and underlined their strength in Test cricket. Bavuma led from the front in that series with a career-best 179 in the second Test at Gqeberha, and he credited Tendulkar's technique for influencing his compact movement at the crease.

Tendulkar's remarks are a reminder that India's selection system in the 1990s asked a captain to deliver results without giving him the tools to build the side.

A leader who sat in the room as a non-voting attendee, while zonal selectors pushed names according to regional quotas, was always going to struggle to shape a balanced eleven, and the Bridgetown collapse of 1997 showed what could follow when composition and temperament did not fit the task.

The deeper problem was accountability. Selectors chose the squad, yet the captain answered for every defeat, and his record of four Test wins in 25 matches was judged without much thought for the fact that he rarely had his preferred backups. A system in which responsibility and authority sit with different people tends to produce muddled outcomes, and that is what Indian cricket often got in that decade.

Regional quotas also meant that the best available player was not always the one who played. Merit became one factor among several, and the captain was left to make the best of whatever he was given. That is a hard standard to meet in any era, and the later move to give captains a real say over squads is the clearest sign the old way was flawed.

The Toronto Raptors completed a double-digit comeback to defeat the Los Angeles Clippers 125-118 at the Intuit Dome.

Toronto, which did not take its first lead until the final two minutes, came through with a clutch fourth-quarter rally to secure the win.

The Raptors found themselves in a similar position against the Lakers the previous night, but their comeback attempt fell short. This time, however, Toronto learned from that experience and finished the job with a hard-fought victory.

The Raptors continued to experiment with their options at centre, giving Trayce Jackson-Davis an opportunity last night before turning to Collin Murray-Boyles tonight, as Jakob Poeltl did not play.

Both teams traded possessions early, with neither side looking particularly sharp offensively. Trading baskets remained the theme for much of the opening quarter, as both teams struggled to find a consistent rhythm.

However, the Clippers began to create some separation behind their three-point shooting. Kobe Sanders led the charge late in the frame, scoring 11 points on 4-of-6 shooting, including 3-of-4 from beyond the arc as the Raptors had no answer for him.

Los Angeles closed the quarter on a 17-5 run, extending its lead to as many as 13 points before heading into the second quarter with an 11-point advantage.

Toronto looked sloppy down the stretch and simply didn't do enough to start the game.

The Raptors showed some signs of life to start the second quarter, with Immanuel Quickley getting Toronto on the board before Scottie Barnes added his first basket of the night. Barnes, who entered the game questionable, had been relatively quiet through the opening stretch.

RJ Barrett also provided a spark offensively, knocking down a three-pointer before scoring on a post-up jumper against former teammate Gradey Dick to bring his total to 16 points.

Toronto's three-point shooting and defensive effort improved, but the Clippers continued to respond whenever the Raptors threatened to build momentum.

Brook Lopez continued to give Toronto problems, taking advantage of the Raptors' smaller lineup on both ends of the floor.

Turnovers also became a major issue for Toronto, with seven giveaways leading to nine Clippers points. Dick continued to put together a strong performance as Los Angeles extended its lead to as many as 15 points.

Toronto also had to manage much of the quarter without Barrett, who picked up his third personal foul. The Raptors had plenty of work to do after heading into halftime trailing 63-52.

Toronto came out of the halftime break with much better energy, as Barnes, Walter and Murray-Boyles helped spark a 6-0 run to cut the Clippers' lead to five. Dick and Sanders continued to build on their impressive nights, with Dick making an impact across the floor and Sanders knocking down a three-pointer to cap an 11-3 Clippers run.

Toronto continued to struggle offensively, with Barrett providing a strong performance but receiving very little help from the rest of the lineup.

Jamison Battle provided a much-needed spark off the bench, knocking down back-to-back three-pointers to bring his total to 12 points. Battle was particularly effective from beyond the arc, shooting 4-of-5 from three-point range.

Although Toronto showed some improvement towards the end of the quarter, the Clippers maintained control and carried a 13-point lead into the fourth. The Raptors needed a strong final quarter, similar to last night if they wanted to make a comeback.

Toronto opened the fourth quarter with back-to-back baskets from Alijah Martin and Scottie Barnes, who quietly recorded a double-double. Barnes and RJ Barrett began to find a rhythm together offensively, helping Toronto chip away at the deficit, while Immanuel Quickley added a pull-up three-pointer to cut the lead to eight.

However, foul trouble continued to be an issue for the Raptors, with Ja'Kobe Walter picking up his fifth personal foul and Barrett his fourth, allowing the Clippers to extend their advantage back to 12.

Barnes followed with a difficult turnaround fadeaway to give Toronto its first lead of the night. Some clutch free throws from Barnes, Murray-Boyles and Quickley, combined with vintage defensive intensity down the stretch, helped the Raptors complete the fourth-quarter comeback and escape Los Angeles with a hard-fought victory.

Although it was far from a perfect performance, the Raptors showed resilience and refused to give up, earning a crucial victory.

Barnes, Quickley and Barrett led the way for Toronto with strong performances. However, there is still room for improvement, particularly with their three-point shooting, free-throw efficiency and ability to get off to a stronger start.

#2716. 2026 season could highlight the unfairness of the eight-division structure

From time to time, the NFL’s current structure has created unfair results, with the best of four bad teams assigned to a predetermined division earning a playoff berth and the home game that goes along with it.

This year, the NFC has two very strong divisions, one so-so division, and one very weak division.

Here’s the basic reality. With the four NFC division winners getting tickets to the playoff party, the wild-card berths will go to three teams. And, currently, there are three teams in the NFC North and two in the NFC West that are potentially better than whoever will win the NFC East and the NFC South.

Between the Vikings, Bears, Lions, Packers, 49ers, Seahawks, and Rams, two will be crowned division winners. That leaves five for the wild-card berths.

Ultimately, two of them will be frozen out of the playoffs — even if both of those teams end up with better records than the best teams of the NFC East and NFC South.

During last Friday’s episode of PFT Live, I threw out an alternative approach that would be far more fair to all teams.

Instead of two conferences with a quartet of four-team divisions, why not pivot to four eight-team divisions?

NFL East, NFL North, NFL South, NFL West. The easiest configuration would consist of slapping the current East, North, South, and West divisions into one conference each. While some tweaks could be needed to better align things geographically, it would be far more fair to guarantee a playoff spot (and a home game) to the best of eight teams, not the best of four teams.

Decisions would have to be made about scheduling. The home-and-home series (a vestige of the days when there were far fewer teams) would need to be retired. Each team would play the seven other teams in its conference, with 10 (or 11, inevitably) other games.

The playoffs would consist of the four conference champions (with the best two getting byes) and 10 wild-card teams. And there would be an added benefit — it would be possble to have the best two teams meet in the Super Bowl, without regard to the traditional AFL-NFL/AFC-NFC separation.

It would be one league. One playoff tree. Any combination of teams would, in theory, be possible for the Super Bowl. When the dust settles on the semifinal round, the best two teams would remain.

That said, it won’t be easy to get the owners to give up the current format, which entails in any given year a one-in-four shot at hosting a playoff game. But if the goal is to constantly strive for ways to create more compelling matchups, an eight-team, four-conference approach makes a lot more sense than the current structure.

Football is a meritocracy. A configuration of four, eight-team conferences would be far more conducive to that ideal.

Will it happen? Probably not. Should it be taken seriously by the league? Absolutely.

Maybe this year, when the NFC East and NFC South provide none-of-the-above champions and two very viable teams are sent home after Week 18, will spark a real conversation about meaningful change.

#2709. The Day After the Day After: The Houston Texans resume their season after the bye

The Day After the Day After…when the raw, immediate emotions from the aftermath of a game diminish into the realm of clarity and the proverbial (or literal) hangover no longer haunts the mind. With that, a review of Houston's Bye Week:

Where does Houston stand vis-a-vis the league after the bye? While Houston took the week off, the chaos didn't stop. That will likely continue when Houston gets back to their schedule. When they kick-off next Sunday in LA, they will be no better than 2.5 games back of the Jaguars, possibly down 3.5 games. They still have three division games (all at home) left. As for a Wild Card, sitting 11th in the conference does not help their situation. They sit 2.5 games back of New England for the final spot, with Cleveland, Las Vegas and Baltimore still ahead of them. They have three remaining non-conference games, but all of those are on the road and in December/January. While they are a maddening 0-4 at home, they somehow have a winning road record at 2-1. Given that the remainder of the schedule is 6 road games/4 home games, that may not be the worst thing in the world. On the opposite end of the spectrum, Houston holds the 8th pick in the 2027 draft. Just based on numbers, Houston could remain in the draft top 10 if their struggles continue. If the franchise gets solid play from Stroud in spite of bad team play and decides to give him that second contract, it could make Houston game for some wheeling and dealing related to that draft pick.

The criticality of November: At 2-5, Houston finds themselves well back of the conference leaders. Still, there are 10 full games left. To be in legitimate position for a playoff berth, Houston will likely need at least double-digit wins. To get to the usual 10-7 record, Houston has to go 8-2. In particular, this squad can't go any worse than 3-1 in November. Arguably, that will need to be 4-0. On one hand, this past week offered Houston one of the best schedule hands it could have been dealt. The LA Chargers are a league worse 0-7 and are as hard broke as any team in the league. The Cleveland Browns have the best record of the November slate at 5-3, but Watson's play is falling off and they could possibly overlook the Texans, who will have a losing record when they go to Cleveland in two weeks. The Colts come to Houston, but they have been in fire-sale mode and might just be without long-time Texans' nemesis Jonathan Taylor when they play late in the month. The calendar ends with a visit from the usually nightmarish Baltimore Ravens, but after this weekend, when they lost their QB1 and QB2 for significant time, they might be in a weakened state.

On the other hand, all of that relies on Houston playing to its potential and not surrendering the explosive plays like they have. How often have golden paths been paved with fool's gold for this franchise? November takes on added significant due to those games being conference matchups, and upping that conference record is going to be critical for overcoming the slow start for the team if the playoffs are to happen.

Will the result on LA change anything for the Texans' roster? A win means the team can still hold out hope for a run. A loss? It doesn't mathematically eliminate the Texans, but for all intents and purposes, the team will be out of the running. That matchup will end under 48 hours from the trade deadline. Houston added Harrison and they likely aren't done talking with other teams. However, if Houston loses, do they start off-loading players to try to recoup for the offseason? Houston hasn't said as much, but especially if the squad can't overcome the worst team in the league, that would force some tough discussions on the flight back. As it stands, Houston doesn't have a lot of easily tradeable players. Sure, a player like Danielle Hunter would be on a lot of wish-lists, but how many teams could accommodate this contract and salary cap number? Maybe Xavier Hutchinson is traded not for an improvement, but for some draft capital for next season.

How much improvement can a bye really offer? In theory, a bye offers a chance to fix some issues. Yet teams only have a week. It is not like teams can engage in a full-up training camp and fix all the issues. Maybe they can throw in some new plays or adjust some facets of their strategy. Coaches can be fired and new personnel put it, but that doesn't always spark the desired change. The desperation firings of Chris Palmer as OC in 2005 did nothing to help that hapless offense and the sacking of Bill O'Brien in 2020 did not salvage that season.

Could Houston get flexed out of their prime-time slots? The schedule-makers back-loaded the Texans' primetime appearances, with a Week 11 Thursday Night game against the Colts, a Week 13 Sunday Night matchup against Pittsburgh, a Week 16 Christmas Eve duel against the Eagles and an Week 17 Monday Night game against the Packers. The Colts game is ineligible for flexing. The Christmas Eve game is also locked in, for better or worse. However, the Sunday Night Matchup at Pittsburgh and the Monday Night Game against Green Bay can get flexed. The league would need to give 12 days' notice and there would be a lot of horse-trading going between the networks. Much depends on Houston remaining in the playoff mix. Pittsburgh and Green Bay rest in playoff position and have rather strong fanbases that help ratings. However, if Houston is playing out the string by Thanksgiving, look for one or both of those games to get moved. The Texans did have one scheduled Sunday Night Game in 2013 flexed to an early afternoon kickoff (their home game against the New England Patriots).

1-2: Houston's record post-bye under Ryans. 2023 saw Houston exit a bye week only to lose an ugly matchup with a bad Panthers' team on the road. 2024 saw the team return from a late bye to beat the Dolphins to clinch the division at home after a Colts' loss later that day. Last season, Houston came off an earlier bye only to lose a tough Monday Night matchup at the eventual Super Bowl Champion's home in Seattle.

.703: Houston's post-bye winning percentage in the regular season during the Ryans' regime: Remember the whole 8-2 target? Well, it might not completely be out of the norm for a Ryans' squad. In 2023, the team exited it bye with that bad loss to Carolina but still finished the year 7-4. The late bye skews some of this, as Houston had a Week 14 bye before a 3-game stretch in 11 days, finished the year 2-2. Last season's 9-game win streak did most of the lifting for a 10-2 finish.

Given that there were no games or major news of note good or bad for players, we'll forgo awarding of game balls or declarations of idiocy. Those will resume next week.

The second part of the season starts in LA against the 0-7 Chargers. Kickoff is slated for 3:05 CST with coverage on CBS/Paramount+ (unless the game were [deservedly] flexed to local public access at 5:30 a.m. Sunday morning). See y'all there.

#2707. Josh Jacobs needs to display more (or any) contrition

In May 2026, Packers running back Josh Jacobs crossed a line that should never be crossed. And neither he nor his representatives are acting accordingly in what should be an effort to seek redemption.

He pleaded no contest to battery of a woman. He's fighting in court to keep the video secret. He's responding to additional allegations through a strident statement from his lawyers attacking the accusers.

The most tone-deaf gesture of all came last Thursday night, when he celebrated a touchdown by pretending to wear, and to be released from, handcuffs.

His implausible explanation, which accused Prime Video of not showing enough of the celebration and attacked the media for interpreting the images with their lyin' eyes, was contradicted by the full video of the event.

That's not the way to play this. His no-contest plea is equivalent to saying, "I did it." He should be contrite. He should be apologetic. He should be seeking redemption.

The Packers continue to stand behind him, primarily because he's the best running back on the roster and they want to win games. Their reported interest in Colts running back Jonathan Taylor strongly suggests that, if the Packers could get Taylor, the support for Jacobs would immediately evaporate.

Here's the basic reality. If the Packers were to cut Jacobs, would anyone sign him? The Chiefs took plenty of heat last week for adding kicker Justin Tucker to the practice squad; they may not be inclined to give another second chance to a player whose arrival would compound the negative reaction to Tucker's arrival.

The reality, in every sport at every level, is obvious. If the player has enough skill and ability, someone will find a way to justify behavior that shouldn't be tolerated by an industry that relies so heavily on support from the public, both directly through ticket sales and TV ratings and indirectly through taxpayer funding for stadium projects.

Still, Jacobs has done himself no favors by adopting a posture of defiance. He did something no man should ever do. He's lucky he's good enough at football to not lose his job over it.

If he was at the bottom of the depth chart in Green Bay, he would have been gone a long time ago.

Here are three giant obstacles the Mavs will have to climb in order to get a win against last year's NBA Finalists from the Western Conference.

We're just 10 days removed, as of this writing, from the season's first matchup between the Spurs and the Mavericks, San Antonio suffocated Dallas, which was without second-year superstar Cooper Flagg do to a shoulder injury, 122-106, in that one.

Without Flagg, who was nursing a shoulder injury, and with Kyrie Irving sitting out suffering from "injury management" on the second night of the first back-to-back set of the season, the young Spaniard Sergio de Larrea took the reins for the Mavericks and turned heads for 21 points on 9-of-15 shooting (3-of-4 from 3-point range) in just his third-ever NBA game. The undermanned Dallas bunch kept it close for three quarters before San Antonio put the Mavs away late behind a balanced effort that saw Wembanyama score a game-high 23 points and Dylan Harper add 22 more.

The Mavs will show the Spurs a completely different look this time around, with Flagg and Irving fully operational for the marquee matchup. Irving was taken off the injury report after sitting out his second game of the year against the Kings. The pair combined for 68 points in the last game they appeared in together, last week's surprise 116-111 win over the Houston Rockets.

There's nothing figurative about the next tall hurdle the Mavs will have to get over (or through) if they want to get an ever-elusive win in San Antonio. They'll have to contain Wembanyama.

His 23 points, seven rebounds and four blocked shots in the teams' first meeting is a pretty good reference point. In that one, it wasn't really Wemby who overwhelmed the Mavs as much as it was the trio of swingmen in De'Aaron Fox, Stephon Castle and Dylan Harper, who got anything they wanted against Dallas "swinging door" defense.

Daniel Gafford will no doubt be instrumental in Dallas' effort to rein Wembanyama in on Wednesday. He's strung together two really good games, is averaging 1.9 blocked shots of his own so far this season and has pulled down seven or more rebounds in five of the team's first seven outings — the last five, actually. He's been much more effective and efficient than he was last season, when he was hampered by nagging injuries throughout the year. He's been an important cog while the Mavs wait on the rest of the tall tall trees, in Dereck Lively II and Santi Aldama, to get healthy.

Aldama is close, inching ever closer to making his Mavericks debut, as his progress on the injury report suggests. He has been upgraded to questionable for Wednesday's game as of Tuesday night. But for now, the tall task of limiting Wembanyama falls primarily on the shoulders of Gafford, who stands at least six inches shorter than the Frenchman.

Let's see how many bodies the Mavericks throw in Wemby's direction on Wednesday.

After yet another "injury management" related absence in what ended up devolving into an embarrassing loss to Sad Sack Sacramento, Kyrie Irving is not listed on the Mavericks' injury report going into the matchup against the Spurs. He needs to be the catalyst on offense at San Antonio — not to make up for the loss his absence could have prevented, no. But because when he's the catalyst on offense, the Mavs have a chance to take down even the league's better constructed teams.

Friday's win over the Rockets is just the latest evidence. The Mavericks don't have another player on the roster who can do the things that Irving can do — namely, dribble the basketball. He'll be the best-rested guest in the West, so there are no excuses, either.

In order for the Mavs to have a big night, it starts with a big night from the point guard position. Look for Irving ot log at least as many minutes (35) as he did against Houston and for the Mavericks to make this one a nail-biter down the stretch because of his disruption.

The Mavericks and the Spurs will tip off on Wednesday at 8:30 p.m. The game will be televised on ESPN, which means tip-off probably won't be until about 8:50 in reality. You can catch the stream on MavsTV, and the radio broadcast will be on KRLD 105.3 The Fan.

The Chicago Bears have won three straight games in the most impressive fashion imaginable. Caleb Williams is the 1st quarterback in Bears history to lead his team to 30+ points in three consecutive games with no turnovers. The Bears also never trailed in any of these three games, and that 3-game streak of scoring 30 points while never trailing is tied for the second-longest streak in franchise history. They went four in a row three times, all in the 1940s (1941, 1942, and 1948). Those teams were led by Hall of Fame quarterback Sid Luckman, who is the only quarterback to win a league MVP for the Bears.

There was some buzz around Williams as an MVP candidate before the season, and that was amplified following the Bears' 59-point explosion in Week 1, but the hamstring injury seemed to derail that because it kept him out of the next three games.

In his weekly NFL MVP Tracker at NFL.com, Kevin Patra wrote about the historical unlikelihood of Williams winning it.

In the post NFL-AFL merger era (since 1970) in non-strike-shortened seasons, only one player has missed three games and still won the NFL MVP award: Joe Montana in 1989. Cool Joe battled through various injuries that season, missing Weeks 6, 8, and 15, and portions of others.

While a long shot, the Bears did just beat last year's Super Bowl participants in back-to-back weeks on primetime. They also have three more stand-alone games on the schedule, including a third straight primetime affair this Sunday.

Patra also explained why Montana's performance in 1989 won it that year and how Caleb could have a similar path.

Despite missing three games, Montana was the best QB on the best team in the NFL, winning the MVP vote in a landslide (62 of 70 votes). The 49ers QB overcame the lack of counting stats by leading the NFL in all the efficiency categories: 70.2 percent completion rate, a 6.7 TD% rate, 53.7% success rate, 9.1 yards per attempt average, 270.8 yards per game, and set the then-record with a 112.4 passer rating — when 100 passer ratings were uncommon.

That's Williams' path to the MVP: Be the most efficient passer on the best team.

Caleb may not hit gaudy passing yard or touchdown numbers, but if all his other numbers are among the best in the NFL, while the Bears keep winning games, how could he not be a finalist?

#2703. Avalanche sign star Cale Makar to largest contract in NHL history at $163.2 million

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

This has been the summer of spending in the NHL, and the Colorado Avalanche just broke the bank for star defenseman Cale Makar. On Friday, the team announced that Makar signed an eight-year extension worth $163.2 million.

The contract is the richest in league history -- both in total value and annual value at $20.4 million per year. Makar is the first player in NHL history to cross the $20 million salary threshold.

At 27-years old, Makar is arguably the best defensemen in the NHL, and he will remain in that conversation for quite a while. Makar has already won the Norris Trophy twice, and he was a key factor in Colorado's Stanley Cup run, which ended with him winning the Conn Smythe Trophy.

This past season, Makar posted monster numbers from the blue line yet again as he tallied 20 goals and 59 assists in 75 games. Since entering the NHL in 2019, Makar leads all defensemen in goals (20) and points (507).

"I am so excited and humbled to continue to wear the Avalanche sweater and represent this incredible organization and community," Makar said in a statement. "I would like to thank the Kroenke family, Joe Sakic and the entire Avalanche organization for their commitment, trust and belief in me. I would also like to thank my wife and family for their constant support, as well as Scott, Brian and Steve Bartlett for their guidance and assistance.

"To the Avalanche fans, thank you for your continued support and for welcoming us to Colorado years ago. Colorado has truly become a second home to us, and we are so grateful to be here. I look forward to getting back on the ice with my teammates and continuing to work toward our goal of bringing the Stanley Cup back to the Mile High City."

Over the last three seasons, Makar's impact has been immense in all three zones. He's posted a five-on-five expected goals share of 54.5%, per Natural Stat Trick. With Makar on the ice in those situations, Colorado has outscored its opponents 220-157. In two of the last three seasons, Makar has hit the 90-point mark, and he has 100-point potential at his best.

Makar's $11.4 million raise kicks in in at the start of the 2026-27 season, and it will make things significantly tighter for the Avalanche as they navigate the salary cap. The bright side for Colorado -- and the key in getting this deal done -- is that the team now has each of its core players signed through at least 2031.

There may be some sticker shock upon seeing the $20.4 million average annual value, but that's the new reality in the NHL as the cap rises exponentially. The previous record for highest salary in NHL history was just set earlier this offseason when the Anaheim Ducks signed center Leo Carlsson to a contract worth $18 million per year, and the Chicago Blackhawks announced a $75 million extension for Connor Bedard.

The next domino to fall will be an extension for Minnesota Wild defenseman Quinn Hughes, who is neck-and-neck with Makar as the best defensemen in the world. Waiting until after the Makar deal was announced to sign Hughes could prove to be a mistake for Wild general manager Bill Guerin.

#2700. 2026 NHL free agent tracker: Patrick Kane returns to Blackhawks on two-year contract

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

NHL free agency has slowed down in late July, but some notable names are still coming off the board. Most notably, Patrick Kane is returning to the Chicago Blackhawks on a two-year contract worth $16 million, the team announced on Thursday.

Already a Chicago legend and future Hall of Famer, Kane won three Stanley Cups and a slew of individual awards with the franchise that selected him with the No. 1 overall pick in 2007. Kane's first stint with the Blackhawks lasted 16 seasons, and he piled up 446 goals and 779 assists in 1,161 games. Kane ranks inside the top five of just about every statistical category in franchise history, and he will get the chance to keep climbing those lists over the next two years.

The Blackhawks sent Kane to the New York Rangers at the 2023 NHL trade deadline, and he played just 19 regular season games there before hitting free agency the next summer. Hip surgery delayed Kane's decision until November of that year, but he ultimately landed with the Detroit Red Wings, where he's spent the last three seasons.

Last season was Kane's best with Detroit, and it proved that he still had some gas left in the tank, at least offensively. Kane posted 16 goals and 41 assists in 67 games -- with 19 of those points coming on the power play.

In his second stint with the Blackhawks, Kane will add another level of playmaking to the power play, and he should strengthen a top six forward group that's bereft of proven talent. Kane will also be an excellent mentor and sounding board for fellow No. 1 overall pick, Connor Bedard, who is set to miss the first month of the season after undergoing shoulder surgery.

Kane isn't the player he once was, but he'll give Chicago a bit more pop at the top of the lineup, and his first game back in a Blackhawks jersey will be a huge night for the city.

#2699. Doom and Gloom: Overreactions to Utah’s slow start to the 2026-27 season

This has not gone as well as we had hoped. Seven games into the season, and all that the "winning time" Utah Jazz are bringing to show and tell is a solitary one-point win against a subpar New Orleans team and a head bowed in shame. It was a depressing show-and-tell presentation for this premature Jazz team.

But growing pains are part of the deal. Winning in the NBA isn't as simple as a change in mindset; it's a change in identity. A fundamental shift in the direction of a franchise will take time to set, especially one as drastic as going from hunting the number-one overall lottery odds to walking the thorn-riddled path toward the Western Conference playoffs.

Just as Michael Scott learned that it takes much more than shouting in the office to declare bankruptcy, Utah is learning firsthand that flipping the "winning" switch is much harder than simply making a declaration. The Jazz wanted and expected to win many more basketball games this season; they clearly still have some growing up to do before they can reach that switch.

Still, it wasn't ridiculous to expect more from this team by now. They traded for Jaren Jackson Jr., one of the best front-court defenders in basketball and a multiple-time All-Star, to pair alongside Utah's in-house All-Star, Lauri Markkanen. They drafted Darryn Peterson, a player touted as one of the best guard prospects in recent memory and a future star. They re-signed Keyonte George, rewarding him for his steady growth and remarkable leadership.

But 1-6 is 1-6, and the Utah Jazz are way off course at this larval moment in the 2026-27 season. Not all is lost, but much needs evaluation and careful reconsideration. So let's play a game that I like to call "Doom and Gloom". The rules are simple: I'll share an opinion that I've thought myself or heard from others about Utah's unsettling beginning and determine whether said opinion is "Doom", a bad omen and an imminent issue, or "Gloom", an overreaction that, while based in reality, doesn't tell the whole story.

SAN ANTONIO, TX – NOVEMBER 2: Ace Bailey #19 of the Utah Jazz drives to the basket during the game against the San Antonio Spurs on November 2, 2026 at Frost Bank Center in San Antonio, Texas. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this Photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Adam Hagy/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images

No, the Utah Jazz are not winning basketball games. Yes, that is a massive problem, and a legitimate cause for concern for a team whose goal is to win basketball games.

But this problem, as with all others, deserves some context before it stirs up panic.

The biggest factor, I believe, is the Jazz's strength of competition. According to ESPN's RPI, the Jazz are tied at number-one for the hardest schedule in the entire NBA. They've faced the reigning Western Conference champions, San Antonio, twice while the Spurs were at full strength. Who could have foreseen the Memphis Grizzlies, who Utah faced twice, starting the season at 6-1? In fact, all the teams that beat the Jazz at this point of the season are a collective 22-6.

Despite the majority of this Jazz core having played together for years, this is a team still discovering itself. Give them time.

Injury luck has not flipped in Utah's favor early — five big men have been injured at some point in the season — but to blame their shortcomings on injuries is disingenuous.

Jusuf Nurkic hasn't been available since the first game of the preseason, Jaxon Hayes went down with an injury against Los Angeles, and then Markkanen and JJJ went down in the same half against Memphis. Markkanen and Hayes returned quickly, but shortly thereafter Mo Bamba — who has been unironically excellent — rolled his ankle in San Antonio.

That's bad luck, and Utah will obviously underperform without their best players on the court. But playoff-caliber teams regroup and find ways to win while shorthanded. If the Jazz can't win while JJJ recovers from his MCL injury, their playoff chances were slim from the start.

Alright, it's time for some therapeutic pessimism. On the topic of Utah's young players, I have to be painfully honest: Utah's tanking-fueled draft yield has been tragic.

Let's look at the Jazz's body of work in terms of draft picks. Of their four lottery picks, only two are still on Utah's roster. First to leave was Taylor Hendricks, who spends his days at the end of Memphis' bench and doesn't appear likely to sign an extension at the end of the season. It's a similar story for Cody Williams, who, despite generating plenty of preseason static in Minnesota, has appeared in five games and scored zero points.

Utah traded up to pick Florida star Walter Clayton Jr. last year, and he's already on his third NBA team.

As for the draftees still on Utah's roster, Isaiah Collier's team option was just declined, and Kyle Filipowski hardly sees the court even as injuries pile up in Will Hardy's frontcourt rotation.

Sensabaugh's minutes have been uneven, but he's filled his role well and had the trust of his head coach to replace Darryn Peterson in the lineup when their first clash with San Antonio entered overtime. Still, his status with the team is uncertain as he approaches the final year of his contract.

That list doesn't inspire much optimism, but it isn't all bad in terms of the youth of Utah.

Keyonte George has been excellent this year, with the exception of a stinker against San Antonio. Ace Bailey is a revelation, making winning plays with and without the basketball, playing stellar defense, and becoming an offensive rebound magnet. And Darryn Peterson, despite looking uneven out of the gate (more on this later), has still shown flashes of what makes him such an enticing prospect.

Semi-Doom is a bit of a cop-out, I'll admit. But there's still reason to believe in Utah's young core, even if the majority of their swings have inarguably whiffed.

Even worse than seeing Utah lose five consecutive games is seeing how the team has responded to adversity.

Without a rallying cry or an increased sense of urgency, this team is full of players with no experience winning at an NBA level. They haven't been able to hit that next gear, and the team mopes on the court, on the sideline, and in timeouts.

This is all about perception, so I might be out of line, but winners turn losing streaks into winning streaks. Utah is giving its fanbase little reason to expect a turnaround because they don't appear to expect one themselves.

Being a guard in the NBA is incredibly difficult, and development isn't linear.

What we're seeing in Peterson isn't a lack of basketball talent, ability, or confidence. In fact, he's displayed all three of those qualities in droves in his young career. Instead, we're observing the metamorphosis of a college star into an NBA-level player. Darryn Peterson joins a Utah Jazz team where he is the fourth offensive option behind Markkanen, George, and Jackson Jr. Finding his place in the rotation and getting accustomed to his new circumstances was bound to bring growing pains.

The biggest concern has been his lack of athletic burst and top-end speed, keeping him away from the basket. Instead, he's sustained himself on a diet of floaters and mid-range jumpers, while getting comfortable with a quick-trigger three-point shot.

For every poetic dribble combo leading into a buttery-smooth jumper, Peterson is due for a forced off-balance fling. He's playing in the big leagues, which means the competition is bigger, stronger, and faster than he's ever faced.

And I'm still highly encouraged by what he's displayed to this point. The jumper looks slick, comfortable, and will find its target with greater consistency over time. Keyonte was a sub-40% shooter from the field as a rookie; he shot 45.6% in his third year.

Alright, I'll wave the red flag for this one. Utah's offense has been abhorrent this season, and we can't blame tanking on their ratings anymore.

Currently possessing the 29th-ranked offense in the entire NBA, the Jazz have scored under 100 points in their last two games. Lauri Markkanen played in both of those games and has performed well beneath his standard. At just 16.5 points per game, the player who has been Utah's offensive pillar and averaged over 26 points per game a season ago is shooting below 40% from the field.

Against San Antonio on Monday, Markkanen and Peterson were the only Jazz players to score in double digits.

The absence of Jusuf Nurkic has been devastating to Will Hardy's offensive game plan. Heavily reliant on ball screens and passing from the center position, Jaxon Hayes simply isn't the playmaker this system requires to succeed. Nor are Mo Bamba or Tony Bradley.

Having to adjust on the fly, the Jazz offense has been clunky, ineffective, and overly dependent on self-creation to pose any real threat. Either one player's injury has truly been that catastrophic to Utah's offensive integrity, or Will Hardy is struggling to conjure up an alternative play style. Either way, none of this is good.

Calvin Barrett is the Associate Editor for SLC Dunk and a Utah Jazz columnist for the Standard-Examiner. Originally from Springville, Utah, he currently writes from his desk in Japan.

#2698. How Conrad Thompson Used Wrestling Nostalgia To Build a Podcasting Empire

It's often said that nostalgia is a powerful feeling, one that can drown out the present as we search for what we once considered better times. Throughout its history, sports has consistently leaned into nostalgia, revisiting historic games, legendary players and defining moments that evoke powerful emotions. Those memories remind us of how different things once felt compared with today. In the podcast ecosystem, few creators lean into nostalgia more than Conrad Thompson, who hosts five professional wrestling podcasts featuring some of the industry's most recognizable personalities.

"A lot of people may mis-categorize what I do and say, 'He talks wrestling.' That's technically true, but our content is essentially nostalgia. Because we're all chasing things the way they used to be," Thompson explained.

Thompson describes his entry into podcasting as a happy accident. A longtime wrestling fan who grew up marveling at the industry's legends, he never envisioned himself becoming a public-facing personality. Instead, he pursued a career as a mortgage banker, helping people achieve their American dream of homeownership.

However, a chance encounter with legendary wrestling icon and close friend Ric Flair changed everything. After Flair received an offer to host a podcast with CBS, the "Nature Boy" needed help with the first episode. A few days before recording, Flair asked Thompson to join him and conduct an interview from a fan's perspective.

"I had some guest hosting experience on local radio, so he [Flair] knew I could do radio because he had seen me do some of these radio hits. But I had never hosted a podcast, and honestly, I wasn't even a big podcast listener," Thompson explained. "But I wanted to do a good job for Ric Flair's first podcast. So, I put together a lot of notes and was prepared, but Ric didn't tell CBS I was coming to do this. But afterward, they asked if I could come back next week."

That first episode of Wooooo Nation launched an opportunity that would benefit both Thompson's mortgage business and his growing presence in on-demand content. Through his podcast with Flair, Thompson began networking with other wrestling legends about replicating that success while expanding his mortgage business's licensing into all 50 states.

Podcasting gave Thompson a way to turn the six figures he had spent on local radio advertising in Alabama into a revenue-generating marketing operation that attracted leads from across the country.

"I never planned to be on camera or on air, but it was out of necessity. I had seen it work. Instead of selling mortgages one to one, I was selling one to many," Thompson said. "I understood that if I was trying to sell mortgages effectively, why not just be sincere and share these success stories and how I was doing it? It's really me helping you out, and that really worked well."

Today, Thompson hosts five podcasts featuring personalities from wrestling's past and present. His lineup includes former executives such as Eric Bischoff, third-generation promoters such as Jeff Jarrett, and renowned performers and broadcasters such as John Bradshaw Layfield, Jim Ross and Tony Schiavone.

Rather than focusing on live coverage and immediate reactions, Thompson's shows emphasize reflection. Although conversations occasionally touch on current topics, they rarely chase the latest controversy. Instead, Thompson builds discussions around the strengths and experiences of each contributor, giving them room to share stories that remain relevant long after the news cycle moves on.

"I think the reactionary content to wrestling in large leans negative. What everyone is looking for is hot takes, controversy and things that will make people mad. I don't think people necessarily want to buy anything when they're mad," Thompson noted. "The negative content today is second-guessing and also stunting the growth of the performers now. Reactionary content is disposable, like a Solo cup. Evergreen content you can talk about for the next 40 years."

For generations, professional wrestling operated under a code of kayfabe, maintaining the illusion surrounding its characters, rivalries and storylines. Today, very little about the business remains secret. Between documentaries and social media, fans have greater access to the industry's inner workings and a deeper understanding of the entertainment they have followed for generations.

Thompson doesn't view kayfabe's decline as an entirely negative development. His podcasts explore the stories behind wrestling's biggest moments, but he believes the industry has moved too far forward to return to its former secrecy.

"I can't imagine a situation where we put the genie back in the bottle," Thompson said. "We've now embraced that it is theater. Live stuntmen doing their thing as actors. Professional athletes, sure. But they do their own stunts. As a result of everything being so public, the surprises are more genuine. In addition, performers can start to establish that connection with a fan base on their own. They're not starting from square one."

Authenticity remains central to Thompson's approach. Conversations are unscripted, and he doesn't need to ask his guests whether certain subjects are off-limits. Instead, he considers their perspectives and determines which topics his podcast partners can discuss comfortably and which they should leave alone. That mutual understanding has helped build the trust that underpins his successful podcast portfolio.

That trust and the credibility Thompson has established over the years have also created opportunities to work with wrestling companies. He says those relationships have included conversations with All Elite Wrestling (AEW), whose CEO, Tony Khan, has discussed plans to develop a podcast network of the company's own.

"I've had a lot of conversations with AEW for a long time about a number of things. I want to be a value add for all things wrestling no matter what company it is," Thompson said. "I like to consider myself a resource for everyone. One of my main goals is to leave wrestling better than I found it. If and when there's an opportunity for me to be helpful, I jump at that chance."

Thompson also acknowledges previous discussions about working with active roster members across several promotions. However, he believes the politics surrounding professional wrestling can make it difficult for talent to speak freely. For him, authenticity is an essential ingredient in a successful podcast, and performers need the freedom to express their thoughts without constantly measuring every word.

Despite the growth and influence of wrestling content, traditional sports radio has yet to fully embrace it as a regular programming opportunity. Thompson believes broadcasters are missing a chance to connect with a substantial audience. He also argues that mainstream media and advertisers continue to hold outdated perceptions about wrestling fans.

"The big challenge with mainstream media is monetizing advertising for wrestling. There is a perception that wrestling fans are low class, uneducated, and low income. That's not reality. I can tell you firsthand because I've done thousands of mortgages for fans of my podcasts. Our average credit score for a listener of my podcasts is 741. That guy has a house worth a half a million dollars and has a household income over $175,000," Thompson explained.

As a longtime, high-volume advertiser on traditional radio, Thompson has firsthand experience with those misconceptions. He previously had to defend his advertising decisions to market managers and general managers who questioned where he chose to spend his money.

"The guy who had the Metallica album poster on his wall is now driving a Mercedes and he's a surgeon. Radio never seemed to understand who the demographic for wrestling is," Thompson said. "Trying to crack the code on wrestling may feel like pushing uphill for radio. But I've had conversations this year with two terrestrial radio networks who were interested in syndicating some version of our shows. There's nothing wrong with that. But I don't know what their ability to sell ads for wrestling radio would be. That still remains to be seen."

For Thompson, the opportunity in professional wrestling content extends well beyond revisiting the biggest matches, most memorable characters and defining moments in the industry's history. It's about understanding why those memories continue to matter and creating a space where the people who helped shape them can tell their stories on their own terms.

In an era when reactionary content often disappears as quickly as it arrives, Thompson has built a business around conversations that remain relevant long after the final bell.

His approach also offers a lesson for traditional sports radio and content creators. Audiences don't always need another immediate reaction or another debate about what just happened. Sometimes, they want to reconnect with the personalities, stories and experiences that made them fans in the first place. Thompson found that opportunity by combining his passion for wrestling with a willingness to challenge conventional thinking about how the industry could be covered and monetized.

As he looks toward 2027, Thompson has no plans to slow down.

"I am going to be adding some writing to what we do. I've been thinking about a new concept for a show while chasing a white whale," Thompson hinted. "My hope is to announce something very big by the end of the year for 2027. An all-time performer who has never really shared their stories. If I can land it, and I think I can, it's first and goal, and I'm going to take every stab at it. I'm certain it will get a lot of attention in 2027."

Looking ahead, Thompson has already demonstrated that nostalgia isn't simply about longing for the past. It's about building on the foundation of that success and finding new ways to bring meaningful stories to audiences. When paired with authenticity and a willingness to explore the stories behind the spectacle, nostalgia can become more than a reminder of what once was. It can be the foundation for something that lasts.

The Bavarians will be eager to return to winning ways in Europe's premier club competition, having drawn 3-3 against Viking FK and 2-2 with Arsenal in their last two Champions League outings. Those results have left them 14th in the league phase table with five points from three games.

A 1-1 Champions League draw against another Bundesliga side – VfB Stuttgart – was followed by domestic wins over Deportivo La Coruna (1-0) and Levante (2-0), giving Diego Simeone's men a positive run of results heading into Tuesday's clash. Atletico currently sit second in La Liga.

The two sides have met six times over the past 10 years, with Bayern winning three games, Atletico claiming two victories and one ending in a draw. Bayern have never beaten Atletico away from home and will be keen to change that on Tuesday.

Atletico Madrid will have to manage without Morten Hjulmand after he was shown a straight red card against Stuttgart. Johnny Cardoso (thigh) and Koke (muscle) are both doubts.

As for Bayern Munich, assistant coach Aaron Danks will continue deputising for head coach Vincent Kompany, who remains absent after collapsing and being diagnosed with meningeal irritation.

The German champions suffered a triple injury blow at the weekend, as Ismael Saibari, Serge Gnabry and Michael Olise were all forced off during their 2-2 draw with Borussia Dortmund.

Saibari (ankle) and Gnabry (muscle) are both facing longer spells on the sidelines, but Olise could potentially feature after taking part in Bayern's final training session ahead of the game, albeit with his right knee bandaged.

Manuel Neuer also took part in the session and could return from a foot injury, with Jonas Urbig ready to deputise for the veteran goalkeeper once again if he is not passed fit.

Luis Diaz (muscle), Jamal Musiala (thigh) and Bara Sapoko Ndiaye (appendectomy) remain unavailable.

#2693. Vic Fangio: J.J. McCarthy was a "steal" for the Giants

In late September, the Vikings sent quarterback J.J. McCarthy — the tenth overall pick in the 2024 draft — to the Giants for only a fifth-round pick. And the Eagles, who are trying to end a six-game losing streak, have to deal with McCarthy on Sunday.

On Tuesday, Eagles defensive coordinator Vic Fangio addressed the various changes the Giants have made since last season, capped by his take on the Giants landing McCarthy to replace Jaxson Dart, who's out for the year with a knee injury suffered in Week 2.

"They've got a really good offense," Fangio told reporters. "They've got skill at the receiving position. They did a nice job raiding the Ravens, not only for John [Harbaugh], but for [tight end Isaiah] Likely and [fullback Patrick] Ricard. They've got a lot of the Ravens type offense that they had when [New York Giants senior offensive assistant] Greg [Roman] was there, and they've intermixed Kansas City type passing in there with [offensive coordinator] Matt [Nagy]. They've got it going right now. They've got good wideouts, good tight ends, two good backs. The quarterback has come in, in a short period of time and really done a nice job, for them to get him for a sixth-round pick is a steal."

It was a fifth-round pick, not a sixth-round. But it was still a steal.

The Giants were desperate for help at quarterback. The Vikings were, apparently, desperate to unload McCarthy. Desperate enough to take a fifth-round pick, even though the Vikings possibly would have needed him to play at some point this season.

The end result is that the tables have quickly turned, and that the Giants are now the top dogs while the Eagles are currently all alone in one of the weakest divisions in football. And the idea that the Eagles beating the Giants in Philadelphia would be viewed as an upset says it all.
