#2692. ‘Kobe (Bryant) Didn’t Do What (Michael Jordan) and Bron Do to You’ — LeBron James’ Ex-Teammate Draws Surprising Line in NBA GOAT Debate

The debate over where Michael Jordan, LeBron James, and Kobe Bryant rank among the NBA's all-time greats has gone on for more than a decade, and Jordan himself has answered questions about it along the way.

Iman Shumpert, who played alongside James on the Cleveland Cavaliers, waded into that argument as a guest on "The Lou Young Show with TreyDay." The 2016 NBA champion put Jordan and James on one side and Bryant on the other, for a reason that came down to what each man could do physically.

The episode, hosted by comedian Lou Young, was billed as a conversation about fatherhood and Shumpert's life after the NBA. The GOAT question still came up, and Shumpert started by pushing back on how James gets judged against Jordan before turning to Bryant.

"I can't continue to move this goalpost on LeBron. It's just not his fault he was born later," Shumpert said before pushing the point further. "There's nothing from the '60s to the 2000s to now that can deal with Bron."

Their draft years offer some context for the generational comparison. James went No. 1 overall in 2003, 19 years after Jordan was picked third in 1984 and seven years after Bryant was taken 13th in 1996.

READ MORE: 'This Is Next Level Hate,' 'Ends the Argument' — NBA Fans React As LeBron James' Ex-Teammate Backs Michael Jordan In GOAT Debate

Bryant is where Shumpert's argument turned, starting with the defenders who guarded the five-time champion.

"We've seen plenty of people deal with Kobe. Kobe was just insane. I'm saying Kobe didn't do what Mike and Bron do to you athletically because he mimicked Michael Jordan's game so much," Shumpert said.

The difference, as Shumpert described it, showed up in how Bryant's possessions played out: "Kobe wasn't coming down, picking up the ball, palming it, and just having a physical and athletic advantage over you every time."

He then turned back to Jordan and James: "I'm telling you LeBron James and Michael Jordan have relied on athleticism."

That difference also shaped how Shumpert explained Bryant's hold on fans: "That's why people love Kobe. You love Kobe because you could be Kobe. You can't [expletive] be Mike. … You can't be Bron. You can't. You physically can't. But you can be Kobe."

Shumpert then walked through what Bryant did instead, laying out the reads the Hall of Famer made from his spots on the floor:

"If I get to this spot and my left shoulder is outside your right shoulder, I'm gonna go. If I get to this spot and my left shoulder is even with that shoulder and that shoulder is tilted back there, I'm pulling up … he drilled it. That's what made him great. He had the blueprint."

The trophy cases put Jordan ahead in championships and individual accolades, though the order behind him varies by award. The Chicago Bulls legend won six championships in six trips to the Finals, along with six Finals MVPs and five regular-season MVPs.

Bryant, meanwhile, spent all 20 of his seasons with the Los Angeles Lakers and won five titles, two Finals MVPs, and one regular-season MVP.

James, now playing for the Philadelphia 76ers, owns four championships, four Finals MVPs, and four regular-season MVPs, and he is 4-6 across his 10 trips to the Finals.

READ MORE: 'It Really Might Be Over,' 'Father Time Undefeated' — NBA Fans Sound Alarm As LeBron James Botches Alley-Oop Finish Off Flashy Feed From Jaylen Brown

Jordan has weighed in on Bryant versus James before. The matchup came up again in 2017 at his Flight School camp in California, and the Bulls icon did not hedge.

"Would I rank LeBron over Kobe in terms of best of all time? No. There's something about 5 that beats 3. Now he may be better than that, but Kobe won five championships. LeBron won three," Jordan said.

Though James won a fourth title after those remarks, that still leaves him one behind Bryant.

Bryant's 20 seasons and Jordan's 15 are complete, and James, still playing, is chasing a fifth ring in a 76ers jersey. As for the GOAT debate between the three NBA legends, it will take a while for the dust to settle.

This article originally appeared on Pro Football Network.

#2691. 2026-27 NHL season predictions: Expert picks for Stanley Cup playoffs, champion and major awards this season

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Following a brief offseason and an expedited preseason, the 2026-27 NHL season has arrived. Before the puck drops on opening night, we have some predictions to make.

If this season feel like it's staring earlier than usual, that's because it is. The NHL is adopting an 84-game regular season, which just means more hockey for the rest of us. That also means a long and arduous journey to the Stanley Cup is ever so slightly more difficult.

So, what will that journey look like? The Carolina Hurricanes are looking to defend their title as Cup champions, but they'll have to contend with a deep Eastern Conference and some real juggernauts in the Western Conference. With that in mind, we logged our expert predictions for the playoff field in each conference -- and there were a few surprises -- before making our Stanley Cup Final selections.

We also called our shot on the winners of each major individual award. Connor McDavid is looking for his fourth Hart Trophy, but he's got some competition from an up-and-coming superstar in his own division. Races for the Norris Trophy and Vezina Trophy should be pretty wide open, and unexpected candidates always emerge throughout the season.

It should be a fun season in the NHL, so follow along with all our coverage at CBS Sports. Let's get things kicked off with the season preview and predictions, which will of course be 100% accurate.

Baumgartner: I don't see many new faces entering the conversation when it comes to the Eastern Conference playoff race. A healthy Florida Panthers side will slot themselves right back towards the top of the Atlantic, and a revamped Washington Capitals side should be able to make some noise in the Metropolitan. Besides that, I have six 2026 playoff teams returning to the dance in 2027.

Nivison: As much as I hate to go with chalk in preseason predictions -- because it rarely happens that way -- there's no denying the top dogs in the West. The Avalanche and Stars are the class of the Central Division, and the Golden Knights should pound a pitiful Pacific Division into a pulp. Things get more interesting behind those clear Cup contenders, and I'm projecting another significant leap forward from the Mammoth. I also think Macklin Celebrini will be successful in dragging the Sharks to the playoffs in his third NHL season.

Nivison -- Columbus Blue Jackets: The Blue Jackets have been agonizingly close to the playoffs in each of the last two seasons, and I think they get over the hump in 2026-27. There are still questions in Columbus. Can Adam Fantilli be a franchise player at center? Is the forward group as a whole good enough to keep pace in a competitive Eastern Conference? Still, I am sure the Blue Jackets have a really strong blue line, led by Norris Trophy winner Zach Werenski, and goaltender Jet Greaves is on track to become a Vezina Trophy candidate. Internal improvements from the young core will then get Columbus above the cut line.

Baumgartner -- San Jose Sharks: The Sharks narrowly missed out on the 2026 Stanley Cup Playoffs, finishing just four points short of the second wild card. San Jose added a good group of veterans over the summer, but the most important offseason move was selecting Ivar Stenberg with the No. 2 pick in the Draft. Stenberg joins the youth movement in San Jose, which is spearheaded by new captain Macklin Celebrini, who broke the Sharks single-season points record with 115 last season. The Sharks are a better team than they were last year, and with Celebrini entering his third season as a legit Hart Trophy contender, this team won't be fun to play against.

Nivison: Yes, the Mammoth have a brutal path coming out of the Central Divison, but just close your eyes and imagine this scenario with me. Logan Cooley becomes a superstar center. Dylan Guenther hits 50 goals. Dmitry Simashev asserts himself as a budding top-four defenseman. Anders Lee and Vincent Trocheck provide necessary veteran depth. Now open your eyes. Utah is your Western Conference champion.

Unfortunately for the Mammoth, they will run into a refreshed Panthers team that now has double-barreled Tkachuks. Last season, we found out that all it takes to stop Florida is to hope all of its key players miss significant time with injury. The long offseason was probably a blessing in disguise as it allowed the Panthers to get healthy, and that's bad news for everyone else. The structure in front of the crease will limit some of the volatility we saw from Jacob Markstrom in New Jersey, and Florida wins its third Stanley Cup in four years.

Baumgartner: Before last season, the Carolina Hurricanes' kryptonite was the Eastern Conference Final. The Hurricanes were able to overcome their demons and win the East before ultimately taking home the franchise's first Stanley Cup since 2006. In the West, the Dallas Stars have been running into the same problem. After three straight seasons ending in the Western Conference Final, the Stars regressed last postseason, flaming out in the first-round to the Minnesota Wild. The Central Division will once again be a gauntlet, but I'm ready for Dallas to take the next step and reach the Stanley Cup Final.

While Dallas has continued to fall short in recent years, the Panthers have done the opposite. The Panthers made three consecutive Stanley Cup Final appearances, winning back-to-back Cups in 2023-24 and 2024-25. Last season, Florida's three-peat attempt came to a halt on day one of training after captain Aleksander Barkov went down with a non-contact injury, tearing both the ACL and MCL in his right knee. An offseason of healing for Barkov, and the rest of the banged up Panthers, has the team refreshed entering September for the first time in years. With nearly the entire 2025 Stanley Cup winning core still on the team and Brady Tkachuk added to the fold, Florida looks ready to win its third Stanley Cup in four seasons.

Nivison: Celebrini should have won the Hart Trophy last season, but for some incomprehensible reason, he wasn't even a finalist. This year, Celebrini replicates that performance and gets San Jose to the postseason to take home his first MVP award at age 20. Hughes posts a career year in his first full season with the Wild, and Spencer Carberry gets his flowers for winning the Metro Division after missing the playoffs last year.

Baumgartner: McDavid's ability to take over a game was evident nearly every time he touched the ice last season. His 24 points (11 goals,13 assists) in the final 14 games of the regular season -- without Leon Draisaitl in the lineup -- was one of the many reasons I put him No. 1 on my Hart Trophy ballot. With just two years left on his current contract, desperation may start to kick in to get the job in Edmonton, which would lead to another MVP-caliber season. Barkov is healthy and the frontrunner to win his fourth Selke, and Dahlin will have another strong season to take home his first career Norris Trophy.

#2689. Chaos Incarnate: Canucks’ Special Teams Sink Them in Loss to Ducks

Five fights. One of the worst calls of the season. Chaos incarnate is the apt description of the latest Vancouver Canucks game, as they wrapped up their homestand with the 10th annual Diwali Night at Rogers Arena with one of the most entertaining games of the season so far. However, it was not a celebratory night for the Canucks, as they fell to the Ducks, 5-4. The Canucks had won 14 of the last 16 meetings against the Ducks coming into tonight's action.

Tom Willander tweaked something this morning and did not dress for this game. It is a lower-body injury. Willander had been one of the team's top performers over the last week. He led Vancouver with a 65.71 CF% (Corsi-For Percentage) at even strength against the Toronto Maple Leafs on Saturday. In his 18:54 of ice time, the Canucks had 23 shot attempts while giving up 12. In addition, Vancouver outchanced Toronto 12-4 and had a 6-3 edge in high-danger opportunities while Willander was on the ice. As a result, Zeev Buium moved up to the second pairing, and Guillaume Brisebois slotted in on the third pairing. Combined with other injuries the Canucks have sustained, this could be a big loss for the team if it keeps him out of the lineup for significant time.

Kevin Lankinen made his first start since October 22 against the Detroit Red Wings. It was yet another poor game for him, as pucks continued to zip by him at a high rate. It is not so much just the quantity of goals against that is concerning; it is how they are going in. Concern was there already for Lankinen's performance, and those problems were exacerbated tonight. Do questions about a potential buyout need to be had? A bit extreme to think about considering the cap consequences, but it is an option. One thing is for sure: the net is Leevi Meriläinen's to lose.

The Canucks surrendered a penalty early to the red-hot Anaheim power play, which capitalized as Ducks captain Mikael Granlund was open in the bumper position and fired it home past Lankinen at 4:04 to take a 1-0 lead. The Ducks converted on nine of their last 15 power plays coming into this game. 10 for 16 now.

Liam Öhgren scored into an open net with chaos in the blue paint, as Drew Helleson pushed Paul Cotter into Laurent Brossoit.

Öhgy getting it done on the power play. 🫡 pic.twitter.com/CAqOiWOEge

Öhgren would continue his good work on the night, as he thought he put one home late in the period. Much to his and the fans' chagrin, it was called off, as a stick lift was called a hooking penalty. A sketchy call, to say the least, as his stick merely grazed Jackson LaCombe's glove during the stick lift. This would have been a highlight reel play.

I absolutely LOATHE how the NHL is weirdly militant about calling stick lifts that touch or breeze near a player's hands, but that is how they've consistently called it for a couple seasons now. No goal for Liam. pic.twitter.com/c4maEx8cO6

— Wyatt Arndt (@TheStanchion) November 4, 2026

On the ensuing power play, the Ducks got another goal on a slot one-timer from Cutter Gauthier and took a 2-1 lead. 11 for 17 now. "Refs you suck" chants rang loudly in the arena as this could have been a massive turning point in the game. Incredibly frustrating for the Canucks as they played well at five-on-five in the first.

🚨 Cutter 🚨Another power play goal! We lead 2-1. pic.twitter.com/cuXjAftAot

— Anaheim Ducks (@AnaheimDucks) November 4, 2026

The Canucks went on a power play early in the second, but their frustrations compounded. Brock Boeser made a blind pass to Filip Hronek, which got the Canucks panicking as the Ducks came up ice, with Leo Carlsson scoring a short-handed goal. The Canucks have now given up three short-handed goals this season, leading the NHL.

🚨 Leo Shorty 🚨What a SNIPE!That shorthanded goal gives us a 3-1 lead! pic.twitter.com/qjP7gf9Xaj

— Anaheim Ducks (@AnaheimDucks) November 4, 2026

Jacob Quillan would then have his second fight of the game, against Travis Mitchell, after he clipped Ducks goaltender Laurent Brossoit in the pads. Quil the Thrill, anyone? Once again, that may have sparked the team, as Linus Karlsson scored shortly after to cut the Ducks' lead to 3-2. Great forechecking by Drew O'Connor to create space for Karlsson.

NICE WITH IT, 94! pic.twitter.com/kHggL4uhVx

— Vancouver Canucks (@Canucks) November 4, 2026

Jamie Oleksiak got into a fight with Jeff Malott, marking the third fight of the night. This time, it did not lead to a Canucks goal right after, as Cutter Gauthier would fire home his second of the night on the power play. 12 for 18 now. Once again, the shot came from a one-timer from the left circle.

🚨 Cutter X 2 🚨Another power play goal! That one looked oddly familiar…We lead 4-2! #FlyTogether pic.twitter.com/3lBwK5NqQ2

— Anaheim Ducks (@AnaheimDucks) November 4, 2026

Cutter Gauthier got yet another hat trick, his second of the season, as he extended the lead to 5-2. He is the first in Ducks history to register hat tricks in back-to-back games.

🎩 HAT TRICK CUTTER GAUTHIER 🎩Back-to-back hattys for Cut! The FIRST consecutive hat tricks in Ducks history! #FlyTogether pic.twitter.com/fKUK6WAK5M

— Anaheim Ducks (@AnaheimDucks) November 4, 2026

More fights broke out, as once again, Brossoit was clipped, leading to a Max Sasson fight against Noah Warren. During the same stoppage, Paul Cotter also got into a fight with Sam Colangelo. The second fight resulted in 10-minute misconducts being handed out to Cotter and Colangelo. Shout out to the Canucks DJ for playing "Hit Me With Your Best Shot" after the fights.

Once again, a Canucks goal followed a fight, as Jake DeBrusk made a filthy play to slide it under Brossoit, cutting the Ducks' lead to 5-3. That extended Brock Boeser's point streak against the Ducks to 10 games.

BROCK ➡️ EP40 ➡️ DEBRUSK 🚨 pic.twitter.com/fDznMhwaIj

— Vancouver Canucks (@Canucks) November 4, 2026

Jamie Oleksiak then fired a puck toward the net, and DeBrusk deflected a goal home for his second of the night with 10:26 left in the third, livening up the crowd again as the Ducks' lead was cut to one. Déjà vu from last week's game?

— Vancouver Canucks (@Canucks) November 4, 2026

Déjà vu, it was not, as the Canucks could not muster up another goal. 5-4 Ducks is the final.

The first graph from NaturalStatTrick.com is the shot attempt advantage. The second is the expected goals advantage. A pretty even game, all things considered. Both teams have a lot to work on in terms of defence and goaltending, as shot volume was low, yet the goals came fast and furious.

The Canucks will face off against the Winnipeg Jets on Thursday at 5:00 p.m. Pacific Time (PCT). You can catch that game on Sportsnet.

#2686. 15 players to watch amid NFL trade deadline buzz

Take a look at the NFL standings. There's no sure thing this season.

Once the Los Angeles Rams got off to a rocky start, it opened things up around the league. There is no runaway team this season, and there is also a group of teams already looking ahead to 2027. That could lead to a ton of activity before the NFL's trade deadline, which is on Nov. 10. There has been plenty of action well ahead of the deadline, with players like guard Quenton Nelson going to Seattle, defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons landing in Chicago, defensive tackle DeForest Buckner heading to San Francisco, cornerback Joey Porter Jr. being shipped to Dallas and receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. being dealt to Houston.

That's already a lot of big trades and we're just getting started. Here are the 15 names to watch between now and the deadline:

There was a quarterback change in Arizona on Sunday and it will stick. Brissett was removed late in the third quarter for Gardner Minshew, who led a wild comeback win over the Cowboys in overtime. The Cardinals announced Monday that Minshew will start Week 9 with rookie Carson Beck being the backup.

All of a sudden, the Cardinals have a third quarterback who could be moved. Minshew can handle the starting job as well as the struggling Brissett was doing, and Beck will get starts at some point. Teams don't usually trade their backup quarterback, but Brissett isn't even the backup anymore and is expendable. And he has plenty of starting experience, though his $15.5 million salary for this season would have to be managed to swing a deal with most teams. He's the most likely quarterback to move at the deadline for any team desperate for a stopgap starter (perhaps the Ravens?). – Frank Schwab

If we take the Browns at their reported word, Sanders is not likely to be traded at the deadline. You can never say never until the deadline passes, but for now it appears Cleveland will continue to carry four quarterbacks, which includes Sanders. He has been QB2 behind Deshaun Watson and has replaced Watson for a handful of snaps after Watson got hurt. Watson was sacked eight times Sunday, and the 5-3 Browns might fear a more serious Watson injury as they sit just outside the current playoff picture after Week 8's defeat to the Steelers.

Given his cost-controlled salary, low draft pedigree and Cleveland's crowded QB room, Sanders might normally be considered a higher-likelihood trade candidate. So far there has been little apparent traction. We'll see if that changes over the next week. Perhaps there's even a world where Sanders is in the mix to start in Cleveland if the free-agent-to-be Watson is not brought back in 2027. – Eric Edholm

The Eagles reportedly won't trade Barkley. That also doesn't make much sense. Philadelphia is going nowhere, Barkley is turning 30 years old in February, his production has declined since 2024 and the Eagles have never been overly sentimental about player moves. Barkley brought great memories and was the superstar on a Super Bowl champion, but the Eagles should listen to calls. They could pass if teams try to get Barkley cheap, given his current injuries, but it seems like he'd have more value to a contending team this season than the Eagles going forward.

Maybe the Eagles are serious and Barkley is indeed off the table. That won't stop speculation. It makes a ton of sense for Philadelphia to move Barkley now. That's why we're still keeping an eye on Barkley as the deadline approaches. If they don't move him, that decision will be discussed not only at the deadline but beyond. – Frank Schwab

It would be a surprise if Taylor isn't traded, after the Colts sent off guard Quenton Nelson and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner. The question is who lands Taylor and his 8,208 career rushing yards. He's still one of the NFL's best runners and plenty of teams have a need. The Giants, Broncos, Packers and Vikings top the list. While other backs are likely available, nobody else would pop like Taylor. Other players might be more prudent from a football aspect (Jeffery Simmons to the Bears, most notably) but no player acquisition would generate more buzz than nabbing Taylor. – Frank Schwab

Pollard has said he doesn't want to be traded, and the Titans reportedly have rebuffed offers, but a 1-7 record and a reasonable proposal could change their minds. He's in the final year of a three-year deal, makes fairly modest starting RB money and would provide the Titans with some salary cap relief if they moved him.

Pollard has averaged a robust 4.5 yards per carry, has back-to-back 100-yard rushing outings (and five TDs in two games) and remains in his relative prime at age 29 with fewer than 2,000 career touches. On paper, he checks every box for a sale candidate if the Titans want to add more draft assets before the deadline. And for teams looking for RB help, he might come far cheaper than some of the other players mentioned above. – Eric Edholm

The memories of Thomas' rookie season might last forever. They could lead to some team thinking it can revive his career. Thomas was a first-round draft pick in 2024 and had 1,282 yards and 10 touchdowns. He looked like a future star. In the season and a half since he has fewer than 1,000 yards. He has fallen well out of the Jaguars' hierarchy at receiver, leading to plenty of trade speculation. The Jaguars, who look like Super Bowl contenders, could keep Thomas just in case there are injuries at receiver. But teams like the Seahawks, Chiefs or Commanders would likely be interested, hoping Thomas rediscovers his rookie form in a new situation. – Frank Schwab

Interestingly, Jennings was rumored to be a target of the 49ers, trying to bring him back into the fold, but declined the offer, saying he didn't want to go back to San Francisco. That's especially interesting considering his best production came with the 49ers, notching a 975-yard season in 2024 and a nine-TD campaign a year ago before leaving on a one-year deal in Minnesota. Jennings has been almost a ghost with the Vikings, with only six catches in his six games and only modest upticks in his activity lately.

The Vikings need all the offense they can find, but Jennings hasn't been a great fit. If they can include him in a deal for a running back or defensive depth, the Vikings might consider it. – Eric Edholm

Downs has requested a trade, saying he's "open to whatever" when it comes to moving on from the Colts. The team has already kick-started its offloading efforts with Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner, and don't appear to have strong intentions to keep Downs. The 25-year-old receiver is in the final year of his rookie deal and has stepped up as the Colts' leading option with Alec Pierce hurt. Downs doesn't fit a WR1 profile but could be a quality complement for a team seeking an upgrade to its unit, similar to the Seahawks' deadline trade for Rashid Shaheed last year.

Downs is a smaller slot receiver and might be a fit for only certain teams, but with his trade request and the seeming league-wide need for WR help, he figures to be a candidate who possibly moves on soon. – Eric Edholm

Jeudy has always been mercurial. He came into the NFL as a first-round draft pick and was fine early on with the Broncos, but wore out his welcome and was traded to the Browns. With the Browns, he had a stellar 2024, with 1,229 yards and a Pro Bowl nod. But he has dipped again and with the Browns turning toward rookies Denzel Boston and KC Concepcion, Jeudy has just 171 yards this season. Still, Jeudy has one of the biggest plays of the Browns' 5-3 start, a 33-yard catch against the Ravens to set up a game-winning field goal.

Jeudy, 27, could be an intriguing gamble for a team that needs juice at receiver. He's no sure thing, but the talent is there. – Frank Schwab

Mack isn't the same player he was when he was a first-team All-Pro three times in four years. His peak might lead him to the Pro Football Hall of Fame. He's 35 years old now, but still is an effective player. And with the 0-7 Chargers going nowhere, it would make sense for the team to move on and allow Mack a chance at playoff success in what might be the final season of his career. Mack is in his 13th season and has never been part of a playoff win.

Mack would add leadership and a strong edge defender down the stretch for a contender. Mack has 8.5 sacks in 19 games over the past two seasons, including three in seven games this season. Given his age, he might not cost that much. A reunion with the Bears seems like the perfect fit. – Frank Schwab

When the Eagles drafted Smith in 2023, draft experts lost their minds. They gave the Eagles a consensus grade point average of 4.12 — better than an A. While the Eagles' first pick, defensive tackle Jalen Carter, worked out very well, Smith has not.

Smith has just 14.5 career sacks but still has the draft pedigree and enticing athleticism. The Eagles picked up Smith's fifth-year option for 2027, which means they won't be looking to give him away. But for a floundering Eagles team, the idea of recouping some value on Smith during his fourth lukewarm season has to be a possibility.

There are a lot of Eagles on this list. Philadelphia becomes the seller to watch as the trade deadline approaches. For some contender looking for a shot on a sleeper, taking a stab at Smith at age 25 could pay off nicely. – Frank Schwab

Sweat reportedly requested a trade in August, and the Cardinals very publicly said they had no interest in honoring that request. Could they have a different mindset now? Arizona has won two of three and is a fairly respectable 3-5, albeit in a very tough division the Cardinals are unlikely to win. Sweat's play has not been as impactful as a year ago, when he notched 12 sacks and four forced fumbles, but he had a huge sack in overtime of Dak Prescott in Dallas on Sunday.

Speaking of Dallas, the Cowboys figure to be among the teams that could have interest in Sweat, along with the Packers, where Jonathan Gannon (his former coach) is defensive coordinator. Sweat's contract kicks up to $23.6 million salary cap hits each of the next two seasons, which puts him outside the top-10 edge rusher deals, but there have been rumors of Sweat wanting a new deal after this season, which could complicate things. – Eric Edholm

There are conflicting reports on the 25-year-old Ojomo and whether the Eagles might consider dangling him. Normally, they'd want to build around an emerging defensive tackle who has started the past three games and been more productive recently than highly paid DTs Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis. But Ojomo is set to hit free agency, and it's unlikely the Eagles can afford him after what they paid Carter and Davis. If the Eagles have designs on re-signing Ojomo, they'll have to be creative. They are 2-6, losers of six straight, including back-to-back thumpings in prime time, and QB Jalen Hurts (along with others) is on injured reserve. The Jeffery Simmons trade to Chicago had to be an eye-opener for Philly, value-wise, and might cause the team to consider moving him before the deadline. – Eric Edholm

Baker has been tremendous for the Cardinals over his 10 seasons with the team, making eight Pro Bowls. But it might be time for a rebuilding club to move on. Baker can provide playmaking at secondary, as he has for a decade. He is signed through 2027, with a reasonable salary of a little more than $16 million for next season. So he wouldn't be a short-term rental for a team.

It would sting for the Cardinals to move on from Baker, one of the team's best players and only positive lights in the post-Larry Fitzgerald era. But it's prudent for a team looking for the future. And it would be a big get for a contending club that needs a difference maker in the secondary. – Frank Schwab

Following his three-pick game Sunday against Joe Burrow, Hooker is the NFL's INT leader with five, and his 114 return yards off those picks also is first. The 28-year-old veteran has quietly carved out a nice career over eight seasons with the Titans and is enjoying one of his better years, tackling and covering well. The Titans signed him to an extension last summer through the 2028 season with a fairly reasonable salary outside the top 10 safeties.

Given their 1-7 record at the bye, the Titans could offload more vets after trading Jeffery Simmons. – Eric Edholm

#2685. Samberg lifts Jets past Canadiens 5-4 with OT goal to complete comeback from 4-goal deficit

MONTREAL (AP) — Dylan Samberg scored in overtime as the Winnipeg Jets snapped a nine-game losing streak by storming back from a four-goal deficit to beat the Montreal Canadiens 5-4 on Tuesday night.

Montreal led 4-0 when Cole Caufield scored his second of the game and 10th of the season 46 seconds into the third period.

But Winnipeg scored four goals in 2 minutes, 8 seconds to tie the game with 32 seconds remaining in regulation on Kyle Connor's power-play strike, his second goal of the game.

It was the latest four-goal comeback in NHL history.

Tyrel Bauer and Morgan Barron started the rally to break Montreal goalie Jacob Fowler's shutout bid for the Jets, who were coming off a 7-0 loss to the Carolina Hurricanes on Sunday.

Stuart Skinner made 18 saves, while Mark Scheifele and Dylan Demelo had two assists each.

Owen Beck and Josh Anderson also scored for Montreal and Juraj Slafkovsky added two assists. Fowler stopped 42 shots. On Beck's goal, Arber Xhekaj and Florian Xhekaj became the first brothers to record a point on the same Canadiens goal since Andrei Kostitsyn and Sergei Kostitsyn on Jan. 17, 2009.

Nick Suzuki missed his sixth consecutive game with a hand injury. The Canadiens captain had played 546 straight regular-season games to begin his NHL career. He appears close to returning after practising without any obvious limitations Monday and Tuesday morning.

Winnipeg reunited its prolific top line of Scheifele, Connor and Gabriel Vilardi in search of a spark. The Jets piled on the shots and eventually broke Fowler late in the game.

Jets: Host the Vancouver Canucks on Thursday night.

Canadiens: Host the Utah Mammoth on Thursday night.

#2684. Brewers win the 2026 World Series: Where the Brew Crew ranks among the best recent MLB champions

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

ST. PETERSBURG -- The Milwaukee Brewers are World Series champions. There's so much weight in such a statement on its own, but let's consider for a second all the context behind it.

The 2026 Brewers won 103 games in the regular season and then, more impressively, went a ridiculous 11-2 in the playoffs, never facing elimination, never even trailing in a series. They were one loss away Not only that, but they came so close to being the first team ever to go 8-0 in the League Championship Series and World Series. The 1976 Reds were the only team to sweep both the LCS and World Series, but that only got them to 7-0 because the LCS was five games until 1985. The best playoff record in the era of multiple wild cards was the 2022 Astros at 11-2, and the Brewers have tied that. The 2005 White Sox went 11-1 and so did the 1999 Yankees. We're already up in rarefied air. But there's more.

Think about how hot the Brewers closed. They finished the regular season by winning 15 of their last 18 games. This means they went 26-5 after Sept. 6. Further, look at who they decimated in the playoffs. The Padres were riding a run of 19 wins in 22 games, including a two-game sweep in the Wild Card Series. The Brewers went 3-1 in that NLDS. The Dodgers were the two-time defending champions who swept the Brewers in the NLCS last year. They won 100 games in 2026. The Brewers swept them in four games. The Rays won 98 games in the regular season and were 7-2 thus far in the playoffs. The Brewers took them down in five with their only loss coming in 12 innings.

Remember the Bob Uecker line from "Major League?" There's nothing left but a vapor trail.

That's the Brewers' path to the championship. They just became an absolute killing machine down the stretch, pulverizing everything in their path.

Statistically, they can't touch the 1998 Yankees (114 wins, +309 run differential, 11-2 playoff record including World Series sweep) and certainly can't get to the 1927 Yankees (110-44, +376 run differential, swept World Series). But what about more recently?

Such an exercise is subjective, but let's figure out where these Brewers rank in recent memory. Probably really close to the top, if not all the way up. This wasn't a team loaded with future Hall of Famers, as the Dodgers were last season, for example, but the numbers say these Brewers take a back seat to very few, if any, teams in the past couple of decades.

In fact, let's sort through it. I'll go with the multiple-wild card era, so we're starting in 2012. Let's narrow it down to teams that won at least 100 games and also won the World Series. Yes, the World Series title is a requirement, so we can safely say goodbye to the 2021 Giants and 2022 Dodgers.

We'll compare the teams via regular-season record, run differential, playoff record and how they fared in the World Series. As you'll see, the Brewers will have the most impressive resume here.

An absolute juggernaut in the regular season outside of a wretched stretch before the All-Star break, the Cubs finally broke the faux curse and won it all. They had the regular-season MVP and two Cy Young candidates, in addition to the Cy Young winner from the previous year. On the downside of this argument, they trailed in both the NLCS and World Series (three games to one). Coming back is impressive, but the most dominant teams didn't fall behind.

The first World Series title in franchise history came with a young and (at least it felt like it at the time) fun team. They had the MVP and a former Cy Young winner and also traded for future Hall of Famer Justin Verlander. They needed seven games in both the ALCS and World Series.

The highest win total on the list is right here. They also never faced elimination in the playoffs, though they did trail 1-0 in the ALCS. The MVP of the league was again on the champs and they also had three Cy Young winners (Chris Sale hadn't won his yet, but he was the undisputed ace).

After a 106-win regular season, the Astros steamrolled through the American League side of the bracket, going 7-0. They did lose Games 1 and 3, though, to fall behind 2-1 in the World Series after seeing the Phillies club them for a bunch of home runs in a 7-0 Game 3 win. The Astros righted the ship thereafter, though, and won the next three games, including two nail-biters.

Though the regular seasons are pretty comparable in that chart above, the Brewers were easily the top dog in the postseason. They lost one game between the NLCS and World Series.

We should probably loop in the 2013 Red Sox, the 2015 Royals and the repeat champion 2024-25 Dodgers as well.

If I had to rank them, I think the Mount Rushmore in this era would be:

The 2025 Dodgers were a tough omission, but they didn't even earn a bye due to a relatively low regular-season win total.

I'm willing to hear arguments for the Brewers over that Red Sox team, too. After all, the Red Sox did lose a whole three playoff games, even though they never faced elimination.

The bottom line is that the 2026 Milwaukee Brewers are one of the best, if not the greatest, champions in recent history.

Contreras also went 10 for 14 in ABS challenges behind the plate and 4 for 9 throwing out basestealers.

"I don't have words to say for how I'm feeling," Contreras said through an interpreter following Game 5. "I'm just appreciative of my teammates, appreciative of (manager Pat) Murphy. I want to thank all of them."

"This team's not what it is without this guy," ace reliever Aaron Ashby said after Game 5. "He wants to compete every day. He's our bulldog and we love this dude."

#2677. MLB Lockout 101: Everything to know about baseball's likely upcoming work stoppage

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026 Major League Baseball season is over, and the Milwaukee Brewers are World Series champions for the first time. The Brewers finished off the Tampa Bay Rays on Wednesday night in Game 5 of the 2026 World Series. MLB Opening Day for 2027 is scheduled for March 24. But whether fans are watching baseball again or not in less than five months is very much up in the air.

Major League Baseball's players and owners are in the process of negotiating a new collective bargaining agreement, or CBA. The CBA is the accord that governs the working relationship between the players, as represented by their union, the MLBPA, and the clubs. It covers pretty much every aspect of that relationship that you can imagine, all the way from the overarching salary and payroll structure to daily meal money and days off during the season.

Not surprisingly, it's the economic platform of the game that's the toughest to negotiate because that is always, in essence, a fight over money, or how the league's substantial revenues will be divided up between teams and players. That's keenly relevant right now because players and owners are sparring over whether or not MLB will have a cap on salaries moving forward. The owners have renewed their push for a salary cap after not aggressively (or at least not this aggressively) pursuing one since the 1994-95 players' strike.

Matters are such that the owners are expected to implement a lockout of the players after the current CBA expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1 of this year.

There are two kinds of labor stoppages in MLB: the strike and the lockout. A strike is when the labor side – players as represented by their union, in this instance – puts a halt to operations. A lockout is when the management side – team owners and the commissioner's office doing their bidding, in this instance – initiates the stoppage. In plainspoken terms, a strike is a refusal to work, and a lockout is a refusal to permit work to be done. For those on the outside, the result is the same, in that there's no Major League Baseball during a lockout or strike.

When a lockout is in force in MLB, as is expected to be the case after this CBA expires, nothing happens on the major-league front. And we do mean nothing.

There's an almost literal element to a lockout in that anyone on the 40-man roster of any MLB club will be locked out of any team facility for the duration of the stoppage. That also means no access to team trainers or team physicians or members of the coaching staff. Beyond that, there's a transaction freeze in place starting the moment the lockout begins (more on that in a moment).

Additionally, MLB is expected to remove player images and videos from the league's official website, MLB.com, and player images and even names would be removed from articles on MLB.com. A league memo acquired by The Athletic also forbids contact between players and anyone on the club side, at least to the greatest extent possible. The latter extends all the way down to a recommendation against sending holiday cards to players who have been locked out.

Bottom line: A lockout means the sport at the highest level is on hold across all fronts until further notice. "Further notice" almost certainly means when a new CBA is agreed to in principle and then ratified by both sides.

As just noted, a lockout means a transaction freeze, which means no players on any 40-man rosters can be traded and no major-league free agents can be signed for as long as the lockout lasts. Free agency, however, begins on Monday (Nov. 2), so there is roughly one month available for those looking to make trades or signings (once the five-day exclusive negotiating window closes and qualifying offers are extended) before the freeze sets in.

It's worth noting that in the run-up to the last lockout of 2021-22, we saw a swarm of free agent signings just before the lockout began. We could see that flurry of moves again, particularly in light of proposed changes to contract structures that would limit lengths and dollar amounts. Would players like Tarik Skubal, who are eyeing mid-nine-figure contracts, want to get their deals done quickly and hope they're grandfathered in?

That said, there's a lot more uncertainty about what the game's financial structure will look like after this CBA negotiation concludes, at least relative to the last time we did this. That may have a chilling effect on the trade and free agent markets leading up to the lockout date. Clubs don't like mass uncertainty when it comes to making major roster decisions, and they may prefer to see what the league's salary and revenue sharing systems will look like for the next half-decade (the term of each CBA these days) before committing to signings and trades.

If the lockout spans a meaningful amount of time, then that means a great deal of usual winter business will be put on hold. The MLB Winter Meetings and the major-league portion of Rule 5 Draft are typically held in the first half of December, so those could be imperiled. Last time out, the major-league portion of the Rule 5 Draft was indeed canceled, although the November Rule 5 protection deadline had already passed. If the lockout stretches into January, then the exchange of arbitration figures between eligible players and their teams will be delayed. Get well into late January and early February without an agreement, and arbitration hearings and the spring training schedule could be shortened or imperiled altogether. Needless to say, local businesses and elected officials in Florida and Arizona would very much not like that. That, though, could be the least of our worries.

It very well might. It's too soon to say, but there's the real potential for disruption and, perish the thought, maybe even cancellation of the 2027 season. The latter is of course the worst-case scenario, and there's no reason to think there's a strong threat of that possibility, at least this far out. During the last lockout, though, the two sides weren't fighting over quite as much territory, and we very nearly lost games from the regular-season schedule. Lest anyone forget, the last time the owners vigorously pushed for a salary cap, we wound up losing the World Series.

There is a wrinkle of note that may make a worst-case scenario less likely. If the lockout drags on long enough to cancel 60 or more games from the 2027 MLB season, then the fallout could be significant. The Athletic recently reported that if the lockout extends into late May or so and costs at least 60 games, then most of the league's national broadcast and streaming contracts would be extended for another year, through 2029. That matters because Manfred and the league hope to bundle and centralize team streaming rights and share those revenues equally, and the current timeline would theoretically allow that to happen at the same time the national contracts are up for renegotiation in 2028. Tacking on another year to those national contracts would push back the significant windfall that owners and the league are expecting from that new media rights structure. This amounts to a major incentive, at least on the league side, to agree to a new CBA before June arrives.

Just players on the 40-player roster will be affected by the lockout, as mentioned. While that includes some minor leaguers, the vast majority of minor-league players are not on the 40 and thus will not be impacted. Minor leaguers now have their own CBA independent of MLB players, and that CBA is still in force. Thus, they're not being locked out. The minor-league season will proceed as normal, albeit minus those prospects on their respective 40s, just as it did during the 2021-22 lockout. So, yes, there will be affiliated professional baseball going on even if the lockout stretches into the 2027 regular season.

To hear commissioner Rob Manfred tell it, the lockout is designed to hasten negotiations between the two sides and speed up the process of forging a new CBA that, assuming it arrives in time, will cover the 2027-31 MLB seasons. Manfred cited this very reason leading up to the lockout of 2021-22, and during the drumbeat phase of this approaching lockout, he said this:

"In a bizarre way, it's actually a positive. There is leverage associated with an offseason lockout, and the process of collective bargaining under the NLRA (National Labor Relations Act) works based on leverage. The great thing about offseason lockouts is the leverage that exists gets applied between the bargaining parties."

After implementing the 2021-22 lockout, Manfred said the drastic decision was designed to "jumpstart the negotiations and get us to an agreement that will allow the season to start on time."

Actions, though, hold sway over words, and after locking out the players, MLB owners didn't make their first CBA proposal to the players for another six weeks or so. In reality, the purpose of a lockout is to preempt a strike. The union can time a strike so as to exert maximum leverage and apply maximum pressure on ownership, say, during the stretch drive or soon after Opening Day or just in advance of the playoffs. From a fan and observer standpoint, though, at least this gets the clock started before games hang directly in the balance.

Yes. The forthcoming lockout will be the 10th labor stoppage in modern MLB history – five strikes and, soon, five lockouts. Here's a quick look at the nine lockouts and strikes that have already happened:

As you can see, there are occasions in which the stoppage is lengthy and disruptive, and in other instances they barely register. Given the complex nature of the current negotiation, the expectation is that the upcoming lockout won't be resolved quickly. There is, though, some runway between "immediate resolution" and "2027 season greatly harmed."

It's the salary cap, first and foremost. MLB has coveted a capped system for decades, but for the MLBPA, the strongest union in sports, a cap is a complete nonstarter. If the stoppage turns into a war, then it will be because owners continue pushing for a cap and players continue to resist. Let it be known that despite the public narrative, the main advantage of a salary cap for owners is not that it will promote competitive balance, but rather that a payroll cap figures to increase franchise values.

Otherwise, changes to the way the league shares local revenues are also up for negotiation. MLB already shares local revenues at significant levels, but Manfred and owners want to share them more equally among teams, perhaps similar to what the NFL does. The good news is that the union has already shown a willingness to discuss such changes and indeed has proposed something similar. That's common ground on a negotiation that figures to need as much of that as possible. As well, increasing the sharing of local revenues, especially local broadcast revenues, would help achieve what the league claims a cap would achieve and do so without a 1994-95 scale of work stoppage.

Given the all-encompassing nature of the CBA, many other issues will need to be sorted out. Those may include the length of the regular season, postseason format, the minimum salary, any changes to free agency and salary arbitration, the implementation of an international draft, retention of the qualifying offer system, active roster sizes, draft bonus pools and eligibility, and -- if retained -- the structure of the Competitive Balance Tax system. That's not an exhaustive list, and all of it has to be hammered out, at least in terms broadly agreeable to both sides, for the lockout to end. For now, though, the league hasn't moved off its demand for a cap, and until that changes -- or until the union acquiesces (highly unlikely) -- that issue will determine how long the lockout lasts.

Yes, there is. Once we get into spring training and beyond, any continued shutdown costs clubs and players money. MLB owners have a significantly larger war chest than the players do, but neither side relishes missed broadcast and gate revenues or paychecks. As detailed above, there's heavy incentive to get this resolved before the 60-game mark of the regular season because of broadcast contracts. Along similar lines, with attendance continuing to rise and revenues also increasing each year, the game is in a relatively healthy spot. Pace-of-play initiatives are broadly popular among paying customers, as is the implementation of the ABS challenge system. Expansion to 32 teams is probably also on the horizon. All of that adds up to a potentially lucrative glut of national broadcast contracts, and a lockout that cuts the 2027 season to ribbons would do great harm to what may be MLB's most important business-side objective of all right now. The 1994-95 strike also still provides a roadmap to how much damage the "nuclear" outcome can do to the sport.

Every labor stoppage is a skirmish over money, but the prospect of losing a hunk of the money they're fighting over can reveal shared interests and the foundations of compromise. Therein lies the hope for those of us on the outside.

#2676. Pat McAfee Is Having a Howard Stern-Like Impact on Sports Media

Remember Howard Stern? What was his impact on the broadcast radio and media industry? Stern was different. He took risks and made his life its own reality show on his program. He was radio's greatest provocateur, finding an audience with his edge and by pushing the envelope. Today, Stern is revered for taking risks and being unique in an age of uniformity. Is it fair to say Pat McAfee's impact on sports media is similar to Howard Stern's impact on radio?

McAfee has grown an audience all his own, tested boundaries and found opportunities through traditional media before taking ownership of his content and going digital. Does he have the edgy, against-the-grain content Stern had? No. But his impact is similar, as is the reaction to it. Today, McAfee's influence is at a fever pitch. Traditional media figures across every sector are pushing back, but the results continue to impress.

Am I the biggest fan of Pat McAfee? No, but I respect the audience he has earned.

There hasn't been anyone in sports media who has built what McAfee has. He didn't need a traditional network to reach an audience. He founded his own platform, reinforced it through social and digital media, and has rarely said no to an opportunity.

That should be celebrated more than it is. McAfee is an example for every brand, talent, executive, creator and business to study. There are elements of his success that others should attempt to replicate. But this isn't 2023. It's 2026. Today, audiences are quicker to complain than compliment and quicker to engage than ignore.

In many ways, McAfee approaches sports media like a professional wrestler. When business is good in professional wrestling, it's because the act doesn't make people think. It makes them feel. The goal is no different in any form of media. McAfee knows how to flood the zone, play the algorithm, get into your feeds and make you react.

That's why business is good, and why it continues to be.

Over the past couple of weeks, everyone from former congressman and television host Joe Scarborough to former Deadspin founder Will Leitch has weighed in on McAfee's influence on College GameDay. Their criticism centers on how the 40-year-old program has shifted from celebrating college football to being, in their view, diminished by McAfee's presence.

"I've just had enough of this Pat McAfee ruining College GameDay," Scarborough said Tuesday. "I look forward to waking up on Saturday mornings and watching that. I don't know if they haven't got the message yet, but the manosphere that we all thought was brought in in '24, it may get washed aside."

Leitch compared McAfee's presence on GameDay to Mr. Beast, saying, "Eventually, if you don't have anything to actually contribute other than yourself and your stunts and your neuroses, you're going to realize there's no gas left in the tank."

Earlier this year, I wrote that College GameDay would never be the same without Lee Corso. He was a giant of a man who embodied everything the sport stands for: fun, family and football. He was the grand marshal of the Saturday morning parade, always kicking things off with his headgear selection.

College GameDay viewership in 2026 is up 5% through eight weeks compared with last year's regular-season average. The final hour continues to draw more than three million viewers, with last Saturday's edition averaging 3.1 million. McAfee's "Kicking is Easy" competition also generates significant audience spikes, with ESPN reporting an average 10% increase in viewership from the start of the segment to its conclusion.

Those numbers don't mean McAfee alone is solely responsible for the show's growth. However, they do demonstrate that the program continues to attract an audience despite the criticism surrounding its changing identity.

Yes, McAfee isn't for everyone. The demographics prove that. He skews younger, and always has. His weekday program just recorded its best October audience since joining ESPN in 2023, averaging 483,000 viewers across linear and digital platforms. If anything, McAfee has also become a fresh face on ESPN's Monday Night Countdown. Remember the concerns from many of his critics about oversaturation on ESPN?

Monday Night Countdown is averaging 1.6 million viewers per show, up 26% from last year's figures.

ESPN's slogan continues to be, "Serving Sports Fans. Anytime. Anywhere." McAfee is Exhibit A, B and C when it comes to fulfilling that mission. The reason he's everywhere on ESPN comes down to one thing: He generates attention. People love him. People hate him. Either way, more people are watching, and they're watching for longer periods of time.

Just like Howard Stern did for so many years.

Love him or hate him, Pat McAfee isn't going anywhere. ESPN isn't going to scale back his presence because a vocal minority believes he's changing the network for the worse. The audience is telling a different story. Viewership is growing, his influence continues to expand, and ESPN keeps finding more opportunities to put him in front of sports fans.

Howard Stern faced plenty of the same criticism throughout his career. He wasn't universally loved, nor did he need to be. He understood how to make people pay attention, and McAfee has figured out how to do the same in a different era.

The media landscape has changed, but one principle hasn't: Audiences gravitate toward personalities who make them feel something. As long as McAfee continues to deliver that, ESPN will keep giving him the airtime.

The critics can keep complaining. The audience has already delivered its verdict.

#2674. Key MLB offseason dates: When does free agency start? What else will happen before potential lockout?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026 MLB season is complete and the Brewers are World Series champions. They defeated the Rays to clinch the first title in franchise history. We were assured a first-time champion this season and the Brewers won it. The Rays will try again for their first title next year. With the World Series now complete, the 2026-27 offseason has officially begun, and several significant events are right around the corner.

Of course, this all comes with a disclaimer. When the current collective bargaining agreement expires on Dec. 1, the owners are expected to lock out the players until a new deal is reached. That could take days, weeks, months, who knows? It may affect spring training and even the 2027 regular season, or they may find labor peace before the spring. Regardless, the likely lockout will all but certainly affect some of the calendar. MLB free agency will still begin in early November, but transactions will all come to a halt the minute there is a lockout.

Here now are the important dates and deadlines for the coming weeks and months.

As of 9 a.m. ET, eligible players (i.e. those with at least six years of service time) are free agents. Free agents cannot sign with a new team just yet. They have to wait five days for that. The first five days of the offseason are an exclusive negotiating period during which free agents can only talk money with their most recent team. Very few players re-sign during the exclusive negotiating period. Edwin Díaz returning to the Mets four years ago is by far the most notable in recent memory. Once players get this close to free agency, they typically test the market. Also, trades involving 40-man roster players resume on this day for the first time since the summer's trade deadline.

This year's Gold Glove winners will be announced during an ESPN broadcast at 8:30 p.m. ET. The Cubs and Blue Jays lead the way with five Gold Glove finalists each. In addition to the nine individual positions in each league, there is also a utility Gold Glove and a team Gold Glove.

Most contract option decisions are due on this date. Some contracts specify a different date (the Yankees had to make a decision on Zack Britton's 2022 club option in November 2020, for example), but the vast majority have to be made within five days of the end of the World Series. Club options are controlled by the team, player options and opt-outs are controlled by the player, and mutual options are kind of pointless. They're a way to shift money to the next year's payroll more than anything.

Some option decisions are no-brainers, like the Braves picking up their $17 million club option on Ronald Acuña Jr. or Luis Severino picking up his $22 million player option with the Athletics. This offseason's notable contract option decisions include Michael King (can opt out of two years and $58 million with Padres), Bo Bichette (can opt out of two years and $84 million with Mets), and Luis Robert Jr. (Orioles hold $20 million club option).

The qualifying offer is a one-year contract worth the average of the top 125 salaries, or $23.15 million this offseason, according to the New York Post. To be eligible for the qualifying offer, a free agent must have spent the entire 2026 season with one team and have never received the QO previously. The Mariners can make Randy Arozarena the QO, but the Dodgers cannot do the same with Tarik Skubal because he was traded during the season.

The five-day exclusive negotiating period ends and free agents are truly free. They can negotiate and sign with any team as of 5 p.m. ET on this date. That said, much like the regular season, MLB's free agency is a marathon, not a sprint. We (probably) won't see a rush of signings on Day 1 because MLB is not a salary-capped league (not yet, anyway), and free agents aren't worried about getting left out in the cold when cap space runs out.

Rookies of the Year on Monday, Managers of the Year on Tuesday, Cy Youngs on Wednesday, and MVPs on Thursday. The awards will be announced during an MLB Network broadcast at 7 p.m. ET each day. Awards finalists will be announced Nov. 2. The All-MLB Team, Comeback Players of the Year, and Relievers of the Year will also be announced on Nov. 11.

Generally speaking, the GM Meetings are used to handle off-the-field matters like rule changes, but when you put all 30 GMs in one place, deals inevitably get discussed and sometimes completed. The Angels signed Travis d'Arnaud and the Braves traded Nick Allen to the Astros at last year's GM Meetings, for example. Also, the groundwork is often laid this week for deals that are completed at a later date.

If Silver Sluggers are your thing, this is the date for you. Four years ago, a utility player Silver Slugger was added, then three years ago, MLB and Louisville debuted a team Silver Slugger. Finalists will be announced Nov. 2.

The deadline for free agents to accept or reject the QO is 4 p.m. ET.  Players who accept the QO sign that one-year, $23.15 million contract and remain with their team (and cannot be traded until June 15 without their consent). Free agents who reject the QO are attached to draft pick compensation. Their former team receives a draft pick if they sign elsewhere, and their new team has to forfeit a draft pick(s) and, in some cases, international bonus money. Arozarena and Seiya Suzuki are among the free agents who will surely reject the QO and sign more lucrative contracts this offseason.

That is a fancy way of saying this is the deadline for teams to add eligible minor leaguers to the 40-man roster to protect them from the Rule 5 Draft. Generally speaking, college players drafted no later than 2023 and high school players drafted no later than 2022 are Rule 5 Draft eligible this winter, as are players signed internationally no later than 2022. Among the notable Rule 5 Draft-eligible prospects this offseason are Dodgers righty Christian Zazueta and Nationals righty Travis Sykora. Those two and many others will be added to the 40-man roster on this date. The deadline is 6 p.m. ET, specifically.

It should be noted that there are usually several minor trades in the days leading up to the Rule 5 Draft protection deadline as teams get their 40-man roster in order. Four years ago, the Rays traded Xavier Edwards to the Marlins in the 40-man roster management move at the Rule 5 Draft protection deadline.

The now triannual owners meetings cover big-picture business matters and are rarely a source of hot stove news or rumors. Three years ago, the owners voted on and approved the Athletics' proposed relocation to Las Vegas at their November meetings. With the collective bargaining agreement set to expire on Dec. 1 and talks with the MLB Players Association ongoing, the owners will likely use this week as one last strategy session.

This is the deadline for teams to offer contracts to their pre-arbitration and arbitration-eligible players for 2027. Contracts do not have to be signed yet. An offer just has to be extended. Players who do not receive a contract offer before the deadline are considered "non-tendered" and immediately become free agents. Notable players are non-tendered every offseason as teams determine that their salary outweighs their performance and the trade market turns up nothing worthwhile. Adolis García and Nathaniel Lowe were among the players non-tendered last offseason.

Specifically, the CBA expires at 11:59 p.m. ET, and it is very likely the owners will lock out the players at that time. It is possible MLB and the MLBPA will agree to a new CBA before this date, sure, but it would be a major surprise. All major league transactions get put on hold during the lockout. There will be no trades or free agent signings involving 40-man roster players, or even any negotiations. Here is our timeline of CBA talks and proposals. Because a potential lockout would bring so much uncertainty, any events and deadlines listed after this date are subject to change. We'll put asterisks as a reminder.

These are the extra draft picks given each year to teams that fall in the bottom 10 in revenue and/or market size. There is overlap between the two groups, so there are typically 14-15 competitive balance picks awarded each year, not 20. Competitive balance picks are MLB's only tradeable draft picks. Last offseason, picks were included in the Shane Baz, Brendan Donovan, and Caleb Durbin/Kyle Harrison trades. Five years ago, the assignment of competitive balance picks was pushed back until after the lockout.

Voting results for the Hall of Fame's Contemporary Baseball Committee for Managers, Executives, and Umpires will be announced during an MLB Network broadcast. The Hall of Fame has restructured its veteran committee three times in the last 14 years, and this year's Contemporary Baseball Committee will consider "candidates whose primary contribution to the game came since 1980." The 16-person committee will consider eight candidates on the ballot. This has nothing to do with the CBA and the announcement will take place as scheduled.

This is typically when all hot stove hell breaks loose. The Winter Meetings are the busiest period of the offseason and feature plenty of trades, free agent signings, and rumors. It is three-plus days of nonstop hot stove action. Historically, the biggest moves of the offseason are completed at the Winter Meetings. GMs can talk face-to-face with agents and other GMs to get things done. Last year, Pete Alonso, Edwin Díaz, and Kyle Schwarber signed during the Winter Meetings while Jose A. Ferrer and Harry Ford were among those traded. The Winter Meetings were canceled during the last lockout. It seems likely they would be canceled again during a potential lockout this offseason.

In an effort to curb tanking, MLB and the MLBPA agreed to a lottery to determine the top six picks of the annual amateur draft as part of the current CBA. The 18 non-playoff teams each have a shot at the No. 1 pick, though the worst teams have the highest odds. Here are this year's odds for the No. 1 selection in the 2027 Draft (via Baseball America):

Teams that pay into revenue sharing cannot pick in the lottery in back-to-back years, so the Giants (No. 4 pick in 2026) are not eligible for the lottery this year. The Pirates, meanwhile, cannot get a lottery pick this year because teams that receive revenue sharing can not pick in the lottery in three consecutive years. They had the No. 6 pick in 2025 and the No. 5 pick in 2026. The Giants and Pirates cannot pick higher than No. 10 overall in 2027.

The lottery determines the top six draft picks. Picks 7-18 are the remaining non-playoff teams in reverse order of the standings. Picks 19-30 are the 12 postseason teams ordered by their finish, with the Wild Card Series losers coming first and the World Series winner picking last. The draft lottery was not yet a thing during the last lockout. It's unclear how MLB would handle it during a potential lockout this offseason.

By rule, players selected in the Rule 5 Draft must remain on their new team's MLB roster all season in 2027; otherwise, they must go through waivers and be offered back to their original team. Teams don't often find difference-makers in the Rule 5 Draft. They usually look for middle relievers, platoon bats, and lottery tickets. Most Rule 5 Draft picks don't stick and wind up back with their original team. Last offseason's notable Rule 5 Draft selection was Blue Jays righty Spencer Miles, who gave them 95 ⅔ innings with a 2.63 ERA. The Rule 5 Draft was canceled and not held during the last lockout. There is a minor-league phase that still took place, however, because that phase does not involve 40-man roster players.

This is the deadline for teams and arbitration-eligible players to submit salary figures for 2027. The player files what he believes he should be paid while the team files what it believes the player should be paid. This date is only the filing deadline, and the two sides can still agree to a contract of any size even after filing salary figures. The vast majority of arbitration-eligible players agree to a contract before the filing deadline and avoid this headache. MLB Trade Rumors released their 2027 salary arbitration projections a few weeks ago. The entire arbitration process (submit filing figures, hearings, etc.) was pushed back until after the lockout five years ago.

The 2027 international amateur signing period opens at 9 a.m. ET. The annual signing period used to run from July 2 to June 25, though MLB and the MLBPA agreed to push the start of the 2020-21 and 2021-22 signing periods back to the following January because of the pandemic, and now the January start is permanent and the signing period is neatly confined to a single calendar year. These are non-40-man roster players and the international signing period opened as scheduled during the last lockout.

The 2027 Hall of Fame class will be announced during a live MLB Network broadcast. The Hall of Fame ballot will be revealed on Nov. 16, votes are compiled over the following weeks, then the results are announced in January. Newcomers to this year's ballot include Jon Lester and Buster Posey. This is Omar Vizquel's tenth and final year of eligibility. This is also Year 6 on the ballot for Alex Rodriguez and Year 4 for Chase Utley. Among holdovers, Utley was closest to getting in without actually getting in last year. He received 59.1% of the vote, well short of the 75% needed for induction, but he's made huge gains in his three years on the ballot and is trending toward induction.

Inevitably, a few arbitration-eligible players and their teams will be unable to come to terms on a contract, and wind up in front of an arbitration panel. Each side states their case -- hearings can be contentious because the team will outline the player's shortcomings and explain why he deserves a lower salary than he believes -- and the three-person panel picks either the salary the player filed or the salary the team filed on Jan. 8. Nothing in between. Again, teams and players can work out a contract of any size prior to a hearing, even after filing salary figures. Skubal and Kyle Bradish were among the players to go to an arbitration hearing before the 2026 season. Hearings were pushed back until after the lockout five years ago, and in some cases they took place during the season.

Spring training camps open across Arizona and Florida in the middle of February. Each team sets its own reporting dates for pitchers and catchers and then position players, though they'll all be up and running by the second full week of February. All 30 teams are scheduled to play their first exhibition game on Feb. 19. If the lockout extends into February, the start of spring training will be delayed. During the lockout five years ago, MLB announced spring delays one week at a time, piece by piece.

March 24 is the exclusive Opening Night game on Netflix (teams TBA). The other 28 teams will begin their seasons one day later. There's Rivalry Weekend, a special series in Las Vegas and more. Of course, if the lockout extends in March, Opening Day and other games will be pushed back. Five years ago, the regular season started a week late and teams picked up the existing schedule. A new schedule was not drawn up. Missed games were made up with doubleheaders and on mutual off-days throughout the year, with a few extra days tacked on to the end of the season as well.

#2673. Gauthier scores 2nd straight hat trick in Ducks’ 5-4 win over Canucks

VANCOUVER, British Columbia (AP) — Cutter Gauthier scored a hat trick for the second game in a row and the Anaheim Ducks held on for a 5-4 victory over the Vancouver Canucks on Tuesday night.

Mikael Granlund added a goal and two assists for the Ducks, while Leo Carlsson put away a short-handed tally and Beckett Sennecke had four assists.

Laurent Brossoit stopped 19 shots in the Anaheim net.

The Ducks came into the game with the league's second-best power play (34%) behind only the Utah Mammoth and went 3 for 3 with the man advantage. Two of Gauthier's goals came on the power play and Anaheim has 10 power-play goals on 12 chances over its last three games.

The Canucks got two goals from Jake DeBrusk, and one each from Liam Ohgren and Linus Karlsson. Elias Pettersson notched a pair of assists. Vancouver goalie Kevin Lankinen made 17 saves.

The Ducks took a 2-1 lead into the intermission when Gauthier fired a shot in on his team's second power play of the night at the 17:07 mark of the first.

Gauthier also scored three in Anaheim's 6-3 comeback victory over the Ottawa Senators on Sunday, and is the first player in Ducks history with back-to-back three-goal games.

The 22-year-old American has eight goals in his last three games after going the previous nine without finding the net.

#2672. Alexander Ovechkin announces this will be his last NHL season: 'Let's have fun'

Alex Ovechkin's 22nd NHL season will be his last, the Washington Capitals superstar announced on Monday."This is gonna be my last year," Ovechkin told his teammates in a video the Capitals posted to social media. "It's sad, but it is what it is. We have an unbelievable team this year. There are 82 games left. Let's make the playoffs, and let's have fun."

Ovechkin has already established himself as the greatest goal-scorer in hockey history with 929 tallies, and he still has 82 games to add to that total before he hangs up his skates.

The No. 1 overall pick in the 2004 NHL Draft, Ovechkin immediately established himself as a prolific scorer by notching 52 goals en route to winning the Calder Trophy as a rookie.

Since then, Ovechkin has won the Rocket Richard Trophy as the NHL's leading goal-scorer a record nine times. The Capitals legend's resume also features an Art Ross Trophy and three Hart Trophy wins.

The crowning achievement in Ovechkin's illustrious career is leading Washington to its first Stanley Cup in 2017-18. After coming up short in a number of postseasons prior to that, Ovechkin led all playoff performers with 15 goals and won the Conn Smythe Trophy as a result.

Following the 2025-26 season, there was speculation that Ovechkin could retire, but he signed an incentive-laden one-year deal with the Caps.Sensing that this could be Ovechkin's final season, the Capitals loaded up to give their franchise icon one more shot at the Stanley Cup. Washington signed former Buffalo Sabres winger Alex Tuch in free agency and acquired winger Jordan Kyrou from the St. Louis Blues via trade.

No team is as loaded on the wings as the Capitals, and they have one of the best rosters in the Metro Division. Washington has the ingredients to challenge the defending Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes and get Ovechkin one more ring before he rides off into the sunset.

Despite Michael Olise and Manuel Neuer both taking part in Bayern Munich's final training session ahead of Tuesday's Champions League away clash against Atletico Madrid, it remains unclear whether – and to what extent – either player will feature.

Olise, who was forced off in the second half of Saturday's 2-2 draw with Borussia Dortmund, trained with his knee bandaged on Monday. Meanwhile, Neuer returned to team training after missing the previous three games due to a foot problem.
