#2669. NBA rumors: Injury-plagued Thunder eyeing player 'they've already had,' and one surging star makes most sense

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Last season, a total of 11 players gave the Oklahoma City Thunder at least 900 minutes of service. Three of those players now play for other teams: Lu Dort, Aaron Wiggins and Isaiah Joe. Two of them, Jalen Williams and Cason Wallace, have already suffered injuries that may end their seasons. Another, Alex Caruso, has a sprained ankle. For Wednesday's game against the Dallas Mavericks, Chet Holmgren is also out with right knee patellar tendinitis and Ajay Mitchell is questionable with a right ankle sprain.

In other words, most of Oklahoma City's core rotation from a year ago, aside from Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, is not available right now. Inevitably, that has sparked quite a bit of speculation. The Thunder are as asset-rich as any team in the NBA. They have the picks to go trade for a difference-maker and a roster spot to add a free agent. The question here is who, and on Wednesday, ESPN's Brian Windhorst stirred the pot with an intentionally cryptic rumor.

"And this is one thing that I've talked to executives about, and I don't mean to be cryptic, but I'm being cryptic," he said on his Hoop Collective podcast. "If you're going to, if they're going to acquire a player, it would not be a surprise if they acquire a player they've already had."

This makes plenty of sense on paper. The Thunder are very particular about their culture. Bringing in someone new is far riskier than reacquiring someone they already know, and given their asset surplus, they can afford to be picky. Given Windhorst's track record of cryptic reporting leading to seismic transactions, let's take a look around the league to see which former Thunder players, if any, make sense as reacquisition targets.

The Thunder traded Dort, Joe and Wiggins last offseason. Given how things have played out, Oklahoma City may regret doing so, and given this rumor cycle, fans will inevitably call for them to try to reacquire one of last season's core pieces. Alas, Dort, Joe and Wiggins are functionally not obtainable to the Thunder. The NBA does not allow teams to reacquire players they have traded until the following season. That means Dort, Joe and Wiggins are off limits for now.

There is a very narrow exception to this rule, but it is not likely to come up. If the player is traded a second time and then gets waived, the original team can re-sign him upon clearing waivers. This happened with Mike Conley and the Minnesota Timberwolves last season. Of course, no team is likely to waive Dort, Joe or Wiggins, so we should assume for the sake of argument that they are off the table.

The Thunder have been so well-run for so long that the NBA is now littered with extremely accomplished Thunder alumni. Of course, these players are, in most cases, either so expensive that they would be impractical for Oklahoma City's purposes or so vital to their existing teams that they likely are not functionally available. So let's roll through those players now:

The players listed above are all currently under contract with teams trying to win today. There are, however, quite a few famous Thunder alumni who are theoretically much more gettable. Four stand out:

A reporter asked general manager Sam Presti on Monday about potentially bringing back retired team legend Russell Westbrook. Presti gave a typical non-answer. Fans would certainly love to see Westbrook in a Thunder uniform again, but the question here is whether he'd be able to accept a small enough role for this to be worthwhile. Westbrook, who announced his retirement in August, is a high-usage player whose value is mostly derived from having the ball in his hands. His issues as a shooter are well-documented, and while he's capable of the sort of intense on-ball defense the Thunder prefer, he's never been consistent as a team defender. All in all, Westbrook is probably just too high-maintenance an addition given what the Thunder could expect out of a 37-year-old.

The point guard Westbrook was once traded for, Chris Paul, makes a bit more sense. He and Gilgeous-Alexander thrived together during the 2019-20 season. However, Paul fell off a cliff during his brief return to the Clippers last season, and he's a notoriously demanding locker-room presence. He's now 41 and has shown no interest in playing in the NBA again after announcing his retirement in February, so we can probably cross him off the list.

Here's a sneaky one: Victor Oladipo. He spent this offseason trying to fight his way back onto an NBA roster. The Sacramento Kings worked him out, but did not sign him. He has not played since the 2022-23 season, but is still only 34. The healthy version of him fit into Oklahoma City's defensive culture, and after several years out of the league, he'd likely be happy with any role the Thunder could offer him.

The only non-guard in this section: Al Horford. The Thunder, again, have plenty of front-court depth. If they did elect to trade one of their bigs for help elsewhere, though, Horford is still useful in a smaller role and the Golden State Warriors simply aren't competitive enough to turn away offers for players in their 40s. The Thunder have several trade exceptions big enough to fit Horford, and his salary is just below the $6.9 million in second-apron space they currently have available.

Any of these three players theoretically could have landed in one of the last two categories. For reasons I'll explain, I wanted to separate them:

George is more expensive than any player we've covered thus far. The only scenario in which this would make sense is one in which the Thunder trade Jalen Williams to Boston (along with a few other contracts, for the sake of legality). That, obviously, is enormously unlikely. It just isn't so crazy that it should be taken off the table altogether. The Celtics already showed a willingness to take a step back this season in the name of the longer view when they traded Jaylen Brown for George in the first place. The Thunder, however, have much more at stake this season given their impending financial cliff. George, with his player option, could actually help on that front by potentially renegotiating a slightly longer deal that suits the Thunder's needs. There would have to be draft picks going to Oklahoma City, and George would have to be willing to take a team-friendly contract that pays him less than Williams is due next season. But if you squint hard enough, you can see something that sort of makes sense here.

The Thunder traded Giddey in part because his shooting made him an iffy off-ball fit next to Gilgeous-Alexander. Well, Giddey has made at least 38% of his catch-and-shoot 3s since coming to Chicago. The Bulls have a new front office that didn't bring Giddey in, and he's struggled to start this season. That doesn't mean they'll give up on him, but it means he could be gettable at the right price. Alas, price is the biggest hurdle here. The Thunder have no obvious way to cobble together the $25 million in tradable salary they'd need to match Giddey's contract without incurring an untenable first-apron hard cap. This would have to be a part of something bigger we can't foresee, so it's unlikely, but if the Thunder do something surprising, there might be a pathway here.

The Thunder could fit him into the trade exception they have leftover from sending out Dort, though they'd have to shed money elsewhere to duck the second apron. Schröder would likely be gettable for second-round picks later in the season (especially if Charlotte rookie Christian Anderson shows he can handle real minutes), and he'd simply be a spare ball-handler on point-of-attack pest defensively. He wouldn't have a big role in Oklahoma City, but the Thunder know him and what he brings to the table. Truthfully, though, the Thunder would probably just prefer to stick with what they have... unless things get worse.

Alright, we've spent the bulk of this story writing about players who wouldn't fit. Let's talk about the players who could. There are two standouts here:

The Thunder ironically chose Dieng one selection ahead of Williams in the 2022 NBA Draft, but Williams outplayed him and Dieng could never find a role in a crowded Thunder rotation. That rotation is less crowded now, especially at forward, and Dieng took advantage of all of the extra playing time he got for the Milwaukee Bucks after the trade deadline last season. Dieng has held a much smaller role for the Bucks this season, so he's theoretically gettable. He can't be traded until Dec. 15 because he just signed a free agent contract, but the Thunder likely don't want to rush into a move anyway.

This is the likeliest big swing on the table for Oklahoma City, if any is even possible. Jerome is in the middle of a breakout season for the Memphis Grizzlies and could be well on his way to an All-Star selection. He's also 29, has serious durability concerns, and is functionally on an expiring contract considering his player option. If the Grizzlies view this as a flash in the pan, or a chance to sell high on someone they don't want to give a big contract to next summer, the Thunder could be their chance. His cap figure is only around $9 million, so he's very obtainable. His shooting makes him an easy fit on any roster, and the Thunder have quite a bit of experience managing the workloads of high-impact players with durability concerns like Alex Caruso.

Jerome is a bit duplicative of Ajay Mitchell, but beggars can't be choosers. If the Thunder have to reorient their roster more around offense to maintain this season's title window, they should do so. Oklahoma City has enough of a draft surplus to trade for even an expensive rental. The question simply comes down to whether or not the Grizzlies view Jerome as a long-term fixture or a pleasant surprise they're willing to cash out. The former is likelier, but we can't rule out the latter.

#2666. Tyrese Haliburton becomes latest injured NBA star: Pacers guard 'week-to-week' with hamstring strain

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Tyrese Haliburton's return to the Pacers lineup after missing the entire 2025-26 season with an Achilles tear has hit a speed bump, as the All-Star guard deals with a hamstring strain four games into the year.

Pacers coach Rick Carlisle said Wednesday that after meeting with doctors, Haliburton would be considered "week-to-week" with his hamstring strain and is unlikely to play in the next two weeks.

"It's not good news, but it could be worse," Carlisle told reporters (via the Indianapolis Star).

Haliburton, who sat out all of last season after suffering a torn Achilles in Game 7 of the 2025 NBA Finals, has been terrific for the Pacers in his return to the court, averaging 21.8 points, 9.5 assists and 4.5 rebounds per game on 51.6/37.0/86.7 shooting splits over Indiana's first four games. After hitting some clutch shots in the opener, Haliburton was overcome with emotion thinking about his journey back to the basketball court, and now he will have to find that patience once again as he waits for his hamstring to heal enough to play again.

The Pacers will be without Haliburton for a big game on Wednesday night against the 76ers, with games against the Heat, Nets and Hawks up on the schedule over the next week.

Indiana will try to navigate that stretch not only without their star guard, but with Ivica Zubac and TJ McConnell as players also listed as out on Wednesday's injury report, while Andrew Nembhard is questionable with a neck/back injury.

That's a considerable amount of Indiana's guard depth that either can't play or will be playing at less than 100 percent, along with their top center. That shifts Pascal Siakam back into a lead role offensively and forces the Pacers into more small-ball lineups with Obi Toppin at the five.

For a team trying to get back into the conversation in the Eastern Conference after a lost season in 2025-26, seeing injuries pile up early in the year is extremely frustrating and disheartening. The Pacers were a half of basketball away from winning a championship when Haliburton tore his Achilles in Game 7 against the Thunder and have spent more than a year waiting to get him back to try to make the climb again.

While Carlisle noted in a radio interview on Wednesday morning the hope was Haliburton's hamstring wouldn't be a long-term injury, soft tissue injuries always bring some concern. The Pacers will have to balance patience with the desire to not fall too far behind in a suddenly stacked East.

Haliburton's injury continues a frustrating trend in the early NBA season, which has seen a tremendous number of top players listed on injury reports. The list of stars currently on the shelf with injuries is staggering, with the likes of Anthony Edwards, Jalen Williams, Paolo Banchero, Kawhi Leonard, Jaren Jackson Jr., Chet Holmgren and Alperen Sengun all currently listed out for games on Wednesday night. That's not to mention players like Brandon Ingram, Jimmy Butler, Kon Knueppel and Kristaps Porzingis who have yet to make their season debuts.

While it feels like an absurd number of injuries this early in the season, it's much closer to par for the course than the NBA would probably like to admit. Stars being injured has become a constant concern in recent years, but there isn't an obvious solution.

The NBA schedule is often discussed as a reason for the volume of injuries, but this early in the season, it's hard to point to the wear-and-tear of an 82-game grind. Instead, it feels more like a byproduct of a style of play that pushes players to their limits. The speed of the game is tremendous now and players are pushing their bodies to play faster and more explosively, which raises the potential for injuries.

That's an even harder thing to solve than schedule reform -- which the league and players aren't particularly interested in -- because playing with pace and maximizing possessions is proven to be the most effective style in the modern era.

#2665. Will Wade is back coaching at LSU and starts second stint with a season-opening victory

BATON ROUGE, La. (AP) — Will Wade's second act at LSU started on Tuesday night — 1,697 days after his first ended.

Wade was fired on March 12, 2022, just as the NCAA sent LSU formal notice of allegations and later found him guilty of five major recruiting violations.

After a year off, two seasons at McNeese State and one at North Carolina State, Wade is off and running in his LSU sequel. He finally got a 14-man roster cleared, and has already assembled a No. 1-ranked recruiting class for 2027-28 by both 247sports.com and On3.com.

On Tuesday night, he won his regular-season opener, 100-57, in front of 7,919 win-starved fans at the Pete Maravich Assembly Center after consecutive 3-15 Southeastern Conference seasons and 14-18 and 15-17 overall marks under former coach Matt McMahon.

"We're not back for the nostalgia or any of that. We're back to win," the 43-year-old Wade said. "We're back to dominate. We're back to build a championship-caliber program."

Wade won the SEC regular-season championship in his second season of his first stint at LSU in the 2018-19 season at 25-5 overall and 15-2. The team reached the NCAA Tournament Sweet 16, but he couldn't attend because of being suspended by LSU amid reports of cheating and him not cooperating with LSU's or the NCAA's investigation.

He got LSU into two more NCAA Tournaments, but he was fired before the second.

"I would say we're determined to put a good product on the court and something people can be proud of," Wade said.

LSU led LSU-New Orleans 53-17 at the half Tuesday night and got its lead to 50 points in the second half at 68-18. LSU led by as many as 54 at 84-30 with 9:07 to play.

"It was a solid first outing," Wade said.

Donovan Dent, a fifth-year senior transfer from UCLA, led all scorers with 19 points and 10 assists. Five other Tigers scored in double figures, including three who were playing professionally overseas earlier this year.

Michael Ruzic, a 7-foot freshman who played professionally in Catalonia, Spain, and is from Zadar, Croatia, had 17 points and six rebounds.

Forward Saliou Niang, formerly of a pro team in Bologna, Italy, and a native of Dakar, Senegal, in West Africa, finished with 14 points and 14 rebounds. And 6-11 center Brice Dessert, a former pro in Istanbul, Turkey, and a native of Pontoise, France, added 13 points and seven rebounds.

Guard Abdi Bashir Jr., a senior transfer from Kansas State, scored 11 points. And, Mo Dioubate, a senior forward transfer from Kentucky, scored 10 points.

"It's been a long time coming from the summer time," Dioubate said. "It was only four of us at a point. And now we've got our whole team. We've just been ready to go. We've got all the tools to get it done. We're going to shock everyone."

And Wade is only just beginning … for the second time.

"This was just one step in what we're trying to do," he said. "We want to start building a program that can compete on the championship level again."

#2662. Jacob Misiorowski wraps breakout Brewers year with World Series title and a reminder that best is yet to come

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. -- When the Brewers took the field for Game 5 of the World Series, they did so with their ace on regular rest. All that stood between them and their first World Series championship was a win with the best possible formula that they could draw up on the lineup card.

If there was any question, it was if Misiorowski could channel some of his early season magic. In the playoffs, he hadn't been bad, but hadn't been nearly as dominant as in the regular season. He also hadn't gone more than five innings in a start.

He stepped up, as championship-caliber athletes do. He was forced to leave the game late in the sixth inning due to calf cramp, but the Brewers already had a 4-0 lead (the eventual final score) and handed things off to their elite bullpen on cruise control. Misiorowski came through with 5 ⅔ innings of scoreless ball, allowing only two hits. He stifled the Rays until the game felt like it was elementary. Only two pitchers have ever recorded a scoreless start of 5+ innings with two or fewer hits allowed in a potential World Series clincher: Misiorowski and some guy named Tom Glavine in 1995.

And behind their ace, the inevitable Brewers are World Series champions.

"It's awesome," Misiorowski said on the field after the Brewers clinched. "It's awesome for this team, it's awesome for the city of Milwaukee. I just made it work. It didn't matter how we won tonight, just that we won."

There were questions in the aftermath of Game 4 about whether Brewers manager Pat Murphy should have brought Misiorowski in for the bottom of the 12th to close things out. There shouldn't have been. It wasn't Game 7. The Brewers were up 3-0 in the series. Losing Game 4 meant they had full-strength Misiorowski waiting to close the door in Game 5. Unsurprisingly, he did exactly that, despite likely being on fumes from his 2026 workload.

In 2025, Misiorowski only worked 141 ⅓ innings between the minors, majors and playoffs. That was a career high in his professional career. In 2026, he finishes with 193 ⅔. It's a monster leap, and it's why the Brewers held his workloads in check down the stretch. They needed something left in the tank to achieve the ultimate goal. That was the plan all along: for him to do exactly what he did in Game 5.

And we're only scratching the proverbial surface here. Remember what a phenom Misiorowski was in the regular season, especially early in the year? He was the must-see player in the sport. Even with his workload monitored, he finished the season with a ridiculous 1.80 ERA (leading the majors) and 252 strikeouts (again, leading the majors) in 174 ⅔ innings. He also led the majors in WHIP, strikeout rate and had the lowest hit rate.

Between his rookie season and this year, "The Miz" ratcheted up his strikeout rate, plummeted his walk rate, improved his efficiency and, early in the year before workload became a concern, worked much deeper into games. As a rookie, he was a talent to dream on. As a sophomore, he was the dream. He's already as decorated as any pitcher the Brewers have ever had (with the Brewers, that is).

Now, let's keep a few things in mind. Misiorowski is:

After the Brewers swept the Dodgers in the NLCS, Murphy remarked on how they don't have a bunch of Hall of Famers, an indirect shot at Los Angeles' star-studded lineup, but there's an argument that Misiorowski has a strong foundation right now (so does Jackson Chourio, by the way).

Given the improvements that Misiorowski made from Year 1 to Year 2 in the majors, there's every reason to expect that next year he'll be just as good, only he'll have built up more stamina for late in the season.

Could he go 200 innings in the regular season next year and lead the Brewers to back-to-back championships while winning a second Cy Young? I don't see why not. That would have sounded like a pipe dream to Brewers fans if we got in a time machine to the aftermath of last year's sweep at the hands of those dastardly, mega-payroll Dodgers. But, you see, Misiorowski just had a dream season. With a guy with his level of talent, the only answer is to dream bigger.

#2656. INTERVIEW: Philipp Lahm senses Harry Kane would trade Ballon d'Or for Champions League glory

MÜNCHEN (Bulinews) Former Bayern Munich star Philipp Lahm, speaking at a media round attended by Bulinews.com, was delighted with Harry Kane’s Ballon d’Or triumph but feels the striker would trade it in for top honours in Europe.

“It’s a personal award. I think [winning it] is more important for the offensive players rather than the rest. So, [someone like ex-Bayern star] Franck Ribery will be happy Kane won the Ballon d’Or.

“We all know how important the FC Bayern team is for Kane’s success too. Since I never had the chance to win this award, as a captain I think more of the team as a whole.

“I think Harry Kane would exchange his Ballon d’Or for a Champions League title. Most players grew up playing as a team from a very young age,” Lahm explained, alluding to the collective aspect of football teams.

Interestingly, the 2014 World Cup winner went on to explain why he feels it is difficult to win the Ballon d’Or as a German playing in the domestic top-flight. His theory is largely linked to external noise and catching the public eye.

“As for Kane and Michael Olise [ranked 9th in the Ballon d’Or], they came from another country. I think it’s quite difficult for a German player playing in the Bundesliga to win this award. Think of Florian Wirtz for example.

“It’s all about the attention. When you are successful with the German national team then you become visible. Then when you play successful football for a club like Liverpool, the attention in the UK is much bigger.

“That’s important for this award. It [less attention] makes it more difficult for a player to win it in the Bundesliga rather than changing to another league [and club]. But I do hope the best players stay in the Bundesliga.

“I hope with players like Harry Kane that a lot of other players will follow now it’s possible to win [the Ballon d’Or playing in the Bundesliga],” Lahm concluded, underlining his hope that others may be inspired by the Englishman.

#2655. Buyers, sellers or fence-sitters? All 32 NFL teams slotted before the trade deadline

NFC East: Cowboys | Giants | Eagles | Commanders NFC North: Bears | Lions | Packers | Vikings NFC South: Falcons | Panthers | Saints | Buccaneers NFC West: Cardinals | Rams | 49ers | Seahawks

AFC East: Bills | Dolphins | Patriots | Jets AFC North: Ravens | Bengals | Browns | Steelers AFC South: Texans | Colts | Jaguars | Titans AFC West: Broncos | Chiefs | Raiders | Chargers

Where does your team sit as the NFL's trade deadline fast approaches?

Not all needy teams will swing trades prior to Nov. 10, but some certainly will look. On the other end of the spectrum, not all out-of-contention teams will hold fire sales, but with the recent spate of big names moving, there are opportunities to sell now and cash in later.

And, as we know, some teams will sit idly by as the deadline comes and goes. The NFL might be as active, trade-wise, as it has ever been in-season, but not every team is willing to pay the asking prices they're hearing.

Here's how we view all 32 teams, slotting each of them into one of three categories — buyers, fence-sitters and sellers — prior to the trade deadline. Teams are roughly ordered within each section by their perceived fits: strongest at the top, weakest at the bottom.

The Bills are the top seed in the AFC in spite of a defense that clearly needs help. Sunday's blowout of the Ravens notwithstanding, that unit isn't as likely to perform to that level against top-tiered quarterbacks and offenses. There are questions about how much the Bills want to give up in any prospective trade, and they're hamstrung a bit right now by salary-cap space (less than $4 million), but that can be rectified if needed. Safety might be the biggest position of need, although they also could look for extra pass-rush help.

Defensive tackle DaVon Hamilton suffered a torn quadriceps in Sunday's win over the Colts and will miss the rest of the season. It's hard to understate how big a blow this is. Head coach Liam Coen said the Jags will take a committee approach to replacing Hamilton, but finding a nose tackle is easier than finding other positions, so it would not be surprising to see them try to add a plugger up front. Safety is another spot they could consider. The Jaguars (5-2) are steamrolling toward a division title, and are in the hunt for the AFC's top seed. There's no better time to go for it.

They're already buyers after the DeForest Buckner trade, and they might not be done. They reportedly reached out to the Vikings about Jauan Jennings before they found out Jennings wasn't interested in a return. But receiver figures to be a position they consider upgrading, along with edge rusher and possibly cornerback. The 49ers have to be very cautious with Mike Evans; they've been a vastly better team with him on the field. Adding WR insurance, given all the injuries there, feels like a low-risk move that's on the table.

Their first buy of trade season, Jeffery Simmons, sunk his teeth into the Seahawks on Monday night. It's the kind of move that turned a very good team into a downright scary one. You can't blame the Bears if that's all general manager Ryan Poles gets done prior to the deadline, but the one area of concern coming out of the Seattle game had to be cornerback. Jaylon Johnson and Tyrique Stevenson both had rough nights with Malik Muhammad out, so we expect Poles to work the phones for CB help. They also could look for a pass-rush addition, with old friend Khalil Mack a name often bandied about these days. The Bears appear to be in Super Bowl mode now. They're out shopping.

The Vikings' offense could keep them from a Super Bowl, so they figure to seek help on that side of the ball — specifically a running back or an offensive guard. The run game has slowed down, and Aaron Jones Sr. has battled knee issues. The Vikings really could use more of a workhorse to complement Jones and Jordan Mason. They've also been connected to some pass rushers, scary as that sounds for opponents.

The Chiefs are stricken by limited salary cap space, but they figure to look and see what's out there. Wide receiver is the biggest area of concern — again — with Tyquan Thornton out for the season and Rashee Rice seemingly dealing with chronic soft-tissue issues. General manager Brett Veach has a decent history of smaller-to-medium deadline moves, so you can't rule anything out here. They also could mine for pass-rush help, but that might be tougher to find — and afford.

The primary need appears to be on defense, a unit that started strong but has tailed off. The Bengals could use help at multiple spots, although cornerback figures to be the most concerning, especially after watching Cam Ward pick them apart Sunday. A coverage linebacker and another pass rusher would be nice, too. On offense, if there's a need, it's at running back. They're averaging 3.7 yards per rush, with a long run of 15 yards this season.

Dallas is 3-5 yet still in the hunt for how poor the NFC East is. Team owner Jerry Jones says the Cowboys remain on the lookout for more help, and though they had been historically quiet at the trade deadline, Jones backed up his talk with last year's deadline deal for Quinnen Williams and the earlier-season trade for Joey Porter Jr. The Cowboys' defense is getting manhandled now. They badly need pass-rush help, but another corner would also be nice. Then again, so could more LB help. Jones said they won't want to flush more draft picks on a player who isn't under contract long term, but they might be desperate enough to add wherever they can.

The Patriots remain in contention at 5-3 (and a 3-0 mark in the division), but they could have concerns on both sides of the ball. On offense, they could use guard reinforcements after Alijah Vera-Tucker and Mike Onwenu landed on injured reserve. On defense, pass-rush help probably tops the list, but they also could seek LB and DB depth. Following the major A.J. Brown trade this summer, it would be surprising if the Patriots relinquished major draft assets. Any moves they make figure to be on the lower-compensation side, perhaps for a veteran's expiring contract.

Detroit fans have let general manager Brad Holmes know they want action prior to the deadline, especially after seeing the 49ers, Seahawks and Bears add starters last week. The Lions' defense is the biggest concern by far. The injuries to LBs Jack Campbell and Jimmy Rolder have left a big hole in the middle. Safety is in better shape with Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph back, but cornerback remains problematic. Pass-rush help also could be addressed. Can Holmes find the right help in the next week?

After adding Rashid Shaheed last year and Quenton Nelson this year, we know the Seahawks are open for business this time of year. Did Monday's home blowout loss to the Bears change their level of aggression? A struggling run game is an area the Seahawks could seek to help, although Zach Charbonnet's return could make them look elsewhere. They could try to add one more pass rusher and possibly another receiver for an offense that has been too JSN-dependent.

The Giants have found themselves atop the NFC East, and their first in-season trade for QB J.J. McCarthy has borne some early fruit. Could that move portend another (or others) if the Giants keep finding ways to win? Possibly. We know that John Harbaugh personally called Titans owner Amy Adams Strunk about Jeffery Simmons, but that call went to voicemail and Simmons went to Chicago. Defensive tackle figures to be the spot most likely to be addressed, but don't rule out a cheaper running back to stabilize that shakier position.

The Steelers already have been sellers, trading CB Joey Porter Jr. to the Cowboys. But sitting in first place in the AFC North in what's roundly expected to be Aaron Rodgers' final season, the Steelers might try to get back to buying. Not coincidentally, they could use a cornerback. Safety and wide receiver also could be spots they seek to upgrade. This doesn't feel like a team, however, that's prepared to go broke for that proverbial one final move.

They were close to being labeled "fence-sitters" after Sunday's breakout from RB Jonah Coleman. Running back had been the position that seemed most in need of being addressed prior to Coleman's big game Sunday. Now that feels like a luxury. Their most likely target position, if they try to swing a deal, figures to be offensive line or tight end.

This felt like an all-in season at one point, but that was before Myles Garrett and Davante Adams got hurt and the team started 2-4. The Rams have since evened their record at .500, but several tough games remain. The Rams certainly could be active, and another receiver certainly would help, but they've already depleted their trade assets significantly with the Garrett deal and don't have a ton to give up. They might want to add some help, but can the Rams realistically make an impact trade in time? It's unclear.

They've had some recent tailwind as a team, they've gotten Josh Jacobs back and Micah Parsons' return appears to be on the horizon. They also have some possible needs, including cornerback, if they can find the right trade partner. On the other hand, they've just been so historically quiet around the deadline under GM Brian Gutekunst (they actually have been more deadline sellers than anything), that I wonder if they'll do much.

The Texans have already bought, adding WR Marvin Harrison Jr., but is more coming? There are questions in the offensive and defensive backfields, and they continue to struggle to get the offensive line fully right. All those spots are possible. But the Texans are 2-5 and falling farther behind the first-place Jaguars. If Houston makes a move, expect it to be more on the minor end.

How seriously are the Browns taking their 5-3 start, especially after the humbling loss to first-place Pittsburgh? There are plenty of areas they could address, ample draft assets to part with and a general manager in Andrew Berry who has been among the most active in-season traders. But if the Browns don't feel this team has a legitimate chance to make playoff noise, they might be wise to keep their assets and load up more in the offseason. Browns fans would be giddy at a deadline deal, but patience might be preferred.

The Raiders feel like they are in no-man's land. They pulled back to .500 after losing four straight, but is Vegas capable of contending? The big drama now feels like when the Raiders will move off of Kirk Cousins and give the reins to Fernando Mendoza. There might be a case for the Raiders as sellers, with Cousins perhaps an intriguing piece for a team such as the Ravens that recently lost its starting QB. Other possible trade figures include Jackson Powers-Johnson and Adam Butler, but it also feels like the Raiders could ride things out without any major transactions the rest of the way.

The Panthers are a strange team to handicap. Carolina has clear needs, but at 3-4, with two straight losses, is it in position to add help? Oh, and did we mention that record puts the Panthers in first place? The playoffs are still very much a possibility, but this team being one or two moves away from being a Super Bowl contender is a stretch. If the Panthers add somewhere, cornerback feels like the most likely spot. Anything they do likely would have to be more than just a short-term rental at retail price.

Most of the NFC South profiles similarly to Carolina. There's a real shot at winning the division, but at what cost? There's also the chance the Bucs could look to sell, with names such as Yaya Diaby, A'Shawn Robinson and Chris Godwin Jr. being floated. But GM Jason Licht has not made an in-season trade since Tom Brady was QB, and it feels like the chances are greater that the Bucs do nothing.

They're 3-5 and 1-2 in the division, yet Atlanta has enough explosive potential offensively to be potential buyers. Even after Michael Penix Jr.'s four-INT game, the Falcons might think they have a real shot of taking the division. The receiver depth is light, and there are still holes to patch on defense, although they might treat the return of James Pearce Jr. from suspension as their big pre-deadline addition.

I'd put the Saints more in the "sellers" bin, sitting at 2-5 with team owner Gayle Benson already having aired her grievances with the team's performance publicly. A loss to the Browns this weekend might push them closer to moving some pieces. The question is about what players might be available and sought by other teams. If another team wanted Alvin Kamara or Cameron Jordan, the Saints would almost have to sell. Otherwise, there just aren't a lot of tradable assets that might tempt other teams.

The Jets certainly could be sellers, with the season again slipping away and the focus continuing to shift to what could be one of the franchise's biggest offseasons, armed with three first-round draft picks — with all three currently in the top 10. Adding to that should be a consideration. Garrett Wilson and Breece Hall are two big names that could be on the move, but to this point they've publicly pushed back against dealing either. If they are active, I expect lower-profile pieces such as Harrison Phillips or Nahshon Wright to be more likely than the bigger names.

The Commanders kept their season alive in the watered-down NFC East with a win over the Eagles on Sunday night, and there's a chance they could be lighter buyers if they can find a running back who fits their short- and long-term vision. They also could be sellers, with pass rusher K'Lavon Chaisson the most logical piece to try to move. It's hard to get a clear read on what GM Adam Peters wants to do, but he said he's talked to all 31 teams and continues to work the phones.

The Colts have already sold off two major assets in Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner. There's not much stopping them from continuing to put other players up for sale. WR Josh Downs has reportedly requested a trade and figures to be in play in the coming days. RB Jonathan Taylor might cost too much to be moved before the deadline, but the Colts are acting like a team just waiting for a bigger offer to pull the trigger. Lacking a first-round pick in 2027, the Colts need all the draft-pick help they can get.

For years, GM Howie Roseman has been about the most aggressive talent hunter out there come deadline time. This season, following a string of poor developments and six straight losses, the Eagles look far more like sellers on the outside. There is no shortage of players the Eagles could move. They have several expiring-contract candidates, including TE Dallas Goedert, CB Riq Woolen, WR Marquise Brown, DT Moro Ojomo and others. There also are players under contract beyond 2026 who could be available, including OG Landon Dickerson and Edge Nolan Smith. They've already made one trade and could be open for more business with this season apparently shot.

The Chargers have continued to hoard assets for now, but as the league's final winless team, it's worth wondering what they're waiting for. GM Joe Hortiz was turning away calls at one point because the team believed a turnaround was coming. It was not. If they finally become sellers, Khalil Mack figures to be an easy piece to move — a veteran pass rusher on an expiring deal. Teams seeking nose tackle help should probably call on Dalvin Tomlinson. WR Quentin Johnston also could be available if the team doesn't think he can reach his ceiling there. There are deals to be made if the Chargers shift their thinking.

The Dolphins are not making the playoffs this year, although it's reasonable to be encouraged by their competitiveness. Still, this is a sell-off phase for the Dolphins if they can cook up some interest in players such as Zach Sieler, Austin Jackson, Josh Uche or others. The problem is that Miami's roster is already so heavily loaded with rookies and minimum-salary players that there are only so many assets to move. But the Dolphins gladly will vacuum up any draft picks other teams are willing to fork over in this multiyear rebuild.

Shipping out well-liked Jeffery Simmons was a sign that the Titans are in sell-now mode. RB Tony Pollard is probably their most tradable piece, but it's not clear if they want to move him. Anyone can have WR Calvin Ridley for a song, if they want. Edge Jermaine Johnson II also might be a name you hear this week after picking him up from the Jets this offseason. This might not be a fire sale, per se, but they're apparently open for business.

Even after Sunday's dramatic win in Dallas, the Cardinals feel more like sellers than buyers, having already shipped out Marvin Harrison Jr. and sitting at fourth place in one of the toughest divisions. If a QB-needy team wants Jacoby Brissett, the team shouldn't hesitate trading him, especially after benching him for Gardner Minshew in the dramatic comeback. Pass rusher Josh Sweat feels like the biggest player who most reasonably could be moved now, although Budda Baker's name has also come up. They have some assets that could be moved, but will the Cardinals act on that?

In a single moment, when Lamar Jackson suffered his thumb injury against the Bills, the Ravens might have gone from buyers to sellers. The one exception might be at QB, where the Ravens could opt to swing a trade, be it for someone like Kirk Cousins or perhaps Bears backup Tyson Bagent, who played last year with Ravens OC Declan Doyle. But if the Ravens lose Thursday, they might consider moving a few players, including Marlon Humphrey, Mark Andrews and Roquan Smith.

#2653. In Class AA girls' soccer final, Bethlehem outlasts Ballston Spa in PKs

LATHAM - First-year Bethlehem girls' soccer coach Scott Geis spent plenty of time getting his team ready for a potentially season-deciding slate of penalty kicks.

Tuesday night at Shaker High School, that work paid off.

The Eagles played to a thrilling 1-1 draw with Ballston Spa after 110 minutes in the Section 2 Class AA championship game, but Bethlehem stamped its ticket to the state tournament, advancing 4-2 on penalty kicks.

"We practice it non-stop," Geis said. "We practice it with me in the goal. … I would shout, 'Hey, this is the most important shot you've ever taken.' Just pressure, pressure, pressure - and, each time, they laughed it off, they breathed through it and they put it home just like they did today."

No. 2 seed Bethlehem (10-4-4 overall) got a huge momentum burst to start the PKs when junior goalie Kinley Logsdon made a diving save to deny Ballston Spa's first shooter, Abby Werner.

It was Logsdon's first-ever round of PKs in high school, but she's been through them at the club level.

"I know the pressure," she said. "I know I can deal with it."

The fifth-seeded Scotties (9-5-5 overall) were also denied in PKs when Charlotte Haskell's attempt hit the post.

All four Bethlehem players who stepped up to the penalty spot - Maira Braddock, June McCarthy, Mallory Maycrink and Elayna Shersky - calmly converted their attempts.

"As soon as I got it on frame, I knew we had it in the bag," Braddock said. "We've done this so many times in practice. It was just constant repetition. It felt the same. It felt like what we always do."

Ballston Spa coach Tom Rogan, who won 348 games and nine sectional titles during a legendary tenure at Bethlehem, expressed pride in his team's run, but acknowledged the heartbreak of season-ending PKs.

"It's a hard thing. It's almost harder than losing, in a weird sort of way," he said.

Ballston Spa controlled most of the first half, taking the lead on a Haley Wiltsie goal 8:03 before halftime. A spectacular solo effort from Braddock netted the tying goal four minutes into the second half, and the following 36 minutes of regulation and 30 minutes of overtime were a flurry of near-misses on both sides, including a shot off the crossbar by McCarthy late in the first overtime.

"I was up, I was down," Geis said. "I was all over the place. I feel like I lost about 10 years."

Braddock simply wasn't going to be denied the game's tying goal.

Four minutes into the second half, the sophomore standout collected the ball 40 yards from goal and charged down the left wing with a Ballston Spa defender on her hip the entire way. However, Braddock refused to be dispossessed, and when Ballston Spa goalie Avery DiNallo came off her line, Braddock coolly slipped a shot past her that rolled into the side netting to make it 1-1.

"I was definitely fighting for my teammates," Braddock said. "I knew that as soon as we got one, we were back in the game. I just used pure will to get that ball in the back of the net."

That set the stage for a breathless stretch run and Bethlehem's eventual triumph.

Logsdon, the Eagles' junior goalkeeper, was a rock in goal for Bethlehem throughout the night.

After giving up the game's first goal with 8:03 left in the first half, Logsdon and the Bethlehem defense kept Ballston Spa off the board for the final 48 minutes of regulation and another 30 minutes of overtime. Logsdon's performance wasn't marked by a number of highlight-reel saves, but rather by her command of the penalty area and her quick action to cut out dangerous Ballston Spa attacks.

"She was phenomenal," Geis said. "She was everywhere. There must have been three or four real scary breakaway opportunities that she came up with."

In PKs, Logsdon provided the biggest highlight of the night when she dove to her left to deny Werner in the first round and open the door for the Eagles to take charge.

9: Consecutive games without a regulation loss by Ballston Spa to end the season.

7: Years between Section 2 girls' soccer championships for Bethlehem.

Goals allowed by Bethlehem during the Eagles' three Section 2 tournament games.

The Eagles will face Section 3's Fayetteville-Manlius in a NYSPHSAA regional final Saturday at 2:30 p.m. at Stillwater High School.

The Scotties' season has come to an end at 9-5-5.

#2651. Rangers lose star goaltender Igor Shesterkin for season with lower-body injury; what's next for New York?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

#2650. Five ways the NBA's injury outbreak could impact trade season: OKC has work to do, Rockets are in control

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

At a bare minimum we're still six weeks away from the unofficial start of NBA trade season. It's still October, and a bit less than one-third of the league is still not trade-eligible because they signed new contracts in free agency. The moves usually don't begin until Dec. 15, when the bulk of those players become trade-eligible.

The strategizing for those moves, however, is a never-ending process, and even though we've only seen nine days worth of games, the entire league landscape has already been turned on its head by one of the earliest injury outbreaks in NBA history. Let's do a quick roll call: Jalen Williams, Cason Wallace, Jaren Jackson Jr., Tyrese Haliburton, Kawhi Leonard, Anthony Edwards and Paolo Banchero are all out with injuries that should sideline them for weeks or months at best and all season at worst. Their teams suddenly have to figure out how to manage without their best players... but everyone else has to figure out what those absences mean in the long run.

Again... we're barely a week into the season. The market could change drastically again in eight days or eight weeks. We're more than three months away from the deadline. But so much has already happened that it's worth taking a step back and figuring out what this could mean when the deals eventually start coming. Here are five ripple effects the early rash of injuries could have on the trade market.

Think about the trades Oklahoma City tends to make. They're almost always from a position of strength. They traded Paul George to the Clippers when they had them at their mercy during Kawhi Leonard's free agency. They didn't proactively seek out Alex Caruso. They were looking to move Josh Giddey when the perfect role player fell into their laps. They got Jared McCain with a spare first-round pick because Daryl Morey thought he was selling high. The only notable, recent occasion in which the Thunder have added a notable veteran based on an immediate need was Isaiah Hartenstein, who came in free agency. The Thunder typically don't have needs. They develop players to address them before they arise.

Well, because of injuries, the Thunder suddenly do have needs. The bare minimum here is a versatile, forward-sized defender. They tried to steal Spencer Jones from the Nuggets over the summer for this exact purpose. At the time, they likely viewed Jones or Jones-esque defender as a luxury. Now, someone like that is a necessity. Oklahoma City's formerly endless rotation of All-Defense-caliber point-of-attack stoppers is now down to Caruso, who's already sporting an ankle sprain. Their playing style is enormously reliant on this archetype for turnover generation and transition offense.

There are half-court offensive questions as well. We all saw what Victor Wembanyama did to Shai Gilgeous-Alexander without Williams in the Western Conference Finals. Ajay Mitchell is healthy now. He wasn't in that series. How his next few months play out will tell the Thunder whether or not they have to upgrade the offense as well. They can't expect to score on Wembanyama if their offense devolves into nothing but Gilgeous-Alexander mid-range jumpers. Eventually, Alex Caruso is going to miss a playoff 3-pointer.

So for the first time since perhaps the Kevin Durant era, the Thunder, and their endless reserves of assets, go into a trade deadline with obvious needs and an imperative to address them. This roster gets more expensive by the year. The Thunder can't afford to waste a season. Their financial limitations are significant, but Sam Presti is the NBA's best general manager. If there is a way to keep the Thunder up to speed with Wembanyama and the Spurs, he's going to find it.

Oklahoma City's vulnerability trickles down to everyone else. We entered the season assuming a Thunder-Spurs conference finals rematch was inevitable. The Thunder are weakened. The entire rest of the West is one Wembanyama ankle sprain away from 2027 becoming their best chance for the foreseeable future. The Lakers, the Nuggets and the Timberwolves suddenly have far more reason to be aggressive than they did 10 days ago. The problem is that all three of them are working with limited means of improvement:

Minnesota is obviously dealing with the trickiest situation of the three since Edwards is already hurt. They can't justify a win-now move until they have a better sense of how healthy he'll be in the spring. And yet, with Rudy Gobert in his age-34 season and the Thunder more beatable than ever, they might have to roll those dice. Can they really justify holding onto Donte DiVincenzo's contract considering he might not return from his torn Achilles this season, for example? He's someone they hope to keep as a long-term bench fixture. He's also the only notable salary Minnesota can use to add someone who can help now, when the West seems winnable.

The Lakers are starting two minimum-salary wings, and their backup center minutes have been atrocious. The Nuggets are winless against teams besides the Pelicans. These are talented yet flawed teams staring down a future in a conference that features two younger, deeper and better juggernauts. This is an opportunity that may not repeat itself. The ones who take it will be in far better shape than the ones who don't.

The Rockets have the same newfound sense of urgency that the Lakers, Nuggets and Wolves do... under a completely different set of internal circumstances. They have a sizable draft pick surplus. They have salaries of every size to trade. They're also undefeated, including a win over San Antonio that underlined their meaningful advantages in that matchup Alperen Sengun is one of the few bigs in the NBA that tends to enjoy attacking Wembanyama. They have the perimeter defensive depth to handle San Antonio's guards. The Rockets, of those four non-Thunder or Spurs West contenders, probably should feel the best about their ability to win the title right now, with what they already have.

That puts the Rockets where the Thunder usually sit: a position of strength. There's an obvious need to fill when it comes to adding another shot-creator, but their ability to trade for basically anyone across the salary or asset spectrum with the leverage to tell any trade partner "no thanks, we're good enough as is" gives them control of the board. They can outbid just about any rival suitor for just about any theoretically available player if they so choose, effectively giving them right of first refusal over most of the trade landscape unless the Thunder or Spurs are prepared to take on contracts bigger than we'd presently expect.

So much of what's happening in the West starts with Oklahoma City. Those same ripples aren't felt in the East. There, teams are much more concerned with themselves than their competitors.

Take the Raptors. They have RJ Barrett on an expiring contract and a clear need for more shooting. With a healthy Kawhi Leonard, Barrett's individual creation might be a luxury. With him injured, it's a necessity. The Thunder can't really evaluate Barrett's fit on the Leonard-centric version of their team until Leonard returns, and they can't consider whether or not there's a way to flip Barrett into more shooting until they know how important he is to their actual roster.

The Pacers are adapting to playing with a center that cannot shoot 3s. That's a fairly traditional basketball problem, but it's still new to a team that reached the Finals on the strength of its shooting. The Haliburton-Ivica Zubac tandem has only played 52 minutes together thus far, and with Haliburton sidelined, it'll be awhile until Indiana gets a bigger sample than that. Those two are going to be fixtures for the Pacers, but Indiana is still relatively liquid from a draft pick perspective and has serious questions to address on the bench. A clearer idea of where that duo is deficient, if anywhere, would help the Pacers figure out what sort of bench help to target.

And then there's Orlando. Poor, poor Orlando. For the third straight season, Paolo Banchero has suffered a meaningful injury in October or November. In each of the last two seasons, Franz Wagner took on a bigger role while Banchero was out and eventually got hurt himself right around Banchero's return. The Magic are running out of bullets to fire. They've traded most of their picks for Desmond Bane and they've changed coaches by hiring Sean Sweeney. They're headed for a financial crisis with Anthony Black hitting restricted free agency next summer and their total payroll getting dangerously close to the second apron.

The West trade market changed drastically by virtue of what happened to the Thunder. The opposite is true for the East. These teams haven't gotten new information. They're awaiting information they assumed they'd be getting in the early weeks of the season but will instead come further down the line. If the rumors start coming in earlier than expected, you should therefore assume that the West is the conference driving most of that activity.

So we've identified why the West contenders are going to be eager to improve. The East isn't there yet, but give it time. In a conference with no clear favorite, there are usually plenty of teams looking for reinforcements. Here's the problem: we don't know where they're going to get them. The NBA has never had fewer obvious sellers than it does right now.

We're in a post-lottery reform world now. Nobody wants to lose. That's not just true in a single-year setting. There are going to be fewer and fewer teams that proactively initiate multi-year teardowns now that there are slightly more plausible paths to building from the middle. Contenders get stripped for parts every offseason because of the aprons. Teams that might have rebuilt in the past are instead going to attempt to be opportunistic about adding players whose teams can no longer afford them.

Now you throw in all of these injuries. Not only does that create an excess of potential buyers, but it also freezes the potential sellers market because there are inevitably going to be teams that outperform their on-paper talent because the schedule just got a bit easier and teams that should be above them in the standings instead fall short because of absences.

There are only four teams we can confidently call sellers right now: the Kings, Pelicans, Nets and Bucks. If you want an idea of how confident these sellers are in their ability to extract value for their veterans, look at Shamit Dua's reporting on the Pelicans. New Orleans still reportedly wants two first-round picks worth of value for Herb Jones... who is averaging less than 18 minutes per game to start the season.

New Orleans has been notoriously averse to trading its players away under Joe Dumars, but remember, the Nets functioned as buyers this offseason when they added Julius Randle. They have historically held their veterans until they've been offered a premium, most notably Kevin Durant, Mikal Bridges and Cam Johnson. That's something to keep in mind as they consider Michael Porter Jr. offers. The Bucks and Kings are so early into rebuilds that their plans, for now, are a bit of a mystery.

All of this together suggests that the teams that are willing to trade veterans expect to get significant returns for them. There are simply more teams that want to add right now than there are teams that want to subtract. We'll get closer to equilibrium in January and February, but for all of the reasons we've outlined, we'll probably be further from it as a whole than we've been at any point over the last several years at least.

#2648. Jaylen Brown insists he never demanded Celtics trade, pushes back on 'false allegations' from Brian Scalabrine

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The messiest drama in the NBA resides in the Northeast corridor, where new Philadelphia 76ers star Jaylen Brown has yet to reach the stage where bygones can be bygones with his old team, the Boston Celtics.

Brown was floated in trade rumors early in the offseason as the Milwaukee Bucks were trying to trade Giannis Antetokounmpo before ultimately getting dealt to Philly in a stunning in-division deal for Paul George. His old running mate, Jayson Tatum, said he was shocked by the move, which Brown finds hard to believe.

Tatum tried to bury any notion of beef between he and Brown, insisting "this ain't f--kin Shaq and Kobe," but Brown is less eager to move on and said it might not be beef but could be "lamb chops and gravy" between the two former teammates.

Amid all of that, former Celtics player and current Celtics TV analyst Brian Scalabrine tried defending Tatum by claiming on his radio show that Brown asked for a trade and actually gave Boston a list of demands this offseason and wanted to be traded if they weren't met.

Brown's reps called that "10,000% a lie" and Brown was asked about it after the Sixers' win on Wednesday night and elaborated further, via the Philly Voice.

"Yeah, I mean, I guess it is what it is. I saw that. I saw Scal, he made some comments. Never had any issues with Scal. I love Scal, but I guess he's doing what he has to do," Brown said. "I can understand why he feels the need to do that, but I have no interest [in] letting any false allegations [follow] me to my next chapter here in Philadelphia. Never. I never demanded a trade. Never made a list of ultimatums. None of the sort. None of that is true, but as of now, I'm going to just stay focused on what's in front of me here in Philadelphia. I've got a tremendous opportunity, and I'm looking forward to that. So, I'm going to just leave the questions for another time, but during the season, I'm going to just focus on what's in front of me."

This seems to put this weeklong saga to rest for now, but with the Celtics visiting Philadelphia in less than two weeks on Nov. 10, it won't be long before the questions pick up again about what exactly happened that led to Brown's departure.

The reason the questions persist is the Celtics' process for trading Brown felt sloppier and more hurried compared to the more surgical, calculated approach that's been the hallmark of Brad Stevens' tenure in charge in Boston. Brown's name surfaced in the Antetokounmpo talks and then never went away, with reports emerging that Boston was shopping him around the league to anyone who would listen.

Doing that after Brown put together an All-NBA campaign in 2025-26 raised eyebrows, and there has been an assumption around the league that something happened behind the scenes to sour the team-player relationship to the point of no return.

Brown indicates he'll address that at an appropriate time but not during the season. Until then, the speculation will continue about what went down in Boston.

#2647. 2026 NFL trade deadline QB rankings: Mac Jones, Kirk Cousins lead 10 best targets

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026 NFL trade deadline is fast approaching, and already some major deals have come down across the league. For instance, the Chicago Bears just made a blockbuster trade, sending multiple picks (including two first-rounders) to the Tennessee Titans for star defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons. The defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks also landed All-Pro guard Quenton Nelson in a trade with Indianapolis. Those deals may have been the first, but there will certainly be more before the Nov. 10 deadline.

Most of the conversation surrounding the deadline has largely centered around pass rushers, running backs and wide receivers. That said, the quarterback market could also heat up as a few teams across the NFL could be on the hunt for a signal caller. That includes both the Baltimore Ravens and Philadelphia Eagles, who each lost their starting quarterbacks. Then, there's the Minnesota Vikings, who could also eye an upgrade at the position with Kyler Murray struggling despite the team's 6-1 start to the year.

With that in mind, we combed the market and identified 10 veteran quarterbacks who could be available for the right price on the trade market.

Milton is on the active roster of the Eagles after he was signed off of the Cowboys practice squad. He's backing up starter Tanner McKee, who ascended the depth chart in the wake of Jalen Hurts being put on the shelf with blood clots in his lungs. While Philadelphia would lose some depth at the position, Howie Roseman could see shipping away Milton as an opportunity to continue gaining future draft capital, albeit in the Day 3 range.

The 26-year-old was a sixth-round pick of the Patriots in 2024 out of Tennessee and spent his rookie season in New England before he was traded to Dallas in the spring of 2025. He's appeared in five games over the course of his career (one start) and has completed 69.8% of his passes for a 90.4 career passer rating. Milton is still raw, but has ability that could make him an intriguing addition.

Keenum has started games this year for Chicago, so while he may be 38, he has recent starting experience that could be useful for a team looking for a QB. After Caleb Williams and Tyson Bagent got hurt for the Bears earlier this year, Keenum started the club's Week 3 matchup against Philadelphia and impressed. He completed 24-of-34 (70.6%) for 247 yards and two touchdowns, while adding another score on the ground in a 27-7 win over the Eagles.

Keenum also saw some action in Week 5, but the results were not as prolific, completing 11-of-19 for 108 yards and an interception. Still, he's shown an ability to come in and play at a serviceable level, which is really all you can ask for at this time of the year when searching for a quarterback.

Dalton is another notable name who could be had, as he's in a crowded quarterback room with the Atlanta Falcons. The 39-year-old began the year with the Philadelphia Eagles, but was released by the team on Oct. 9. He then signed on with the Falcons, who released Cooper Rush to make room for him on the roster. Dalton is currently in a quarterback room that consists of starter Michael Penix Jr., Tua Tagovailoa, and undrafted rookie Jack Strand.

Dalton made a brief appearance in the Eagles' Week 3 loss to the Bears, attempting one pass that was intercepted. While that doesn't exactly instill a ton of confidence, Dalton is a seasoned veteran who has 16 years and 169 career starts under his belt.

The Colts are blowing it up. They already traded away Nelson and DeForest Buckner, and Jonathan Taylor seems like he could be next if the price is right. If Indy is willing to move that caliber of player, trading Anthony Richardson for any sort of return should be on the table even after benching Daniel Jones late in the Week 8 loss to Jacksonville.

Richardson has been a bust so far for the Colts after they selected him with the fourth overall pick in the 2023 NFL Draft out of Florida. The 24-year-old is 8-7 as a starter and has a career completion percentage of 50.9% to go along with a 68.0 career passer rating. His raw ability and untapped potential could be of interest for a QB-needy team wanting to pick up a lottery ticket. For a rebuilding team like Indianapolis, extracting any value on the roster -- particularly for a player like Richardson, who is going to be a free agent this offseason --  makes too much sense.

Winston is the backup in New York after he lost the starting job to J.J. McCarthy. After Jaxson Dart went down with a season-ending knee injury, Winston initially got the nod and the 12-year veteran largely struggled, despite a 2-1-1 record as the starter. He completed 57% of his throws and had seven passing touchdowns to go with five interceptions over six games played. Most notably, Winston's arm strength appeared diminished, which helped pave the way for McCarthy -- who they acquired in a trade with Minnesota -- to leapfrog him on the depth chart.

While Winston may be past his prime, he's started 13 games over the past three seasons, so he's not the coldest quarterback on the market.

Minshew might be the new QB1 in Arizona, which could eliminate him from this list. However, the Cardinals should eventually see what they have in rookie Carson Beck, so if they can get value for someone like Minshew, it'd be negligent not to pull the trigger. After coming in for the benched Jacoby Brissett, Minshew helped lead Arizona to a fourth-quarter rally against the Cowboys and pulled off the upset win in overtime. The veteran completed 17-of-23 for 188 yards and three touchdowns in the winning effort.

The 30-year-old began his career as a sixth-round pick of the Jaguars in 2019 and has bounced around the league since being traded out of Jacksonville in 2021. In all, Minshew has made stops in Philadelphia, Indianapolis, Las Vegas, and Kansas City before arriving in Arizona, so he is no stranger to jumping into new systems. He's started 47 games over the course of his career and is 17-30 as a starter.

Brissett could be one of the quarterbacks who is truly available on the trade market, especially after he was benched for Minshew against Dallas last week. The 33-year-old started the first eight games of the season for Arizona, owning a 3-5 record while completing 63.3% of his throws and a 79.7 passer rating. Brissett started 12 games for the Cardinals last year and had a 94.1 passer rating, so his production has slipped rather dramatically in 2026, which has since led to him finishing that Week 8 victory on the bench.

If Arizona is going to turn the keys over to Minshew, it makes Brissett expendable, especially with rookie third-round pick Carson Beck waiting in the wings. Brissett has started in 73 games over the course of his career and is 23-50 in those contests.

Caleb Williams is back healthy, which could make Bagent expendable. He was initially the top backup when Williams went down with a hamstring injury earlier this year, but had to give way to Case Keenum as the Week 3 starter after he landed in concussion protocol. Once he was cleared, Bagent did get the nod in Week 4 against New York, where he completed 25-of-34 for 268 yards and an interception.  The following week, he started against the Packers, but was eventually benched for Keenum after completing 57.1% of his throws and two interceptions.

If Chicago feels comfortable with Keenum serving as the primary backup to Williams, Bagent becomes an intriguing trade chip as he's only 26 years old.

Cousins' future in Las Vegas is directly linked to the development of No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza. If the Raiders believe the rookie is ready to ascend atop the depth chart, Cousins becomes expendable on the trade market and maybe the most sought-after quarterback this deadline. After all, he's 4-4 as the Raiders starter, has thrown 19 passing touchdowns, and has a 101.4 passer rating through eight starts. He's had at least two passing touchdowns in seven of his eight games played this season.

In the right situation, Cousins could help a reeling team -- like Baltimore, who just lost Lamar Jackson due to a right thumb injury -- stay afloat in the playoff race.

It's unlikely that he's moved, but if you're ranking veteran quarterbacks who could be traded by the deadline, you have to at least mention Jones. He's arguably the top backup in the NFL, and given how well he filled in for Brock Purdy last year, the Niners would likely need to be blown away to deal him.

In eight starts last season, Jones owned an 8-3 record while completing 69.6% of his throws and averaging 268.9 passing yards per game. He also had a 97.4 passer rating. The former first-round pick has been mentioned in trade rumors in the past, but San Francisco has held a high price, and it's hard to imagine they'd budge now. Still, if a team is looking to truly make a splash, he would likely be atop their wish list.
