#2590. Could Tyson Bagent save Ravens' playoff hopes? Lamar Jackson injury raises a costly trade question

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Ravens are 4-4, Lamar Jackson is headed to injured reserve after undergoing thumb surgery on his throwing hand, and suddenly Baltimore has a much bigger problem than anyone could have imagined even just a few days ago.

Jackson had already missed three games with a high-ankle sprain before returning Sunday against Buffalo, only to injure his thumb on his first play back. Backup Tyler Huntley also left that game with a toe injury; undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano was pressed into action and looked like, well, an undrafted rookie who had taken exactly zero reps with the first team. And with the NFL trade deadline approaching, Baltimore has to decide whether to stick with its current QB room or find help elsewhere.

The Ravens could look to trade for an experienced quarterback. But there's another option worth considering: a younger, largely unproven backup whose upside -- and familiarity with Baltimore's offense -- could make him an appealing target. And that brings us to Bears backup Tyson Bagent.

According to Pro Football Talk, Baltimore could explore trading for Bagent, although acquiring him "won't be cheap." How expensive? Chicago Tribune reporter Brad Biggs suggested back in February that it could take a second-round pick, or equivalent compensation, to convince the Bears to make a deal. That wasn't a reported asking price, but it tells you something about how Chicago values its backup quarterback.

And if you're Baltimore, that's where things get complicated. Because while Bagent might give the Ravens their best chance to remain competitive until Jackson returns -- assuming he returns this season -- we're still talking about a former undrafted free agent with six career starts, three touchdown passes and nine interceptions.

So how much is that worth? And what does history tell us about teams trading valuable draft picks for largely unproven quarterbacks?

There's an obvious reason Bagent's name has surfaced in connection with the Ravens, and it goes beyond their suddenly depleted quarterback room. Offensive coordinator Declan Doyle spent last season in Chicago in the same role, where he worked directly with Bagent.

And Doyle wasn't shy about how he felt about the quarterback.

"Tyson is no-nonsense," Doyle said during training camp in 2025. "He's businesslike. Football's really important to him."

That familiarity matters. Doyle knows what Bagent does well, where he struggles and, perhaps most importantly, what he can reasonably be asked to do. And because Doyle helped implement Ben Johnson's offense in Chicago before bringing elements of that system to Baltimore -- including pre-snap motion, play-action and formation versatility -- Bagent would arrive with some familiarity with the concepts and expectations.

That doesn't mean Bagent will suddenly play like Jackson. And the Ravens wouldn't ask him to. They need somebody who can execute what's being asked, protect the football and give Baltimore a chance to win while Jackson recovers.

But what should the Ravens be willing to give up for that?

We went back through quarterback trades dating to 2007, focusing on players who had started 10 or fewer NFL games before another team acquired them. We looked at their performance before the trade, what their new teams gave up and, most importantly, what happened after they arrived.

And there have been some clear successes, starting with Matt Schaub.

Houston sent Atlanta two second-round picks and swapped first-round selections in 2007 for Schaub, who had started just twice in three seasons with the Falcons. He became Houston's starter for seven seasons, throwing for more than 23,000 yards and helping the Texans reach the playoffs twice.

A decade later, San Francisco sent New England a second-rounder for Jimmy Garoppolo, who also had just two NFL starts. The trade came at the 2017 deadline, and Garoppolo went 5-0 after taking over as the starter for a 1-10 team that finished 6-10. He eventually went 38-17 as the 49ers' starter and helped them reach the Super Bowl.

Schaub and Garoppolo, it turns out, are the exceptions.

Indianapolis traded former first-round receiver Phillip Dorsett to New England for Jacoby Brissett in 2017. Brissett started 30 games for the Colts, with 31 touchdowns and 13 interceptions. Dallas, meanwhile, gave up a fourth-rounder for Trey Lance in 2023 to serve as Dak Prescott's backup. The former No. 3 overall pick started just once for the Cowboys before leaving in free agency.

Then there's Joshua Dobbs, who was traded three times. Jacksonville gave up a fifth-rounder for him in 2019 and never started him. Arizona traded for him in 2023, got eight starts and a 1-7 record, then sent him to Minnesota, where he briefly became one of the NFL's best stories before eventually losing his starting job.

The most encouraging recent example? Malik Willis.

Originally a 2022 third-round pick, Tennessee traded Willis to Green Bay for a seventh-rounder in 2024 after he'd struggled through three starts with the Titans. All Willis did for the Packers was go 2-1 in three starts, throwing six touchdowns without an interception during his time there.

Of the 10 trades we looked at, only five resulted in the quarterback starting at least eight games for his new team. Just three -- Schaub, Garoppolo and Brissett -- made 16 or more starts.

It's not an exhaustive list, but the larger point is hard to miss. Teams routinely trade for quarterbacks they believe can offer more than they've shown. Occasionally, they find a long-term starter. More often, they're giving up future draft picks for somebody who never becomes the answer.

Of course, evaluating quarterbacks isn't as simple as comparing stat lines, particularly when they've barely played.

Schaub found success playing for Gary Kubiak in Houston, while Garoppolo benefited from Kyle Shanahan's offense in San Francisco. And Willis looked like a completely different quarterback when Matt LaFleur built Green Bay's game plans around what he did best.

Matt Cassel offers another example. The former seventh-rounder played well in place of an injured Tom Brady in New England in 2008, then struggled during his first season in Kansas City. But when former Patriots offensive coordinator Charlie Weis arrived in 2010, Cassel threw 27 touchdowns against seven interceptions, made the Pro Bowl and helped the Chiefs win the AFC West. He never sustained that level of success after Weis left.

None of this happens in a vacuum. Coaching, scheme and supporting cast all matter and what a quarterback accomplished in one offense doesn't necessarily tell us what he'll do in another.

Which brings us back to Doyle and Bagent.

We looked at this question earlier in the season when Seattle lost Sam Darnold, and the findings were revealing.

From 2015-2025, 41 teams were above .500 after losing their starting quarterback. Their backups went just 55-82, yet 24 of those teams still made the playoffs. Twelve won at least one postseason game, and four eventually won the Super Bowl.

So, yes, good teams can survive losing their starter. But there's a catch, and it's a big one.

Among those teams, 67.9% made the playoffs when the backup needed to start just one to three games. That fell to 38.5% when the replacement started at least four games, and just 16.7% when the absence stretched to seven or more starts.

Baltimore currently isn't above .500, but the point remains: Asking a backup to keep a talented team competitive for two or three weeks is one thing. Asking him to do it for two months -- or potentially the remainder of the season -- is something else entirely. Especially when the quarterback you're asking to do all this may not be on the roster right now.

And that's what makes Jackson's uncertain recovery timeline so important. The Ravens aren't necessarily looking for somebody to replace their franchise QB. They're looking for somebody who can keep the season from getting away from them before he returns.

Based on history alone, a fourth-round pick might seem reasonable for Bagent, given that he's played so little in his career. But there's no reason for Chicago to accept such an offer when it values Bagent as Caleb Williams' backup and has him under contract through 2027.

Which means Baltimore may have to look elsewhere. One possibility is recently-benched-and-demoted-to-QB3 Jacoby Brissett, currently of the Arizona Cardinals, but for how long is up in the air. The Cards haven't indicated they're shopping him, but his experience – and his current place on the depth chart – could make him a consideration before the trade deadline.

Yes, Schaub and Garoppolo proved that teams can find legitimate starters on somebody else's bench. Both were Day 2 picks, however, while Bagent went undrafted out of Division II Shepherd University. But there are plenty of examples of teams paying for potential and getting little in return. And Baltimore's immediate need for a quarterback doesn't automatically make Bagent more valuable.

Doyle knows Bagent better than most coaches around the league, and that familiarity could give the Ravens a better chance of making this work. History says a capable backup in the right situation can keep a season alive, particularly if the starter's absence is relatively short. And, by the way, Baltimore just signed Austin Reed to its practice squad -- another quarterback who worked with Doyle in Chicago last year.

But if Chicago really wants something approaching a second-round pick, Baltimore has to decide whether it's paying for a quarterback who can help save the season -- or simply paying a premium because it's running out of options.

#2589. Nikita Kucherov trade request: Five potential landing spots for the reigning NHL MVP

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

One of the greatest players in Tampa Bay Lightning history may soon be wearing a different jersey. According to Sportsnet, Nikita Kucherov has told the Lightning he won't sign a contract extension and has requested a trade.

Kucherov, a two-time Stanley Cup champion and two-time Hart Trophy winner as league MVP, is one of the best players of his era. The 33-year-old just passed the legendary Steven Stamkos for the all-time franchise lead in points and has shown no signs of slowing down.

Just last season, Kucherov posted 44 goals and 86 assists en route to his second Hart Trophy win. His underlying numbers were even better with a five-on-five goal differential of plus-38 and an expected goals share of 57.0 percent. Only a select few players can drive play from the wing like Kucherov, and that makes him a unicorn of sorts.

Kucherov is in the final year of a contract that pays him $9.5 million per season, and with the salary cap rising rapidly, he's due for a gargantuan raise next summer. It sounds like Kucherov and the Lightning were too far apart on that number, so the superstar winger has shifted his focuse to a change of scenery.

It's important to note that Kucherov has limited trade protection in the form of a 10-team trade list, but that should be more than enough for the Lightning to find a suitable trade partner. With that in mind, let's take a look at five teams that would be ideal fits for Kucherov as he prepares for the next chapter of his illustrious career.

Right out of the gate, this is the most natural fit of all the potential landing spots. General manager Kent Hughes has done a superb job of locking down his young core on team-friendly contracts, and as a result, the Canadiens have nearly $30 million in projected cap space for next season. They also have a glaring need in their top two lines, and I'd say the reigning Hart Trophy winner would fill that role quite nicely.

Montreal's moment to strike is now. It's an ascendant team with a great salary cap situtation and assets to spend. It's time to make a splash, and this would be a tsunami. Just imagine Kucherov on a power play unit with Nick Suzuki, Cole Caufield, Lane Hutson and Ivan Demidov. Kucherov would also be coached by former Lightning teammate Martin St. Louis, so a rapport would already exist between player and coach. I expect the Canadiens to do everything in their power to land Kucherov.

We already know the Wild are big-game hunting at forward because they've been heavily linked to former Detroit Red Wings captain Dylan Larkin. If I were advising general manager Bill Guerin -- and I'm certainly not -- I would recommend Minnesota package whatever assets it has offered Detroit and redirect them to Tampa Bay. No, Kucherov is not a center,  and that's the Wild's biggest need.

However, Kucherov is a rare breed of winger in that he can drive play better than most first-line centers from the wing. Put him on a line with Kirill Kaprizov, and the only time opponents will touch the puck is when they're pulling out of the net.

With Quinn Hughes also on an expiring contract, acquiring Kucherov would be a risky move for the Wild. What if they give up premium assets only to lose Kucherov and Hughes next summer? I don't think fear can dictate Minnesota's decisions. The team has a top-two defenseman in the world on its roster right now, and it has the opportunity to acquire a top-five forward. Worry about next summer when the time comes. Go all in to win the Cup while you have a chance.

It was no secret that the Hurricanes were in on the Connor Hellebuyck sweepstakes but just missed out. So, if they can't get better at preventing goals, why not get much better at scoring them? Carolina doesn't exactly need any help offensively, but adding Kucherov would go a long way to helping the team repeat as Stanley Cup champions. Besides, Kucherov would provide another level of playmaking and finishing that the Canes don't currently have on their roster.

Carolina has a good chunk of cap space available already, and it wouldn't need to shed much in order to make room for Kucherov. The Canes also have some enticing young players on their roster that might appeal to the Bolts, and they have three first-round picks over the next two drafts. Why not take a shot at landing a superstar winger?

Similar to the Hurricanes, the Mammoth were in the mix to acquire Hellebucyk, and for good reason. The goaltending tandem of Karel Vejmelka and Sebastian Cossa has not been good, so Utah may have to outscore its problems until one of the goalies finds a groove. Offense may be the best defense for the Mammoth -- and if that's the case -- then Kucherov should be in the mix for the Norris Trophy. There is a great young core of forwards in Salt Lake City, and I think Kucherov would be a perfect fit alongside Logan Cooley, who is emerging as a franchise center.

Utah also has plenty of draft capital with which to work, and it's projected for just over $25 million in salary cap space next season. The Mammoth don't have any major pending free agents on their cap sheet, so they're a suitor capable of signing Kucherov to a long-term extension.

Allow me to get a little bold on the fifth and final destination. The Stars have already failed to sign 27-year-old winger Jason Robertson to a long-term extension once. The two sides agreed to a one-year deal worth $12 million prior to the season, but Robertson's future with the team is still very much in doubt. What if Dallas and Tampa Bay executed a true "hockey trade" -- one player for one player?

Dallas would get the better player in Kucherov, but there are no guarantees regarding an extension. The Stars are in win-now mode, and Kucherov could help them get over the Cup hump immediately. Tampa Bay would get a younger player in Robertson, and although he doesn't have the elite playmaking ability of Kucherov, he's still an exceptionally talented scorer. Perhaps the Bolts could get him to join the team's core and sign a multi-year contract. This deal could work for both sides.

#2588. How can Thunder survive Chet Holmgren's absence? Rookie Aday Mara becomes vital as trade rumors swirl

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Oklahoma City Thunder announced that Chet Holmgren underwent treatment on Friday to address a small patellar tendon tear in his right knee, an issue that will keep him out of the lineup for the next 8-10 weeks.

With Jalen Williams out for the season following a gruesome leg injury and Cason Wallace set to miss most of the season after surgery to repair a torn labrum in his left shoulder, the Thunder are now without three of their top six players on the roster less than a month into the season.

The Thunder are off to a 4-1 start so far, but a lopsided loss to the Dallas Mavericks on Wednesday night with Holmgren out offered a glimpse into how challenging life will be with another star on the shelf.

For a team that began the season as the co-favorites in the Western Conference alongside the San Antonio Spurs with a win total over 60, now they face a challenge maintaining a spot in the top four in the West after losing so much of their expected production two weeks into the season.

Oklahoma City has been dominant in recent seasons largely due to its tremendous depth, but this summer saw them take the first steps in shedding that due to the perils of the second apron and rising costs of keeping a talented young core together. Gone are three established contributors in Lu Dort, Aaron Wiggins and Isaiah Joe, and while those were understandable cost-cutting measures, they exacerbate the challenge of dealing with serious injuries to key players at all three levels of the floor.

If there's a silver lining, it's that Holmgren's injury will only cost him a couple of months. But with Wallace and Williams out, losing one of the league's best rim protectors will be extremely difficult to deal with. This was already going to be a challenging season for coach Mark Daigneault without two key backcourt stars, but now he has to shuffle his lineups across the board with Holmgren out.

The Thunder probably hoped to bring their rookie big man along slowly, but with Holmgren out, the 7-foot-3 center out of Michigan will have to take on a larger spot in the rotation. Mara impressed in spot duty in his debut against Victor Wembanyama on opening night, showing why the Thunder drafted him to combat their chief rival with a rare player with the size and length to bother him -- and alleviate the stress Holmgren faces dealing with Wemby.

Mara then picked up his first double-double in a win over the Phoenix Suns on Monday, as he got his first extended burn with Holmgren out, scoring 11 points and pulling down 10 boards in 20 minutes. He was less effective in 21 minutes against the Mavs, and the Thunder will have to navigate the ups and downs of the rookie experience as Mara gets more comfortable in his expanded role.

Offensively, Mara is a play-finisher at the rim. So far this season, 80% of his field goal attempts have come within four feet of the rim and 75% of his attempts have come off of zero dribbles. With Mara on the floor, the offense has to adjust compared to what they can do with the rest of their center rotation. Where Isaiah Hartenstein can be a high post hub and Holmgren and Jaylin Williams can space the floor, Mara has less variability to his game. That doesn't mean he can't be effective, but it does require an adjustment on Oklahoma City's end to put him in the right spots and find ways to still create space for others when he's on the floor.

On defense, Mara gives them a needed rim protector and he's proven to be a high-caliber shot blocker already with seven blocks in five games despite relatively light minutes. However, like many young shot blockers, Mara is learning to navigate an increased minutes load without fouling. He has picked up nine fouls combined in his two games with 20-plus minutes. Defense will be Mara's calling card, and over the next two months, the Thunder will hope to see him continue learning to be impactful without fouling to maximize his time on the floor.

The Thunder never viewed this season as one to focus on development, but at this point they have little choice but to embrace that with Mara. He has the potential to be a key contributor to this team and play an extremely valuable role as they get set for a decade-long battle with the Wemby-led Spurs. With Holmgren out, he's going to get far more extended opportunities to see the floor than expected early in his rookie year, and perhaps that can pay dividends down the road for Oklahoma City.

With Williams out for the year and Wallace out for at least most of it, there were plenty of rumblings about the Thunder exploring their options on the trade market. A deal was unlikely to happen until at least December 15, when players who signed this summer become available, but Oklahoma City figured to spend the next month-plus evaluating its roster and keeping an eye on potential additions from around the league to stay in the contender realm.

With Holmgren out, one wonders whether that changes the calculus for Sam Presti -- or at least the timeline for making a move. Holmgren is expected to return in January, which would allow the Thunder to wait until he's back and see how he's performing coming off of the knee procedure for a couple of weeks before the trade deadline.

The Thunder should be able to manage two-plus months of a center rotation of Hartenstein, Williams and Mara -- with more Kenrich Williams at the four as well -- meaning their focus will still be on adding on the wing and in the backcourt.

Presti may want to see exactly what he has this season before making a significant in-season move. The Thunder could try to weather the storm with the roster they have until Holmgren returns and see where they are in the West before determining whether to make a smaller move or a more foundation-shaking trade.

No one has won three straight MVPs since Larry Bird in the 1980s. For one, it's hard to maintain that level for three straight seasons, but as we've seen over the years, even when the greats do stay in the MVP conversation, voter fatigue typically sets in after a player wins two and voters seek out someone else.

However, with the injuries piling up in Oklahoma City, if there were ever a year for a player to break that drought and become the first to three-peat as MVP in 40 years, it could be Shai Gilgeous-Alexander dragging this Thunder team to another top-four seed with such a depleted roster.

It's been a relatively slow start to the season for Gilgeous-Alexander, averaging 26.0 points, 4.6 rebounds and 3.4 assists per game on 45.9/26.5/87.5 shooting splits. That kind of production obviously won't get him a third MVP award, but if he ups his level and carries this Thunder squad without Holmgren for half the season and without Williams and Wallace for most of it, he will have to garner real consideration.

Some of his candidacy will be determined by who else is in the mix early on -- Luka Dončić seems poised to put up massive numbers in L.A. -- but the circumstances in Oklahoma City this season are so unique that Gilgeous-Alexander could break the run of back-to-back MVPs who have fallen short in pursuit of a third straight.

Gilgeous-Alexander's play will determine exactly how the Thunder proceed this season. If he plays at his typical MVP level and the Thunder look like a threat, Presti may have no choice but to try and make a splash ahead of the deadline to bring in reinforcements to chase a second championship. If it's a down year for Gilgeous-Alexander without some of his top support elements around him, perhaps there's less of a push to go all-in this season and Oklahoma City could look to ride out the storm and hope for better health in 2027-28.

#2587. Khalil Mack trade proposals: Bears reunion headlines 3 deals Chargers could make before NFL deadline

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Prior to their latest loss, the Los Angeles Chargers reportedly remained steadfast in their unwillingness to trade Khalil Mack before the league's Nov. 10 deadline. But after another loss on Sunday dropped them to 0-7, the Chargers may need to seriously reconsider that stance.

Of course, a strong offer could change anyone's mind about trading Mack, a future Hall of Fame outside linebacker who is deep into the back-nine of his career. Instead of spending one of his final years on a team going nowhere, the 35-year-old Mack would surely prefer to have a chance to win a championship, something that has eluded him to this point in his career.

While no longer in his prime, Mack is still a productive pass rusher who can help a title-contending team that needs help in that area. Fortunately for Mack, there are several teams that fit that description. The Chargers are his biggest roadblock.

Realistically, a fifth-round pick would be fair compensation for Mack, but there's probably no chance that happens. The Chargers' reported reluctance and the number of teams that are likely interested in Mack will drive up the price.

Here are three possible mock trades the Chargers could make if they decide to deal Mack.

Despite already trading for Jeffery Simmons, the Bears are reportedly still interested in Mack, who had a memorable, four-year run in Chicago from 2018-21. Mack's arrival in Chicago would further bolster the Bears' Super Bowl prospects.

Let's be clear. The Bears would probably have to overpay for Mack with a third-round pick. That's why they would probably try to get something back in the form of a late-round pick, whether that's in the 2027 or 2028 draft. In this mock trade, the Bears are able to move up a round on Day 3.

Chicago just showed that they are willing to go big if that means getting the player they want. No one will criticize the Bears for trading a pair of first-round picks to the Titans for Simmons if he helps them win a Super Bowl. The same could be said for this mock trade.

Lot of moving parts here, with the biggest one being the Chargers getting a third-round pick for Mack. Los Angeles would also get some players who can help them this season. Palmer played with Justin Herbert from 2021-24 and Chubb adds a veteran.

Buffalo would improve its draft stock and get an extra late-round pick in 2028. The Bills would also get a replacement for Palmer in Johnston, a former first-round pick who could use a change of scenery. Most importantly, Buffalo would get a much-needed pass rusher who can complement Greg Rousseau, who has nearly half of the Bills' entire sack total through eight weeks and is the only Bills player with more than 1.5 sacks.

A trade between Harbaugh brothers? Why not?

The Giants lead the NFC East despite having one of the league's worst pass rushers. They also need help at running back and pass catcher. John Harbaugh is familiar with both Kolar and Mitchell dating back to his time with the Ravens. Jim Harbaugh would get Singletary (who, like Johnston, would benefit from a change of scenery) and draft picks to help jumpstart the Chargers' inevitable rebuild.

#2585. MLB rumors: Padres decline option on key rotation piece, Korean star to be posted

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026-27 MLB offseason is only four days old and already the hot stove moves and rumors are coming in. Here are our top 50 free agents and top 25 trade candidates, and here are the important offseason dates and deadlines you need to know. Here now are Sunday's hot stove happenings.

San Diego's top two starters are now free agents. Two days after Michael King exercised an opt-out clause to become a free agent, the Padres declined their $14 million club option on Nick Pivetta, reports the San Diego Union-Tribune. Had the Padres picked up the option, Pivetta would have held an $18 million player option for 2028. That surely factored into the team's decision.

Pivetta, 34 in February, missed roughly five months with a flexor strain this past season. He returned late in the season and pitched reasonably well in six starts spanning September and the postseason. The San Diego Union-Tribune notes the Padres still have concerns about Pivetta's elbow, but could re-sign him to a new contract with a lower salary and/or no player option.

San Diego signed Pivetta to what amounted to a two-year, $23 million contact with two players options in February 2025. The flexor strain triggered an injury clause that converted the 2027 player option into a club option. We ranked Pivetta as the offseason's 43rd-best free agent.

As expected, the Orioles have declined their $20 million club option for center fielder Luis Robert Jr., reports ESPN. They will pay him a $2 million buyout, so it was functionally an $18 million decision. Robert suffered a hamstring injury and played only three games with the O's after being claimed off waivers from the Mets in late September.

Now 29, Robert again had multiple stints on the injured list this past season. He continued to punish lefties and play solid center field defense when healthy, but injuries have limited him to only 271 of 489 possible regular-season games from 2024-26. We did not rank Robert among our top 50 free agents, though he is an interesting upside play given his age.

The Hanwha Eagles of the Korea Baseball Organization will post star third baseman Si-Hwan Roh for MLB teams this offseason, reports Yonhap News Agency. Roh signed the richest deal in KBO history in February (11 years and $23 million), though as part of the deal, the Eagles agreed to post him this offseason, and Roh agreed to return to the team once his MLB stint is over.

Roh, 26, has been one of the KBO's best players the last several years. He hit .283/.360/.505 with 29 home runs in 2026, and has averaged 35 home runs per 162 games since 2023. Roh is considered a reliable but unspectacular defender at third, plus he has first base experience as well. This free agent class is very thin at the hot corner. Roh should generate a good deal of interest.

KBO players get a 30-day negotiating window once officially posted. If Roh does not sign with an MLB team during the 30-day window, he will return to the Eagles. It's possible that Roh, a right-handed hitter, will eclipse his $23 million guarantee with the Eagles over just a handful of years with an MLB team.

The Astros have acquired Triple-A righty reliever Evan Reifert from the Rays for cash, reports the Tampa Bay Times. Houston is likely to add him to their 40-man roster to protect him from the Rule 5 Draft. The Rays did not have the roster space to do that, so they traded for cash rather than lose him for nothing. Reifert, 27, has an excellent slider and used it to strike out 81 batters in 58 Triple-A innings in 2026. He should spend time in Houston's bullpen next season.

#2584. Luka Dončić teaches Yaxel Lendeborg a lesson, but Warriors bail their rookie out in comeback win over Lakers

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

When Yaxel Lendeborg decided it would be a good idea to start a war of words with Luka Dončić during and after his first career NBA game, basically calling the Lakers superstar a flopping crybaby for whom he "lost all respect," both Stephen Curry and Steve Kerr had the same message for their brash rookie.

Friday night was Lendeborg's chance to do just that when the Warriors hosted Dončić and the Lakers for the start of the NBA Cup's group stage. It did not, to put it politely, go well for Lendeborg, who laid down the worst track of his young career with six points, one rebound, zero assists and five turnovers.

Lendeborg got into early foul trouble and was never a factor on either end. For a guy who has injected so much juice into what looked like an old, disinterested, almost lifeless Warriors team when it faced these same Lakers on opening night, Lendeborg was all but invisible in finishing as a game-low minus-20 in his 24 minutes before fouling out.

When asked what lesson he had taken from a performance like this after shining such a spotlight on himself with the Luka comments, and what he might do differently next time, Lendeborg, with the same brutal honest he has shown at every turn, said he would "try not to wet the bed as bad as I did."

Meanwhile, Dončić -- who was egging on the "Luka sucks!" chant coming from the Chase Center crowd early on -- poured in 21 first-quarter points en route to 37 for the game. He added seven rebounds, five assists, a pair of blocks and a steal for good measure. He outscored the entire Warriors team in the first quarter by himself as the Lakers raced out to a 25-point first-half lead.

Luka Doncic’s face after hitting a 3 over Yaxel Lendeborg 😂 pic.twitter.com/CAiF7LUxDz

Certainly everything you've read so far would suggest the Lakers ran away with this game, but in today's NBA, a 20-point lead is just prologue for a second-half plot twist. And sure enough, the Warriors, behind eight 3-pointers and 31 points from Curry, stormed back to win going away, 112-95, for their third straight victory after opening the season 0-3.

Lendeborg might not have been able to back up his Dončić talk (which, we have to point out, was nothing but the truth, even if you could argue he would've been better off keeping it to himself, at least this early in his career), but the greatest shooter to ever set foot on this planet had his back. This is how you go at Luka Dončić ...

A 3PT MASTERCLASS FROM STEPHEN 📺 @NBAonPrime pic.twitter.com/nIIyrtmuKM

STOP IT, STEPH 🥵 pic.twitter.com/8ns53YenN2

It wasn't just Curry -- who passed Dominique Wilkins for 18th on the NBA's all-time scoring list -- coming to Lendeborg's rescue. It was Brandin Podziemski with 21 points, six assists and five rebounds. It was De'Anthony Melton and Georges Niang tag-teaming for 27 points and seven 3-pointers. It was Draymond Green taking over the Dončić defensive duties and dishing out nine dimes. It was the Warriors' bench outscoring L.A.'s bench 50-7, and a defense that held the Lakers to just 57 points over the final three quarters to fuel an astounding 42-point turnaround.

For Lendeborg, there's a lesson here that goes beyond not riling up a superstar and letting your play do the talking (which, I will restate, was fine; he's a grown man, and he didn't say anything that everyone else doesn't think), which is that it ultimately doesn't matter that Dončić got the better of him individually on Friday, because in the end it was the Warriors that got the better of the Lakers.

This was the message that Kerr had for Lendeborg after the opener in which Lendeborg was all too proud of his individual defense on Dončić.

"He did a good job on Luka one-on-one, but we got torched by Luka as a team," Kerr said. "All those stats that the NBA puts up, like, 'Hey, when he guarded him, who the eff cares?' It's like, they scored 127 on us. That stuff's all bulls---. It's our defense."

Translation: it's a team game. As his career progresses, Lendeborg, a clear alpha, is going to be the one picking up his teammates on plenty of nights, but on this night it was the rookie who needed his teammates to cover for him. Suffice it to say, they did that, and Lendeborg, to his credit, recognized the effort with genuine humility.

"Them boys had my back today," Lendeborg said, noting that in his effort to stay calm and not let the hype of the matchup take over, he actually stayed "a little too calm" and never got into a groove. "Steph Curry, again, did his thing. The bench mob showed up today. It was awesome. They all played a great game. I feel like I was the only Debbie downer on the team. I feel like next time I get into one of these games, just try to be that guy sucking up all the energy."

#2583. Six lessons from Week 8: Bears emerge as top-tier Super Bowl contenders, Chiefs must address glaring flaws

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The NFL is always full of surprises -- season to season, week to week and, on Sundays, hour to hour.

The Week 8 schedule was absolutely loaded, but the two best games of the Sunday slate ended up being Titans-Bengals and Cardinals-Cowboys. If you had Gardner Minshew coming off the bench and throwing three touchdowns to lead a double-digit comeback and Joe Burrow accounting for six touchdowns -- and throwing three interceptions -- go buy a lottery ticket.

And that was only the early window. Later in the day, Bo Nix went from zero to hero again, leading a stunning double-digit comeback against the Chiefs. Overall, there were five double-digit comeback wins, the most of any week this season.

So yes, it may be November, but we're still learning, still being surprised, still finding out what's real and what's not. And the Bears capped a wild weekend by showing they are very much for real.

If you had high expectations for Jeffery Simmons in Chicago -- and I very much did -- they somehow still weren't high enough, at least for one game. The Bears' 34-17 dismantling of the reigning-champion Seahawks was a fever dream for any Chicago fan.

Simmons delivered six tackles, a sack, two tackles for loss and a pass broken up in his team debut, but that outstanding stat line still doesn't come close to telling the full story.

This is what superstars do. They wreck plays, and when they don't, they allow others to. Sam Darnold was running for his life all night en route to just 188 passing yards on 5.0 net yards per attempt. I found it fitting that the Seahawks acquired Quenton Nelson this week, and yet Simmons stole the show. And that's no shade to Nelson. Simmons is that good.

Caleb Williams, meanwhile, was superb. The stats didn't pop, but what makes him so good is that he can have absurd statistical games and he can have just really efficient, high-floor games. Against one of the league's best defenses, Williams had no turnovers and took just one sack. His 7.3 yards per attempt were the best by any player against Seattle this season.

Stars make the world go 'round. They give you a chance. But supporting casts lift you from "having a chance" to "being a force," and the Bears have an awesome supporting cast. Ben Johnson is a top-five coach. Luther Burden III is an ultra-fun wide receiver who eats up one-on-one coverage and has tons of juice after the catch. Outside of his fumble, Colston Loveland was excellent. Rome Odunze is the big, physical guy who wins intermediate/deep throws in the middle of the field, a crucial area to attack. He has been terrific recently. The offensive line is outstanding. Everything has fallen into place.

There are still weaknesses. The cornerbacks are a concern. But the NFL is about figuring out ways to either hide, overcome or fix those weaknesses. Star power is the best way to do it, and the Bears have superstars at quarterback and, now, on defense.

The Seahawks hadn't lost a game by five or more points in nearly two years. They lost this one by 17. The Bears were probably a second-tier Super Bowl contender this time one week ago. After Monday night? Welcome to the top tier, Chicago.

It seems like all the discourse from the Lions' gritty 19-15 win over the Vikings was about how bad Kyler Murray has been. Maybe -- just maybe -- we should focus on Detroit.

The offense is currently third in EPA per play and success rate and sixth in explosive play rate. Jared Goff has thrown for 15 touchdowns and one interception and is playing like a legit MVP candidate. He won't win the award, but he should garner votes. His ability to manage pressure -- long his biggest weakness -- has been at career-best levels this year. Jameson Williams looks like a stud again, and we already know Jahmyr Gibbs, Amon-Ra St. Brown are awesome. Detroit ranks third in run blocking and fourth in pass blocking in PFF's metrics.

The defense, meanwhile, is eighth in success rate and 13th in EPA per play over the past two weeks. Brian Branch's return has been huge. Kerby Joseph could be back soon. The secondary has been miles better since the bye. Up front, Aidan Hutchinson remains a star, and Alim McNeil and Tyleik Williams are playing well inside.

This could be the NFC version of the Bengals: elite offense plus just enough defensive playmaking to be a threat.

In a vacuum, the Chiefs' loss to the Broncos was just that: one loss. Yes, it was a disappointing one, given the chance to put a vice grip on the division, but it's just one loss.

In the big picture, this game revealed multiple significant issues -- issues that will cost the Chiefs when a loss isn't just a game lost, but a season lost.

These are the three things I'm quite worried about:

In the fourth quarter alone, Reid punted on a fourth-and-inches and, up three, had Harrison Butker (who was 2-for-6 from 50+ entering the game) attempt a 54-yard field goal in the rain. Butker missed. Both of those decisions were key moments of the Chiefs blowing an 11-point lead in the final quarter.

Reid has one of the greatest quarterbacks of all time, yet made two incredibly conservative decisions. This is far from the first time. The field goal decision was particularly infuriating because being up six isn't that much more helpful than being up three, and Mahomes is, historically, better on fourth and 8 to fourth and 12 than Butker is from 50+ this year. You can read more of my thoughts on Reid blowing it here.

The short-yardage issues aren't new, either, and they play into Reid's mismanagement. Mahomes has not attempted a quarterback sneak since 2019. If that's how it is, fine. But the Chiefs still have to find another way to consistently get one yard. Kansas City only gains a first down on 62.5% of its plays when it has 1 yard or less to go, 23rd in the league this year. This loomed very large, of course, at the end on Sunday, when Kansas City failed to convert on multiple goal-to-go opportunities at the 1-yard line.

The Chiefs' wide receiving corps is hurting in both the short yardage and the (lack of) big yardage. For the latter, there is no deep threat. Mahomes has gone three straight games without completing a pass 20+ yards downfield. The pass-catching options are, frankly, appalling for a Super Bowl contender. Rashee Rice is a YAC guy. Xavier Worthy just doesn't provide a lot. Even Travis Kelce had two bad drops. And in the short yardage, wouldn't it be nice to have a guy who can win a 50/50 ball? A big catch radius? A guy who wins one-on-one?

George Pickens is the dream add here, but Kansas City must do something. Must. Mahomes is too good. Kenneth Walker III is too good. You just can't pass up many opportunities when you have Mahomes. The Chiefs have extra draft capital. Look at other Super Bowl contenders making big trades this season. If you're not giving Mahomes the best chance possible (within reason) to win a Super Bowl every year, you're being wasteful. It's already bad that the pass-catcher is such a huge issue for a second straight year, but the Chiefs have a chance to change that.

A week ago, I floated Adonai Mitchell as a potential solution for the Chiefs' wide receiver woes. He was coming off a zero-catch game, and Omar Cooper Jr. was emerging for the Jets.

Now? I think Mitchell might be a legit part of the Jets' long-term build. Sunday, he had seven catches for 142 yards and a touchdown. But it's more than the stats. It's how he looked as he accrued them.

Adonai Mitchell set a new career high with 142 receiving yards, topping his previous best of 102.7 REC, 142 REC YDS, 1 TD vs RaidersAcquired in the Sauce Gardner trade, Mitchell is showing serious potential in New York. pic.twitter.com/djWO4vT8Ik

That is legitimate star-level film. I know the Raiders' cornerbacks are young and not great, but Mitchell looked like varsity against JV.

Mitchell was a throw-in in the Sauce Gardner trade. An afterthought. His career was synonymous with a 75-yard catch in which he toasted multiple defenders, only to fumble the ball 1 yard before entering the end zone uncontested. The talent has always been there.

He was off to a strong start this season before a freak finger injury suffered in practice. If he has finally put it all together, the Gardner trade -- already a landslide win for New York -- got even more lopsided.

In all likelihood, you only heard the name Gregory Rousseau in connection to the Lamar Jackson injury. With Jackson and, later, Tyler Huntley out, the Bills crushed the Ravens 36-10, turning a highly anticipated game into a snoozefest.

But if that's all you heard, you missed out on Rousseau being an absolute menace. He only played 30 snaps because of the blowout, but he still managed seven pressures and a sack. Watch him toss Roger Rosengarten aside on the sack.

Greg Rousseau just running through Roger Rosengarten pic.twitter.com/XIY77oqV9z

Shortly thereafter, he destroyed a drive on his own.

Here is the second drive of the second half for the #Ravens. #Bills Greg Rousseau blows up and ruins all three plays.Guy is on the fringe of being a game wrecker this year! #BillsMafia @BuffTrenchTalk pic.twitter.com/IKuhLGHzsp

Here's where Rousseau stands through eight weeks:

He has crucial splash plays -- a strip sack to seal a win over the Texans in Week 1, another strip sack in Week 2 -- and impressive consistency, with at least six pressures in six of Buffalo's seven games.

Will Anderson Jr. is rightfully a comfortable favorite (+250, per DraftKings) to win Defensive Player of the Year. But Rousseau has quietly climbed up to +1200, the fifth-shortest odds. He absolutely belongs in the conversation and has plenty of time to become a bigger part of it.

I can't believe I am "Old man yells at cloud"-ing this, but the Lions' and the Jaguars' uniforms were truly unsightly. Let's start with the Lions, whose uniforms looked like the Panthers had washed their white laundry and their dark laundry together.

Looking fresh 🔥 @LionsMINvsDET -- 1pm ET on FOX/FOX OneStream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/3nDDVhAE9s

Jahmyr Gibbs looks cool because he can make anything look cool. That's what happens when you are cool. But these are bad.

The same thing goes for the Jaguars. A few days later, I feel a little bit better about Jacksonville's getup, but I don't love it.

The @Jaguars NFL x Nike Rivalries uniforms are here 🔥INDvsJAX – 1pm ET on CBS/Paramount+Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/cmXR5YZW81

The helmets being such a departure from the rest of the uniform my biggest complaint. It kind of felt like someone putting together a sensible shirt and pants combo and then throwing on a clashing hat, just because.

The NFL wants alternate jerseys, but some things are better left untouched. Fear not, though, Lions and Jaguars fans. You're still not nearly as bad as the Bills' "Nickel City" eyesore from Week 3. This looked straight out of an unlicensed video game.

#2580. Mets legend Jerry Koosman dies at 83: Pitcher helped New York win 1969 World Series

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Mets team Hall of Famer and two-time All-Star Jerry Koosman died Sunday morning in Osceola, Wisconsin, the team announced. He was 83. The Mets say Koosman battled multiple illnesses before his death.

"Kooz was one of the greatest pitchers in team history and a beloved member of the Mets family," Mets owners Alex and Steve Cohen said in a statement. "The 1969 Miracle Mets were filled with heroes, and the special southpaw from Appleton, Minnesota, was central to their success. He was a fierce competitor on the field, and respected teammate in the clubhouse. His legendary performance in the World Series helped the Mets secure their first Championship in team history. On behalf of the entire Mets organization, we extend our heartfelt condolences to Jerry's family, friends, former teammates and all who loved him."

The Mets discovered Koosman while he was pitching for the United States Army and signed him to a contract in August 1964. He made his MLB debut in April 1967 and moved into the rotation full-time the next season. Koosman threw 263 ⅔ innings with a 2.08 ERA as a rookie in 1968, which earned him an All-Star Game selection and MVP votes, and a second-place finish in the Rookie of the Year voting behind Hall of Famer Johnny Bench.

In 1969, Koosman was again an All-Star, throwing 241 innings with a 2.28 ERA. He was New York's No. 2 starter in the postseason between Hall of Famers Tom Seaver and Nolan Ryan. Koosman made two starts for the Miracle Mets in the World Series, including the Game 5 clincher against the Baltimore Orioles. He allowed three runs in the complete game win and recorded all but one possible out in his two World Series starts.

From 1968-76, Koosman was simply one of the best pitchers in the game, pitching to a 2.94 ERA and averaging 223 innings per season. The Mets traded him to the Minnesota Twins for Jesse Orosco in December 1978 and Koosman finished his career with stints for the Twins (1979-81), Chicago White Sox (1981-83), and Philadelphia Phillies (1984-85).

Koosman retired following the 1985 season with a 222-209 record and a 3.36 ERA that is 39th among AL/NL pitchers with at least 3,500 career innings. He ranks 35th all-time in strikeouts (2,556), 40th all-time in starts (527), 48th all-time in innings (3,839 ⅓), and 77th all-time in pitching WAR (57.0). Koosman went to two All-Star Games and finished second to Randy Jones in the 1976 Cy Young voting.

The Mets inducted Koosman into their Hall of Fame in 1989 and retired his No. 36 in 2021. His 140 wins are the most in franchise history among left-handers and third in team history overall, behind Seaver (198) and Dwight Gooden (157). Koosman is second in Mets history in innings (behind Seaver) and third in strikeouts (behind Seaver and Gooden).

Koosman fell off the Baseball Writers Association of America's Hall of Fame ballot in 1991, his first year of eligibility.

#2579. Ranking NFL's best new coordinators: Packers, Steelers assistants lead top 10 at midseason

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The path from star coordinator to elite head coach is as clear as ever. Look no further than defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks coach Mike Macdonald, Kyle Shanahan, Sean McVay, or, more recently, Ben Johnson and Liam Coen. Finding the next one of those guys could change the fortune of any franchise, and those types of coaches can be found occupying offensive and defensive coordinator roles today.

So which new coordinators are making the biggest, positive impact in their NFL homes through the first half or so of the 2026 season? Here is a look at the top 10 plus a few honorable mentions.

Honorable mentions: New York Jets offensive coordinator Frank Reich, Tampa Bay Buccaneers offensive coordinator Zac Robinson, Buffalo Bills defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard

The Baltimore Ravens were the NFL's No. 7 scoring offense (29.0) through the first four weeks of the 2026 season under new offensive coordinator Declan Doyle when Lamar Jackson was healthy. Without Jackson since Week 5, Baltimore averages just 15.8 points per game, the fifth-lowest in the league. After Doyle surprised the Atlanta Falcons with backup Tyler Huntley in a 30-23 overtime road win, the Ravens have lost three in a row.

If Jackson can shake off his injury woes, Doyle could easily get the Ravens offense back on track. That sadly appears to be a big if at the moment.

The Seattle Seahawks experienced a tough offseason of attrition, losing offensive coordinator Klint Kubiak to the Las Vegas Raiders and Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker to the Chiefs. New offensive coordinator Brian Fleury also got hit with an injury to quarterback Sam Darnold on the first drive of the season, and Darnold has been a rollercoaster the rest of the way: His -0.67 expected points added (EPA) per dropback when pressured is the worst in the NFL this season. Perhaps the addition of Quenton Nelson can help calm Darnold down on that front while he aims to find his footing post-glute injury. Both of Seattle's top running backs, Zach Charbonnet (torn ACL) and first-round rookie Jadarian Price (chest), had yet to be active in the same game until Week 8.

However, Fleury has maintained the staggering production from Jaxon Smith-Njigba. JSN is just one of four players with 900-plus receiving yards and nine-plus receiving touchdowns in the first eight games of a season in the Super Bowl era (since 1966). The other three are Torry Holt (2003), Steve Smith Sr. (2005) and Cooper Kupp (2021). Both Smith and Kupp went on to win the receiving triple crown in their respective seasons.

There was a lot of doubt that the Cleveland Browns' defense could remain among the league's top-half units following the departures of defensive coordinator Jim Schwartz and sack icon Myles Garrett. However, new defensive coordinator Mike Rutenberg has done just that with the NFL's No. 13 scoring defense (21.6 points per game allowed) in 2026.

Despite not having Garrett, Cleveland has remained stout in the red zone, allowing a 48% red zone touchdown rate -- tied for the seventh-lowest mark in the league with the Denver Broncos. Remarkably, Rutenberg's unit is top 10 in the NFL in sacks (21, tied for ninth), sack rate (7.4%, tenth) and quarterback pressure rate (38.8%, 10th) without blitzing at a high volume -- the Browns' 28.2% blitz rate is the 12th lowest in the league. Rutenberg has pulled off a Moneyball approach to the pass rush by replacing Garrett in the aggregate: 11 players have at least one sack and four players have at least three sacks. That's a job well done for the surprising 5-3 Browns.

It would've been easy for Dennard Wilson to feel sorry for himself after Brian Burns went down for the season in Week 3. However, New York has remained afloat with a league-average scoring defense (23.0 points allowed per game, 15th in the NFL). That's largely due to Wilson getting creative with his pressure packages and manufacturing havoc, with the league's third-highest blitz rate (41.9%). Doing so has limited opponents to taking what the defense gives them and checking it down frequently, with the Giants allowing just 6.1 yards per pass attempt, the second-lowest figure in the entire league. That's a job well done for a Giants squad that is the surprise NFC East division leader (4-2-1) through eight weeks.

Losing Jaxson Dart in Week 2 was a crushing blow. Matt Nagy has made the most of a struggling Jameis Winston and Minnesota Vikings castoff J.J. McCarthy at quarterback, and that has led to his unit producing the league's No. 14 scoring offense (23.3 points per game).

The 2026 Giants are the first team since the 2016 New England Patriots to have three different starting quarterbacks win a game before November: Dart, Winston and McCarthy. In their last game out, a 27-21 overtime win at the Houston Texans in Week 7, the Giants had four different players run for a touchdown, marking their first such game since 1950. Nagy is also doing a good job keeping Pro Bowl wide receiver Malik Nabers engaged and involved despite the quarterback carousel: Nabers joined Odell Beckham Jr. as the only players in team history with 100-plus receiving yards in four consecutive games. That's strong work for the NFC East division leaders.

Eric Bieniemy returned to Kansas City for his second tour of duty as the Chiefs' offensive coordinator in 2026, and he adapted his offense well with the personnel at his disposal. From 2018 to 2021, Kansas City's offense was built off of Patrick Mahomes' deep passing game to Tyreek Hill and Travis Kelce, but in 2026, the offense is centered around Kenneth Walker III's talents. That's been a mostly successful formula for the 5-2 Chiefs with Walker III ranking third in the league in rushing yards (770), second in yards per carry (5.5) and second in tackles avoided (59).

Bieniemy needs some help at the trade deadline to truly open up the passing game, but the Chiefs ranking 11th in scoring with a 37-year-old Kelce as the top target represents a job well done. He had Mahomes in position to throw the game-winning touchdown to wide receiver Rashee Rice on Sunday at the Denver Broncos, but a false start penalty by offensive tackle Jaylon Moore nullified the score late.

The San Francisco 49ers are the NFL's No. 1 seed through the first eight weeks of the season, and defensive coordinator Raheem Morris' unit deserves some credit for that. They're the league's No. 6 scoring defense (19.9 points per game), the No. 4 total defense (299.3 total yards per game) and the No. 5 run defense (86.8 rushing yards per game).

San Francisco has the ninth-worst average time of possession margin in the NFL, possessing the football two minutes fewer than their opponents on average, and that hasn't affected Morris' unit at all. Much of that figure has to do with the passing game inconsistencies with all of the 49ers' wide receiver injuries, but the 49ers defense just keeps on chugging.

One could look at new offensive coordinator Drew Petzing putting together the NFL's No. 3 scoring offense (29.0 points per game) and say, "Well, anyone could do that." Detroit has the firepower with Jared Goff, Jahmyr Gibbs, Amon-Ra St. Brown, Sam LaPorta and Penei Sewell. That group alone represents 17 trips to the Pro Bowl.

Petzing's predecessor, John Morton, lost his job after one season and had his play-calling duties stripped by Dan Campbell entering Week 10. Petzing has thrived at giving Gibbs a chance to shine with David Montgomery no longer in the picture. Gibbs totaled his third 150-yard rushing game of 2026 on Sunday in the 19-15 defeat against the Minnesota Vikings after having just two such games in his first three seasons combined.

Petzing also isn't afraid to get creative after having St. Brown line up 10 yards behind Goff on a third-and-8, and the pass play that allowed St. Brown to catch the ball while already moving at near top speed went for a first down against the NFL's No. 1 defense.

Lions ran a play with Amon-Ra St. Brown 10 yards behind the quarterback and it worked pic.twitter.com/4fKrBpEbxV

The Pittsburgh Steelers' defense has come back to life under new defensive coordinator Patrick Graham. They're the league's No. 3 scoring defense (18.0 points per game allowed), No. 6 total defense (305.6 total yards per game allowed), No. 3 run defense (83.9 rushing yards per game allowed), No. 8 third down defense (34.3% third down conversion rate allowed),  No. 2 red zone defense (37.5% third down conversion rate allowed) and tied for No. 3 in takeaways (13).

Having All-Pro edge rusher T.J. Watt turning back the clock also helps. After he had just 7.0 sacks in 14 games last season, Watt has 7.5 in eight games this season, which is tied for the league lead with Houston Texans All-Pro edge rusher Will Anderson Jr. No team has more sacks in the NFL than Graham's unit's 26, one more than the Brian Flores blitzkrieg Minnesota Vikings attack.

The Browns were flying high entering Week 8 with a 5-2 record, but they left Pittsburgh 5-3 after a 27-6 defeat in which the Steelers held them to both season-lows in points (6) and rushing yards (34). Graham is crushing it.

What Jonathan Gannon is doing in his first season as the defensive coordinator of the Green Bay Packers is nothing short of miraculous. The Packers are 5-3 and would be in the playoffs if the 2026 season ended today despite having fewer than 500 yards rushing.

Having the league's worst rushing offense (60.6 rushing yards per game) has heavily contributed to Gannon's defense being on the field for an average time of possession of 31:36, the third highest in the NFL. Micah Parsons isn't expected to return from his torn ACL until Thanksgiving, and top inside linebacker Edgerrin Cooper is out for the season with a torn Achilles. Green Bay is a top-10 scoring defense (20.5 points per game allowed) and a top-10 total defense (314.9 total yards per game allowed).  That is remarkable.

How has he done it? One might think Gannon is like fellow NFC North defensive mastermind Brian Flores, blitzing all day, every day, to compensate for the lack of Parsons, but that's not the case. The Packers blitz at a 33.4% clip, which ranks 13th in the NFL. Gannon has been able to do it the old-fashioned way by developing some of the Packers' talent that has had more potential than it has produced. Edge rusher Lukas Van Ness, the 13th overall pick in the 2023 NFL Draft, produced what was a career-high 4.0 sacks as a rookie in 2023. With Gannon, Van Ness has a career-high of 4.5 sacks, and the Packers still have nine games left to play.

"Honestly man, JG is not scared. He is not shying away from things because we lost a couple of players. He is still going to dial that shit up you know what I mean?" Packers safety Javon Bullard said after Green Bay's "Thursday Night Football" victory over the Carolina Panthers in Week 8, via NBC 26 in Green Bay. "I think that shows a lot of confidence in the players that we have, and honestly that's huge kudos to him because not a lot of coaches dial it up like that. Not a lot of coaches are as aggressive as he is. I think that's what you want in a coordinator, man. You want a nasty defense. You want a rugged defense. A loud defense. A confident defense. Your coordinator has to damn near replicate that. I think we complement each other real well."

He is also maximizing the talent Green Bay has at safety with All-Pro Xavier McKinney (three interceptions) and Evan Williams (two interceptions and a fumble recovery) each having three takeaways this season, tied for the third most in the NFL. Williams, a 2024 fourth-round pick, is actually the NFL's highest-graded safety with a Pro Football Focus defensive grade of 90.6. Packers fans were also ready to run cornerback Keisean Nixon out of town after a couple of less-than-stellar seasons, but his 69.6 passer rating against as the primary defender in coverage is the seventh-best in the league among 52 players with at least 35 passes thrown their way.

Gannon has done a brilliant job coordinating one of the best defenses in football despite always having his unit on the field and missing his best player. That's why he is No. 1 on this list halfway through the season. Just imagine what will happen when he finally has Parsons at his disposal.

#2578. Jeanie Buss accuses siblings of conspiring against her as dispute over Lakers stake continues

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Jeanie Buss has accused her siblings of conspiring against her in a "cloak and dagger" campaign through the media in a court filing this week and has asked a judge to block her siblings' attempts to sell the family's shares of the Los Angeles Lakers, ESPN reports.

According to Wednesday's filing, Jeanie Buss said her siblings -- specifically Joey and Jesse Buss -- are jealous of their father's decision to leave her with governor rights to the team and she does not want them selling the family's remaining shares of the team.

Finality for both sides of the legal spat could come during a scheduled Dec. 8 hearing in Los Angeles Superior Court.

Former Disney CEO Bob Iger and Josh Kushner spearhead an ownership group looking to buy the Lakers from Mark Walter at a valuation of $12.5 billion.

"The conflicts that ensued after Dr. (Jerry) Buss's death (in 2013) were sadly inevitable, and no doubt intensified given that Dr. Buss chose his daughter over four sons to be his successor," representation for Jeanie Buss wrote in this week's filing. "Respondents' obsession with tearing down Jeanie and their inability to accept that she would be a part of the Lakers' future is borne of this classic succession parable."

Jeanie Buss would no longer serve as the Lakers' governor if her family sells its 17.8% ownership stake, which is just above the NBA's 15% minimum for the family to retain control. Iger previously said during an interview with The California Post that the plan was for Buss to remain governor, but "if things change, they'll change."

The latest filing continues an ongoing saga between family members over the NBA's third-most valuable franchise. Earlier this year, ESPN reported that Jeanie Buss contended that a 2017 court order prevents any vote to sell the remaining family shares without her consent.

That was not the first time that the Buss siblings have fought over control of the team. When Jeanie fired Jim Buss as head of basketball operations in 2017, he and Johnny Buss attempted to strip Jeanie of her seat on the Lakers' board of directors.

The two sides ultimately agreed to settle with Jeanie Buss remaining in control of the team.

Now, Jeanie Buss is asking the court to remove two siblings as co-trustees of the trust for breach of fiduciary duty, hold them in contempt of court, and "find Jim, Johnny and Jesse liable for aiding and abetting a violation of the 2017 court order and be reimbursed for legal costs," per ESPN.

If the Buss family sells the entirety of its shares of the team, each sibling receives an additional $371 million per go-along rights. ESPN reported this week that settlement talks have begun.

"Jeanie had no choice but to seek court intervention to enforce the clear terms of the trust and this court's 2017 order," Wednesday's filing states. "Respondents respond (by) casting themselves as victims, when in reality, the entire episode is their own false flag operation.

"The cloak and dagger, backroom 'votes' and 'resolutions' shared with ESPN, rather than their co-trustee and sister, and subsequent refusal to discuss the matter, was intended to force Jeanie's hand, cry victim and again smear her in the media by sharing in advance their specious response."

The winners of the 2026 Rawlings Gold Glove were announced Sunday night by Major League Baseball and, as expected, Cubs wunderkind Pete Crow-Armstrong took home his second straight National League Gold Glove in center field. PCA, who also won a Gold Glove in 2025 and is expected to be named the NL MVP in 2026, was the best defender in baseball this past season based on both the numbers and the eye test.

Here are the game's best defenders in 2026 according to Statcast's Fielding Runs Value, an all-encompassing metric that factors in range and arm, as well as blocking and framing for catchers:

Crow-Armstrong's +26 FRV is the fifth best in a single season since FRV launched in 2016 and the second best by a non-catcher, trailing only Nick Ahmed's +28 FRV season at shortstop in 2018.

Gold Gloves have be awarded since 1957 and are given to the best defensive player at each position in each league. That first year was one MLB-wide honor at each position. In 1958, Gold Gloves were split into AL and NL. Also, it used to be three outfielders per league regardless of exact position. Now the outfield spots are broken down into left field, center field, and right field.

Winners are determined through manager/coach voting (75%) and a statistical component (25%). Team employees can not vote for their own players.

While MLB announced "finalists" for each Gold Glove a few weeks back, remember that the voting was already complete and those finalists were simply the top three vote-getters at each position. #2576. Pressing Impossible: Amorim Loses to Hürzeler – MH

von Next Generation am 21.01.2025 in den Kategorien Premier League mit 0 Kommentaren

Rúben Amorim’s Manchester United faced Hürzeler’s Brighton on Matchday 22. While Manchester United focused on creating a pressing system that was as difficult as possible to bypass, Brighton once again showcased their incredibly challenging vertical play. You can find the tactical analysis of the match here.

Manchester United started in a nominal 3-2-4-1 formation, which transitioned into a classic 3-2-5 shape in possession and a 5-4-1 shape out of possession. Amorim initially placed particular emphasis on a pressing system that varied in height.

Meanwhile, Brighton began in a nominal 4-4-2 formation. In possession, Hürzeler’s trademark positional rotations, vertical runs, and decoy movements for effective vertical play were continuously on display. Accordingly, Brighton operated flexibly from a variety of shapes, such as 4-2-4, 3-1-4-2, 2-3-2-3, and more. This flexibility makes Brighton’s possession game almost impossible to define through formations alone.

Manchester United initially operated out of a 5-4-1 shape with varying defensive heights. This approach made it challenging for the opposition to play through, as different build-up phases required distinct patterns and connections. United’s central midfielders in the four-man line marked Brighton’s double pivot, Ayari and Baleba, man-to-man. The goal was to gain optimal control of Brighton’s central build-up play and apply immediate pressure whenever Brighton played through the middle.

However, Brighton controlled the game during the first 10 minutes. Their holding midfielders positioned themselves close to the backline, creating a large gap between Manchester United’s five-man defensive line and the four-man midfield. This space was then exploited with various runs. When facing high pressing, left-back Estupiñán moved asymmetrically into the left half-space behind United’s first pressing block. This movement utilized the moment when Amad stepped out to press one of Brighton’s center-backs after bypassing Zirkzee.

United failed to adjust their pressing to this build-up variation throughout the match. As a result, this same pattern played a key role in Brighton’s build-up to the goal that made it 1-3.

Against Manchester United’s mid-block, Brighton’s strikers, Welbeck and João Pedro, alternated their runs into the large space between the lines, targeting the gaps. This repeatedly allowed Brighton to bypass United’s first pressing line.

The 1-0 goal resulted from this setup, facilitated by a counter-movement. As striker Welbeck made a run into the space between the lines, he pulled his marker, De Ligt, a few steps out of the five-man backline. Simultaneously, winger Mitoma made a deep run into the space that opened up. De Ligt was caught in a dilemma between applying pressure and covering the depth. A long ball bypassed United’s entire pressing structure, leading to the goal.

Another reason for Brighton’s dominance in the first 10 minutes lay in their defensive work. United built up in a very positionally structured 3-2-4-1(/-5) shape. Brighton countered with a 4-4-2 in their high press and a 5-4-1 in their mid-block. With Minteh marking Diogo Dalot man-to-man on the flank, the two different defensive shapes emerged depending on Dalot’s positioning. Brighton’s two strikers also pressed United’s center-backs, Maguire and Yoro, on that side, applying intense pressure on the ball carriers on United’s left.

On the other side, winger Mitoma positioned himself centrally when De Ligt had possession, cutting off the passing lane to Amad, who was positioned in the half-space. If the ball was played to full-back Mazraoui, Mitoma shifted out from the center to press, creating a cover shadow into the center. This approach effectively prevented United from creating any significant attacking threat on that flank as well.

Around the 10th minute, the game shifted, and Brighton’s dominance began to fade. This was due to several adjustments made by United. To reduce the pressure on the ball carrier on the left side, the highly press-resistant Bruno Fernandes started to drop deeper, while the full-backs pushed higher. The resulting 3-3-4 shape was difficult for Brighton to press, as full-back Veltman, or the half-space defender in the five-man backline, was pulled out, and the space in behind could be exploited by either full-back Dalot or striker Zirkzee. This led to more possession phases for United and fewer pressing phases from Brighton.

Another adjustment United made came from their 5-4-1 mid-block. The half-space defenders, De Ligt and Yoro, became much more aggressive in stepping out from the five-man backline to defend against the strikers making runs into the large space between the lines. This prevented Brighton’s strikers from turning after bypassing the first pressing block. To defend long balls to Mitoma, Mazraoui prioritized covering the space behind the advancing De Ligt. As a result, Brighton struggled to exploit the space between the lines and couldn’t progress as effectively into depth from their own possession.

Additionally, Manchester United no longer pressed situationally from a 5-4-1 in a high press but instead switched to man-marking, with Zirkzee following the goalkeeper. This created much more pressure on the ball carriers for Brighton. Brighton also faced difficulties because the 5-4-1 system is much harder to break down than man-marking in a high press. This became evident in the sequence leading to the penalty goal. United suddenly switched to man-marking and forced the ball loss that preceded the penalty. United deservedly equalized.

After the 1-1, the game became more balanced. Brighton tried to break down the 5-4-1 mid-block, while United focused on their defensive game. When Manchester United switched to man-marking in the high press, Brighton continued to struggle and often lost possession. It is questionable why United didn’t press more boldly and high man-to-man during this phase to maintain better control of the game.

From Brighton’s perspective, a situational, more extreme overload at the moment of transition into high pressing—such as in the central space just behind the first pressing block—could have been a possible solution to challenge United’s man-marking, putting them in a dilemma between applying pressure and defending 1v1 on the wings.

In possession, Brighton’s players frequently adjusted their positioning with small movements, creating new passing lanes, changing passing angles, and occupying spaces that forced the opponent into pressing reactions. Below, I have outlined the main advantages of three of the most frequently used shapes by Brighton against United, as well as the necessary reactions from the opponent.

Another factor that makes Brighton’s vertical play difficult to defend is the continuous variety of space-creating or counter-movement runs into depth. These consistently create dilemmas and positional problems for the defenders. Below, I have graphically illustrated some selected runs used against United:

Despite Brighton’s possession game, Manchester United was able to prevent significant goal-scoring opportunities initially. From their 5-4-1 structure, the center-backs repeatedly defended aggressively, stepping out. Additionally, after bypassing the four-man midfield, it would drop back into position. This “recovery defense” made it difficult for Brighton to develop effective build-up play and exploit opened spaces. Furthermore, United’s players were well-prepared for potential through balls. In particular, the full-backs consistently intercepted balls played behind the defensive line.

Towards the end of the first half and into the second half, small (forced?) mistakes began to creep into United’s pressing. While the failure to step out with Ugarte in the man-marking high press in the 39th minute and the failure to step out with De Ligt in the space between the lines in the 38th minute went unpunished, the delayed step-out by Yoro led to Brighton’s deserved 1-2 at that point.

Especially in the second half, Brighton adapted to the man-marking high press by having center-backs step inside, breaking free from the cover shadow, when pressing the goalkeeper. This allowed them to find the open player in build-up, and Brighton lost possession less frequently.

Longer defensive phases in the mid-block for Manchester United followed. To break down this block, Brighton’s possession play became less positionally rigid. Much more frequently, certain zones were overloaded. In particular, the space between the lines and the half-spaces were repeatedly occupied by multiple players to create numerical superiority and apply pressure.

United, on the other hand, struggled to create any significant goal-scoring chances. The high press could have been more effective with a brief orientation from the player pressing the goalkeeper to position the inward-dropping center-back into a cover shadow. From the 5-4-1 mid-block, too few dangerous ball recoveries and transition situations were created.

Even from their own possession, Manchester United created too few goal-scoring opportunities. When Amorim’s team did get chances, it was typically through a ball played behind the wide players of the five-man backline. At the moment the press was triggered (when Brighton stepped out to the outer center-back), the forward half-space player dropped deep, and the winger made a run in behind. However, the lack of other ways to break the press led to too much predictability in United’s possession play.

As a result, the second half became more one-sided, with Brighton repeatedly pressing and trying to put United’s press under pressure. This ultimately succeeded, leading to a deserved 3-1 victory for Hürzeler’s team.

Amorim’s press, which was difficult to break down, was ultimately cracked by Hürzeler. It is questionable whether more frequent defensive pressing, alternating with situational man-marking high pressing, might have been a better approach against Brighton, in order to better tighten the space between the lines and the area behind the defense, making the game in depth more difficult. Despite a higher mid-block, Manchester United hardly created any dangerous transition situations. This is an area that needs improvement.

Hürzeler’s team, on the other hand, once again played highly attractive possession football. Frequent positional rotations, shifts in formations, overloads, and space-creating runs make Brighton’s possession game very enjoyable to watch. For the opponent, these constant shifts in zones over an extended period are incredibly difficult to defend. It is very likely that we will see more teams adopting similar principles in possession in the future.

Author: “MH” is a young analyst who regularly produces content for Spielverlagerung NextGen and TotalFootballAnalysis. On X, he can be found under Mh_sv5.
